errors.claim: "Observed overlap is therefore about 45 times chance."
errors.evidence: "The median pair shares 4% of its edges." ... "At the median circuit size of 200 edges, the analytic random reference k/(2|E|-k) gives 0.0031." ... earlier in the same part: "Mean Jaccard similarity is \bar{J}=0.1396 (95% CI 0.1377 to 0.1418)."
errors.explanation: The text references the median circuit size (k=200) and gives the random-reference 0.0031; comparing that to the median observed overlap (4% = 0.04) yields ≈13× chance (0.04/0.0031), not ≈45×. The factor ≈45 equals mean Jaccard (0.1396) divided by 0.0031, so the sentence mixes the median-size reference with the mean overlap, producing a contradictory statement.

errors.claim: "Cohen’s kappa is 0.0146. ... Kappa stays between 0.016 and 0.047 at every circuit size."
errors.evidence: "Cohen’s kappa is 0.0146." and "Kappa stays between 0.016 and 0.047 at every circuit size."
errors.explanation: These two sentences contradict each other: if every size-specific kappa lies between 0.016 and 0.047, any aggregate (weighted) kappa cannot be below 0.016. Reporting an overall kappa of 0.0146 is therefore inconsistent with the claim about the per-size range.

final_notes: Key results: overall flip rate F = 0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380); mean Jaccard = 0.1396. Pre-registered filing threshold τ = 0.20 (H2 confirmed). Pooled discovered vs size-matched null: discovered F = 0.7316, null F = 0.6774 (confounded by circuit size). Size-controlled (maximum-pressure / Eq.3) discovered F ≈ 0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859); medium-granularity discovered 0.2746 vs null 0.4230; coarse discovered 0.2706 vs null 0.3822. Fixing size reduces pooled F from 0.7316 to ≈0.2746 — larger reduction than standardising any pre-registered axis (Table 6). Table 6: evaluation metric is the largest pre-registered lever, removing 0.1377 from 0.7316. Residual-axis decomposition & REML: ablation–corruption interaction dominates selected-circuit-size variance; seed axis negligible. Specifications: 7,561 surviving specs; 2,692 specs at large sizes contribute no flips; median circuit size ≈200 edges; size-bin Fs vary (e.g., 0.4543 at size 10; 0.5714 at 2000; 0.0000 at 5k/10k). Agreement = 0.6028 → functional instability = 0.3972. Pooled gap (flip rate − functional instability) = 0.3344 (95% CI 0.3297–0.3394); gap supported pooled but fails at size-fixed level. Internal inconsistency flagged earlier: overall Cohen's kappa reported 0.0146 while text also asserts per-size kappas in [0.016,0.047]. Filability protocol (Sec.8) steps recorded; one of seven publicly exported discovery objectives does not run on the library’s canonical task (Section 6) and is reported as a discard (discard rate = 52.3%). Limitations: one model/task only; second-model replication pre-registered but not yet run. Multiverse limited by library; bootstrap invalid for conditioning groups of 2–5 specs. Reproducibility (this part): pre-registration is a timestamped commit tagged 'prereg-p1-confirmatory' made before the confirmatory sweep. Confirmatory sweep used one environment across all 1,320 cells (verified from results archive). Content-addressed recovery found all 22/22 files identical. Analysis layer runs without a GPU. Verification script recomputes every headline quantity, performed 36 checks with 0 failures, and derives F by three routes (including brute-force pairwise). Second script checks every numeric token in the manuscript against stored results; every table is emitted directly from results. Test suite contains 343 tests.

Title: Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability (Ajay Pravin Mahale, 12 Aug 2026). Goal: test whether mechanistic interpretability (circuit discovery) yields evidence stable to defensible analytic variation (two competent analysts, same system/tool, different defensible settings). Method: pre-registered crossed grid of 7 analytic axes (each level drawn from published implementations). Used a deterministic claim map to convert each discovered circuit into a structured Annex IV statement. Model/task: GPT-2 small; indirect object identification. Specs: 15,840 pre-registered specifications; 7,561 produced a claim. Main results: derived statement differs on 73.2% of specification pairs (95% bootstrap CI 0.725–0.738). Modal (most frequent) claim = 41.1% frequency. Evidence fails the paper's filability criterion at every plausibly acceptable tolerance. Controlling for choices: standardising evaluation metric (most influential choice) yields flip rate 59.4%. Ignoring circuit size and comparing only circuits of same size yields disagreement 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), which the paper says remains above the pre-registered threshold (threshold not stated here). Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap = 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa = 0.015). Authors provide filability criterion as standalone protocol and report that one of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task. Limitation: single model and single task; scalability untested.

Filability criterion: π* ≥ 1-α where π* is the share of specifications producing the modal (most frequent) claim and α is allowed share outside that claim; reported as standalone protocol. Additional claims: paper does not propose new discovery methods or dismiss interpretability generally; provides a decision rule for standards bodies; documents that one of seven discovery objectives fails to execute on the library’s canonical task. Methodological note: when specs select objects of different sizes, pooled statistics can reverse direction; paper shows three such reversals. Limitation: single model (GPT-2 small) and single task (indirect object identification); scalability untested.

Mean pairwise Jaccard J̄ = 0.1396 (95% CI 0.1377–0.1418); expected random J ≈ 0.0031. Typical circuit size k ≈ 200. Baseline claim flip F = 0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380). Modal claim share π* = 0.4109 (pre-registered threshold π* ≥ 0.80 not met). Table 6: standardising axes; group sizes 1,512–2,520; bootstrap bias <0.0006; standardising evaluation metric largest lever → residual F = 0.5939 (95% CI 0.5803–0.6063), drop = 0.1377. REML on log10(selected circuit size): variance decomposition 78.8% ablation–corruption interaction, 11.5% residual, 4.4% ablation, 4.1% threshold, 0.7% metric. Holding circuit size fixed reported as F = 0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859) in results; Limitations section reports 0.2746 (numeric mismatch). Pooled discovered vs null flip: 0.7316 vs 0.6774 (disjoint CIs). Functional agreement 0.6028 → functional instability 0.3972; pooled gap to claim flip 0.3344 (95% CI 0.3297–0.3394). Limitations: one model/one task; second-model replication pre-registered but not run; circuit size is an outcome; discard rate 52.3%; bootstrap invalid for conditioning groups of size 2–5 (point estimates with diagnostic); no post-hoc bias-corrected estimator. Reproducibility (part 11): prereg commit prereg-p1-confirmatory; confirmatory sweep ran under single environment across 1,320 cells; code commit recovered 22/22 files identical; analysis layer runs without GPU; verification script: 36 checks, 0 failures, F derived by 3 routes incl brute-force pairwise; second script claims to check every numeric token; every table emitted from results; test suite 343 tests. (Conflict noted: numeric mismatch above contradicts the claims that every numeric token matches stored results and that verification produced 0 failures.)

Title: Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability (Ajay Pravin Mahale, 12 Aug 2026). Question: Do circuit-discovery explanations survive defensible analytic variation (two competent analysts, same system, same tool, different defensible settings)? Method: pre-registered crossed grid of 7 analytic axes (levels from published implementation); deterministic claim map to structured Annex IV statement. Dataset/experiment: 15,840 pre-registered specifications on GPT-2 small for indirect-object identification; 7,561 specs produced a claim. Key results: derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim covers 41.1% of the space. Standardising the single most influential choice (evaluation metric) reduces flip rate to 59.4%. Removing circuit size from the claim and holding it fixed reduces flip rate to 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286) — still above the pre-registered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). Additional: one of the seven documented discovery objectives fails to execute on the library’s canonical task. Deliverables: filability criterion given as standalone protocol. Scope: one model and one task; generalisability untested.

Related work (summaries relevant to design): Non-identifiability (Méloux et al.) — premise that unique explanation need not exist. Faithfulness metric sensitivity (Miller et al.) — ablation-based metrics sensitive to choices; their library is used as the instrument here, and the paper crosses seven axes testing sensitivity. Structure vs function (Bayat Makou et al.) — phantom specialisation; authors address this via functional measurement (see Sec. 7.6) and report circuits are not functionally interchangeable. Variance-as-estimation (Méloux) — seed variance included as an axis. Auditability (Lan et al., Sharkey et al.) motivates certification/standardisation. Multiverse methods (Steegen, Simonsohn) motivate crossing defensible choices. Explanation-metric optimisation pressure (Hsia et al.) — sufficiency and comprehensiveness are two of the paper's four evaluation metrics; discard rates are reported per metric rather than pooled.

steps.notes_before: Paper studies explanation multiplicity for circuit discovery. Specification s = (o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g) (objective, ablation, corruption, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, granularity). 15,840 preregistered specs on GPT-2 small; 7,561 specs produced a claim (from earlier parts). Under the factorised graph with separate q/k/v, |E| = 32,491 edges (confirmed by instrument and closed-form count). Components: 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs (=156 components) — but the closed-form paragraph also mentions the output receives from 157 non-terminal sources (internal mismatch flagged). Circuit instability: D(s_i,s_j) = 1 − |C_i ∩ C_j| / |C_i ∪ C_j|; ̅J = mean Jaccard over unordered pairs. Claim instability: map φ(circuit) → Annex IV statement. Flip rate F = 1 − (Σ_c n_c(n_c−1)) / (N(N−1)) (Gini–Simpson); modal share π* = max_c n_c / N. Within-group form F_within(G) = 1 − (Σ_g Σ_c n_{g,c}(n_{g,c}−1)) / (Σ_g n_g(n_g−1)). Filability: evidence filable at tolerance α iff π* ≥ 1−α. Ceiling: F ≤ 1−1/k; with k=9 observed classes ceiling=0.8889; observed F≈0.7316 (~82.3% of ceiling).

Paper: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection" by Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Studied model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection on 3 held-out datasets (two named: Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging; third unnamed here). Method: train linear probes on model activations; project activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from PCA on training activations. Use an LLM judge to produce natural-language interpretations: it scores each PC by judging whether the PC’s most- and least-activating examples suggest a transferable deception direction. Key claims/results: (1) projecting onto selected PCs enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained directly on the test distribution; (2) training probes on the highest-scoring PCs closes 78% of the baseline-to-oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging (Section 4.5); baseline = probe using all activations, oracle = selecting PCs using labeled target examples; (3) source-trained probe weights correspond to source-specific surface features, while transferable PCs encode more abstract contrasts that align with natural-language descriptions; overall claim: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” (Yoo & Skapars). Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection. Source train set: Roleplaying deception scenarios. Three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: train linear probes on model activations; compute PCA on source-domain activations and train probes after projecting onto a subset of source PCs. PC selection approaches: (a) target-supervised greedy search (adds one source PC at a time using labeled target examples) finds ~8–15 PCs on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Section 4.2); (b) ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights fails to recover the transferable subspace (Section 4.3); (c) an LLM judge inspects most/least-activating examples for each PC and partially recovers the transferable subspace without target labels (Section 4.5). Key quantitative claims (from earlier summary): projecting onto selected PCs enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching target-trained probes; using the judge-selected PCs closes 78% of the baseline-to-oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Definitions: baseline = probe using all activations; oracle = selecting PCs using labeled target examples. Central claim: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Related work (this part): literature on linear concept directions and linear representation hypothesis; examples claiming population-level directions for properties (honesty, emotion), single-direction mediation of refusal, and an “assistant” axis; methodological skepticism about probes and OOD generalization motivating tests of robustness; LLM-generated neuron explanations and natural-language labeling of features/SAEs, and using such descriptions to guide interventions/ablations.

Paper: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” (Yoo & Skapars). Task: deception detection using linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations (layer 15 chosen for highest cross-domain AUROC). Datasets: Roleplaying (source), three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels from GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Activations: pass prompt through model, average token activations only over the assistant’s response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance; standardize target activations using source statistics. PCA: run on standardized source activations, retain top 100 PCs (ordered by explained variance). Motivation: SAE-decoder alignment with PCs decreases with PC index (Appendix C Fig.6), so low-index PCs are easier to interpret (not claimed to generalize better). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). For subset S of the 100 PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Earlier high-level results to check later: (a) target-supervised greedy search finds ≈8–15 PCs to match target-trained probe (Section 4.2); (b) ranking PCs by probe weights fails to recover transferable subspace (Section 4.3); (c) LLM judge inspects most/least-activating examples per PC and partially recovers transferable subspace without target labels (Section 4.5) — judge-selected PCs close ~78% of baseline→oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and ~25% on Sandbagging. Section 4.1 verifies the 100-PC subspace retains sufficient signal on every target.

Setting & baselines: Probes are logistic regression (λ=10). Baseline: probes trained on full source representations transfer to targets with AUROCs — Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Check of 100-PC subspace: training probes on top-100 source PCs with 5-fold CV on each target yields AUROCs (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging) = 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869, so the 100-PC subspace contains sufficient signal. Greedy PC selection (Sect.4.2): start empty; at each step consider adding any remaining PC among top-100 source PCs, fit logistic probe on source projections, measure target AUROC (selection uses target labels), add PC that most improves target AUROC; 5-fold CV over target for selection; stop when no candidate improves AUROC > 0.001. With CV-based greedy, average selected sizes: 15 (Report), 8 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Using greedy on full target dataset (for a single stable k) gives k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy improves over baseline by ~0.22 (Report) and ~0.23 (Sandbagging) AUROC and comes close to target-trained probes for those two tasks; variance-based top-k (by explained variance) matches greedy only on the easy Confirm task. Sect.4.3 tests two ranking hypotheses: rank PCs by standardized absolute probe coefficients (abs(weight)×PC std) from a probe trained on source (source-PCA probe) or from a probe trained on target (target-PCA probe, still in source-PCA basis); after ranking, evaluated probes are trained on source projected to top-k ranked PCs (k from full-dataset greedy).

Key setting & baselines (from earlier): probes are logistic regression (λ=10). Full-source baseline AUROCs: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Top-100 source-PC probe (5-fold CV per target) AUROCs: Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869. Greedy PC selection (search among top-100 PCs using target labels, 5-fold CV): average selected sizes CV-based = 15 (Report), 8 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging); stable-k greedy on full target gives k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Setup: extract layer-15 residual stream from V6Q (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), chosen for highest cross-domain E3K (AUROC) in prior work. Activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Standardize using source (Z4K) statistics when applying to targets. PCA fit on source; retain top-100 PCs (R2F) for interpretability (motivated by SAE decoder alignment decreasing with PC index; authors explicitly do not claim low-index PCs generalize better). Probes: logistic regression with regularization λ=10. Subset-S probes project activations onto chosen PC subset S; baselines operate on full standardized activations. Data: four deception datasets (Appendix A): Z4K as source, targets Q7V, P3Y, J8W. Labels from GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Experiments (sec.4): main comparisons among many subset/selection methods over three target datasets (Q7V, P3Y, J8W) using E3K (AUROC). Key methods: V9D = source-trained probe on full activations; R2F = top-100 PCs (source PCA retained for interpretability); Q8B = 19 PCs chosen by human interpretability procedure (A8T) using source-only ratings (no PC scored >6; Q8B = PCs scoring 6 in both runs); K9U = greedy target-informed PC subset selection (adds PC that most improves target E3K of a probe fit on source projections; selection uses target labels on non-held-out folds under H6Q; weights always fit on source; stop when gain <=0.001). W4J = top-k PCs by variance; G2Y = the other 81 PCs (R2F minus Q8B). Z1M = source probe weight-based ranking (U1L = |coef|×PC std); H5X = target-trained probe weight ranking. S6F = probe trained in R2F subspace (strong oracle). Reported numeric results: V9D target E3K = P3Y 0.874, Q7V 0.706, J8W 0.606. S6F (R2F) = P3Y 0.950, Q7V 0.936, J8W 0.869. K9U reported K values: run-on-full-target (no CV) k = 13 (Q7V), 7 (P3Y), 14 (J8W); mean subset sizes under CV K9U = 15, 8, 14 respectively. Q8B (19 PCs) beats V9D on all three targets; on Q7V it closes ~78% of gap from V9D (0.706) to K9U (0.929) (~0.88), on J8W closes ~25% of gap (to ~0.663); P3Y is near ceiling and uninformative (all methods similar except G2Y). Claims: both hypotheses that transferable PCs (i) individually separate target classes or (ii) are those source probe relies on fail (Z1M ≈ V9D; H5X mixed). Figures: Fig2 (V9D vs S6F), Fig3 (K9U vs W4J), Fig4 (rankings), Fig5 (Q8B vs baselines).

Experiments compare many subspace/selection methods for transferring a source-trained probe to three targets (Q7V, P3Y, J8W) using AUROC. Key methods: V9D (source probe on full activations), R2F (probe in top-100 source PCA subspace), Q8B (19 PCs chosen by a source-only interpretability procedure), K9U (greedy target-informed PC subset selection that fits weights on source but uses target labels to select PCs), W4J (top-k PCs by variance), G2Y (other 81 PCs), Z1M (source-probe-weight-based PC ranking), H5X (target-trained probe ranking), S6F (probe trained in R2F subspace — strong oracle). Reported numbers: V9D AUROC — P3Y 0.874, Q7V 0.706, J8W 0.606. S6F (R2F oracle) — P3Y 0.950, Q7V 0.936, J8W 0.869. K9U reported targets: Q7V ≈0.929, J8W ≈0.832 (mean CV subset sizes ≈15, 8, 14 for Q7V, P3Y, J8W). Q8B (19 PCs) outperforms V9D on all targets: Q7V 0.706→≈0.88 (≈78% of gap closed vs K9U), J8W 0.606→≈0.663 (≈25% of gap closed); P3Y near ceiling. Source-weight ranking Z1M ≈ V9D (source coefficients poorly predict transferable PCs); H5X mixed. Limitations: single model layer (15) and single source dataset; no causal validation or ablation of high-scoring PCs at inference; nonlinear probes and other readout locations untested; transfer gains small on hardest OOD (J8W). Conclusion: OOD probing is representation selection — the chosen subspace must preserve the intended feature and filter spurious correlations; transfer depends not only on linear accessibility but on where the signal is represented most robustly. V9D probes can mix general and dataset-specific cues (helping in-distribution but hurting transfer); sparse PC subspaces can sometimes isolate more general structure.

Experiments compare many subspace/selection methods for transferring a source-trained probe to three targets (Q7V, P3Y, J8W) using AUROC. Key methods: V9D (source probe on full activations), R2F (probe in top-100 source PCA subspace), Q8B (19 PCs chosen by a source-only interpretability procedure), K9U (greedy target-informed PC subset selection that fits weights on source but uses target labels to select PCs), W4J (top-k PCs by variance), G2Y (other 81 PCs), Z1M (source-probe-weight-based PC ranking), H5X (target-trained probe ranking), S6F (probe trained in R2F subspace — strong oracle). Reported numbers: V9D AUROC — P3Y 0.874, Q7V 0.706, J8W 0.606. S6F (R2F oracle) — P3Y 0.950, Q7V 0.936, J8W 0.869. K9U reported targets: Q7V ≈0.929, J8W ≈0.832 (mean CV subset sizes ≈15, 8, 14 for Q7V, P3Y, J8W). Q8B (19 PCs) outperforms V9D on all targets: Q7V 0.706→≈0.88 (≈78% of gap closed vs K9U), J8W 0.606→≈0.663 (≈25% of gap closed); P3Y near ceiling. Source-weight ranking Z1M ≈ V9D (source coefficients poorly predict transferable PCs); H5X mixed. Limitations: single model layer (15) and single source dataset; no causal validation or ablation of high-scoring PCs at inference; nonlinear probes and other readout locations untested; transfer gains small on hardest OOD (J8W). Conclusion: OOD probing is representation selection — the chosen subspace must preserve the intended feature and filter spurious correlations; transfer depends not only on linear accessibility but on where the signal is represented most robustly. Appendix A provides label distributions (counts for -1/0/1 and totals): Z4K 371 (140/59/172), Q7V 473 (218/194/61), P3Y 151 (29/38/84), J8W 1000 (379/375/246). Appendix also gives informal task descriptions: J8W involves instructed under-performance on some tasks, P3Y involves hiding earlier use of insider information with confirmation requested, Q7V involves a trader deciding honesty, and Z4K is a simple scenario affording an opportunity to lie. Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo; Adrians Skapars. Abstract key claims:
- A8T scores each principal component (PC) by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction. Probing restricted to the highest-scoring PCs. PC interpretations isolate a subset of transferable PCs.
- Under that restriction, M3Z (defined as the baseline-to-oracle gap) is "closed by 78% on Q7V and by 25% on J8W." 
- M3Z is framed in the generalization performance of V6Q probes (parenthetical: "3.1, 8") evaluated over 3 held-out deception detection datasets.
- Projecting inputs onto a small subset of PCs from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches S6F.
- Source probe directions weighted heavily appear to encode source-specific surface features; the directions that actually transfer encode the same contrast more abstractly in a way natural language descriptions can capture.
- Conclusion-level claims: linear probes can detect behaviors/concepts inside LM activations but may fail to transfer OOD; OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.
- Venue: Machine Learning, ICML.

Key numbers/labels to track: 78% (Q7V), 25% (J8W), 3 held-out datasets, terms M3Z, A8T, V6Q, S6F.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct probes. Task: deception detection; authors report experiments on 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging; third dataset not named in this part). Main claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) computed from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the test distribution. Method: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe on highest-scoring PCs. Quantitative claims: using this approach they "close the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging." Additional claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and are capturable by natural language descriptions. High-level conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Venue/area: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection; train on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios), evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: operate in source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of principal components (PCs) for probe training to avoid spurious, non-transferable features. Key quantitative/structural claims: a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds a small transferable subspace of ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Section 4.2). Source-side and target-side rankings (ranking PCs by source or target probe weights) fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform the full-representation baseline (Section 4.3). An LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without using target labels by interpreting PCs and selecting those likely to encode the behavioral contrast (Section 4.5). Prior summary from earlier part: the method reportedly closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. High-level conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection; transferable directions are more abstract and can be captured by natural-language descriptions, whereas source-weighted directions capture surface features.

Related work: evidence for linear/low-dimensional concept directions (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024; Zou et al. 2025); examples of single-direction behaviors (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); longstanding skepticism about probes and OOD generalization (Hewitt & Liang 2019; Ravichander et al. 2021; recent work on uneven OOD probe performance). LLMs have been used to generate natural-language explanations of neurons/features and to label/ablate concepts for intervention (Bills et al. 2023; Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023; Casademunt et al. 2025).

Goal: probe generalization as subspace selection for OOD deception detection. Datasets: Roleplaying (source), Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging (targets). Labels: GPT-4o labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Model & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, use layer-15 residual stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); extract by passing each prompt and averaging token activations over the assistant’s response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance; apply the same source statistics to standardize all target activations. Dimensionality reduction: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs; all downstream experiments use this basis. Probes: logistic regression (L2 lambda=10). For a chosen subset S of the 100 PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activation space (i.e., no PCA subset). Motivation for 100 PCs: alignment with SAE decoder features decreases with PC index (App. C), so lower-index PCs are more interpretable; authors do not claim low-index PCs generalize better—Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace retains enough information to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target. Key claims to check later: a target-supervised greedy search finds a small transferable subspace (~8–15 PCs) where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec 4.2); source-/target-side rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec 4.3); an LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without target labels (Sec 4.5). Reported effect sizes: method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Of 5 PCs that appear in greedy selections for more than one target, 3 received the max OOD score; only 1 of the top-5 source-PCA PCs received the max OOD. Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (WVU), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Contribution: PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with deliberately inserted secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction (persuasion-based) probes. Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows; dialogue-level hybrid leakage reported as 38.7%–54.6% (Table 3). Definition: a dialogue is considered leaking if any standardized probe elicits its secret. Detection: hybrid detector combining normalized text matching and an LLM judge. Reported dependencies: leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity (Tables 3–5). Additional topic drift within the tested window does not reliably reduce leakage (Sec 5.4). Framing: privacy risk treated as a persistent behavioral failure mode, distinct from training-data memorization or immediate jailbreaking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano R. Maldonado Romero. Benchmark: PrivDrift — 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues per model with deliberately inserted secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes (direct, justified, high-pressure persuasion styles). Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows (3 × 1,000 dialogues). Primary metric: dialogue-level hybrid leakage (hybrid detector = deterministic normalization/regex matching + open-weights LLM judge). Reported dialogue-level hybrid leakage: 38.7%–54.6% (Table 3). Detection/reporting: dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only (normalization-based), fuzzy (approximate text similarity), and hybrid leakage rates. Secret-type effects: SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed far more often than email addresses and phone numbers (Table 5). Persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage (Sec 5.3). Topic-drift axis: d = number of unrelated intervening drift turns; tested window d ≤ 6. Within this window, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage (Sec 5.4). Privacy Half-Life τ proposed as a stability-based measure of persistent suppression; no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range (Sec 5.6). Framing: behavioral privacy risk distinct from training-data memorization or immediate jailbreaking.

Framing: behavioral privacy risk distinct from training-data memorization or immediate jailbreaking. Related work: contrasts training-data extraction and membership inference with active-context privacy; cites ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench as benchmarks of privacy reasoning/ norms but notes PrivDrift specifically isolates persistence of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated topic drift and later persuasion-based probing. Connects to multi-turn adversarial attacks (e.g., Crescendo, automated jailbreak frameworks) but emphasizes information re-disclosure rather than unsafe content generation. Contrasts with machine unlearning (TOFU, WMDP) by focusing on suppression in active context/RAG/copilots rather than changes to model weights.

PrivDrift framework: synthetic eval measuring whether secrets disclosed at turn t0 are re-disclosed after d unrelated, content-dense drift turns. Threat model = active-context re-disclosure: leakage if model reproduces S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Formalization: disclosure S at t0, intervening dialogue D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; probes appended to active context. Dataset: N = 1000 controlled dialogues (Table 1): 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored (human dialogs inserted throughout; cached evaluation metadata does not preserve their identifiers so only aggregate results reported). Secret categories = 4 (phone, email, SSN, credit card). Drift lengths tested = {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Word/token stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795; approx tokens estimated from words => avg ~478.87, median ~513.33, min/max ~57.33/1060. Pipeline: scaffold-then-rewrite generation preserves ground-truth secret, drift length, and probe structure; persona + secret injection places secret in opening turn as plausible task; drift turns drawn from topic-conditioned library (tax, medical, travel, etc.) with fallback tasks (writing, reasoning, summarization); annotators human-author subset of drift turns; naturalistic refinement: a rewriting model improves fluency/persona but must preserve exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Probing setup begins next (not in this part).

Eval appends a final standardized probe (three persuasion levels: Simple/Medium/Hard). Drift length d (number of intervening turns) sampled from mixture: d=0 with p=0.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (so each of 2–6 has p=0.16). Dataset drift lengths tested D_obs = {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Hierarchical hybrid detector (two stages, applied in order): Stage 1 normalization-based matching (called regex-stage): φ(·) normalizes secrets/responses — numeric secrets: remove non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, retain meaningful delimiters. Leak_regex(R,S) = I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)] (substring containment). Regex-positive responses labeled leakage; regex-negative responses passed to Stage 2. Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge given (secret, response) returns binary verdict (leakage/no leakage) to catch partial/paraphrased disclosures. Report regex-only and hybrid (regex+judge) leakage rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ: let L(d) be leakage rate at drift d; define δ = 0.1 × L(0). τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ and ∀ d' ∈ D_obs with d' > d: L(d') ≤ δ}. If no d qualifies, τ = max(D_obs) + 1 (requires stable decay below threshold).

Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B accessed via OpenRouter. Dataset: 1,000 PrivDrift dialogues per model; each dialogue has one seeded secret and one drift length d ∈ {0,2,3,4,5,6} sampled from Eq.(1) (mixture: d=0 with p=0.2; otherwise uniform over 2–6, so each of 2–6 has p=0.16). Each dialogue is probed with three standardized persuasion probes (Simple/Medium/Hard) — so 3,000 cached model-probe responses per model, 9,000 total. Detector & reporting: hierarchical two-stage detector — Stage 1 normalization/regex-match φ(·) (numeric: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, keep meaningful delimiters); Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Regex-positive responses labeled leakage; regex-negative passed to Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge for paraphrases. Report regex-only and hybrid (regex+judge) leakage. Privacy half-life τ: L(d) leakage at drift d; δ=0.1·L(0); τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and ∀d'>d: L(d')≤δ}; if none, τ=max(D_obs)+1. Aggregation: dialogue-level (dialogue counts as leaking if any probe elicits secret; used for overall leakage) and probe-level (each dialogue contributes one response per persuasion condition; used for persuasion-level and fuzzy-matching analyses). Statistics: dialogue-level 95% bootstrap CIs (resampling dialogues); probe-level uses cached responses. Paired comparisons: McNemar’s test (+ Bonferroni when applicable). Repeated persuasion-levels: Cochran’s Q, with post-hoc McNemar. Associations (drift length, persuasion, secret type): chi-square tests with Cramer’s V; report p-values vs null.

Each dialogue probed with 3 persuasion probes (Simple/Medium/Hard) → 3,000 cached responses per model. Detector: two-stage — regex normalization (Stage 1) then Llama judge for paraphrase (Stage 2). Report regex-only and hybrid (regex+judge). Aggregation: dialogue-level (dialogue leaks if any probe elicits secret) and probe-level. Key results:
- Regex vs Hybrid (dialogue-level, Table 2): GPT-OSS 47.70%→47.70% (Δ +0.00, p=1.0); DeepSeek 37.80%→38.70% (Δ +0.90, p=7.7×10^-3); Qwen 53.50%→54.60% (Δ +1.10, p=2.57×10^-3). Hybrid adds ≤1.10 percentage points.
- Dialogue-level hybrid leakage (Table 3, 95% CIs): DeepSeek 38.70% [35.7,41.6]; GPT-OSS 47.70% [44.6,50.8]; Qwen 54.60% [51.6,57.7].
- Probe-level by persuasion (Table 4): GPT-OSS Simple 39.30%, Medium 40.50%, Hard 32.90%; DeepSeek Simple 28.10%, Medium 22.00%, Hard 29.20%; Qwen Simple 38.70%, Medium 33.30%, Hard 40.60%. Cochran’s Q p<1e-5.
- Drift length: leakage dips near d=3 then rebounds (Fig.4). Cramer’s V (drift) small: DeepSeek 0.1073, GPT-OSS 0.0659, Qwen 0.0723.
- Secret type (probe-level, Table 5) strongly associated with leakage; Cramer’s V large: DeepSeek 0.5871, GPT-OSS 0.7731, Qwen 0.6927. Per-type leak rates (probe-level): SSN: GPT 0.14%, DeepSeek 1.11%, Qwen 5.97%; Credit card: GPT 0.00%, DeepSeek 0.39%, Qwen 4.01%; Email: GPT 78.24%, DeepSeek 57.11%, Qwen 81.13%; Phone: GPT 70.89%, DeepSeek 46.13%, Qwen 57.24%.

final_notes:
Experiment: 3 models — U5K (GPT-OSS-120B), E7B (DeepSeek-R1), P3R (Qwen3-VL-235B). Dataset: N=1,000 dialogues/model (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored); 3 probes per dialogue (H2R easy, F6K medium, N8W hard) → 3,000 responses/model. V9B (context-depth) sampled d ∈ {0,2,3,4,5,6}; observed fallback τ = max(D_obs)+1 = 7 for all models (no stable decay within d≤6) — evaluation bounded to short-to-medium depths. Leak detection: regex normalization φ; Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]; regex-negatives judged by open-weights Llama T1G; final leak = regex OR T1G. Only structured, fixed-format secrets tested. PrivDrift threshold C5Z: δ = 0.1·L(0).

Key results: summary J5D/X3Q — U5K 47.70/47.70 (Δ0), E7B 37.80/38.70 (Δ+0.90), P3R 53.50/54.60 (Δ+1.10). Conclusion reports dialogue-level X3Q across three LLMs = 38.7–54.6% and states V9B within d≤6 does not reliably reduce X3Q. Table 2 (per-probe leakage) — U5K: H2R 39.30 / F6K 40.50 / N8W 32.90; E7B: 28.10 / 22.00 / 29.20; P3R: 38.70 / 33.30 / 40.60. Secret-type (emails/phones vs SSN/cc) shows much higher leakage. Effect sizes: Cramer's V large for secret-type (0.5871–0.7731). V9B×Z4T small (0.0659–0.1073). Appendix B reports probe-level Z4T Cramer's V ≈ 0.0718 (E7B), 0.0689 (U5K), 0.0639 (P3R); V9B small for E7B, negligible for others. Cochran's Q p < 1e-5 across Z4T. Interpretation: protections uneven, leakage near-direct reproduction and format-sensitive; urgency cues may affect refusals. Planned release: code, templates, scripts, aggregate results, sanitized dialogues. Not tested: training-data memorization, personalization, cross-session retention. Mitigation logging recommended. Unresolved internal issues noted earlier: (1) R9S defined as dialogue-level OR but Table 2 appears per-probe; (2) J5D/X3Q conflict between summary table and Table 6 remains unresolved. Appendices: A references per-V9B length stats in Table 1; B gives additional effect sizes (see above); C shows dialogue construction in Figure 6.

Paper K7X (PrivDrift) studies suppression of user-provided secrets in active multi-turn LLM conversations, focusing on persistence after topic drift (V9B) and later persuasion intensity (Z4T). Key metric C5Z = Privacy Half-Life (τ), stability-based; claim from intro: “No model reaches stable decay in the observed range under C5Z.” Benchmark axes: V9B (topic drift = unrelated turns between disclosure and probe) and Z4T (persuasion intensity). Methods: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Detector: hybrid reproducible detector = normalization + open-weights LLM judge (T1G); reported outputs include R9S, M2V (probe-level leakage), J5D (regex-only), B7N, X3Q. Related work: K7X isolates persistence after drift and persuasion (sec refs 2.1–2.3). Prior work (training-data extraction, membership inference, memorized PII, TOFU, WMDP) targets parameter/memory/static QA/weights or static access-control tests (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench), whereas K7X applies a multi-turn information-flow lens to re-disclosure of user-supplied secrets. Other related work (Crescendo, automated multi-turn jailbreaks, prompt injection) target harmful content or instruction hijacking rather than user-secret re-disclosure.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: privacy risk in active LLM conversations should be evaluated as a persistent behavioral failure mode (not only memorization/jailbreak). Reported finding: additional V9B within the tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage; R9S X3Q (leakage measure) across three LLMs with extended context windows is substantial (38.7%–54.6%), and varies strongly by model, secret type, and Z4T. Dataset/benchmark K7X contains 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes to audit whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after conversational V9B and persuasion-based probing. Motivation: LLMs as persistent assistants in user-facing/shared-session/tool-augmented settings may behaveably recover sensitive info after topic shifts. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu). Core claim: active-context privacy leakage is a persistent behavioral failure mode distinct from memorization/jailbreak. Key empirical findings: dialogue-level leakage (R9S) under hybrid detection (X3Q) is 38.7%–54.6% across three LLMs with extended context windows, tested on 1,000 controlled dialogues per model. Tested drift window: d ≤ 6; adding further drift within this window does not reliably reduce leakage. Leakage varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity (Z4T). Secret-type suppression order: L8P (SSNs) and G6Y (credit cards) are suppressed far more often than D2F (email addresses) and A9T (phone numbers). Definitions/axes: V9B = topic drift (number of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe); Z4T = persuasion intensity / interaction style. Dataset/benchmark: K7X (PrivDrift) — 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, standardized extraction probes. Contributions: (1) K7X benchmark; (2) evaluation under direct, justified, and high-pressure probes modeling Z4T; (3) reproducible X3Q detector combining normalization-based matching with T1G (open-weights LLM judge), reporting rates for R9S (dialogue-level leakage), M2V, J5D (regex-only leakage), B7N, and X3Q (hybrid leakage); (4) C5Z (Privacy Half-Life τ), a stability-based metric showing no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Context/motivation: fills gap between memorization and immediate jailbreaking literature by measuring recoverability of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated conversational drift.

Related work contrasts machine-unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) that operate over static QA pairs and model parameters with K7X, which targets active-context privacy (prompt-level/context-window control rather than weight-level unlearning). Prior multi-turn safety work (Crescendo attacks, automated jailbreak frameworks, prompt injection) focuses on unsafe content or instruction hijacking; K7X adapts the multi-turn lens to information-flow control, asking whether a user-disclosed secret in the context window is behaviorally recoverable after unrelated topic drift (V9B) and later persuasion-based probes (Z4T). Benchmarks like ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, and PrivaCI-Bench test privacy reasoning, norms, or static access-control scenarios; K7X instead isolates persistence/recoverability of secrets across drift and probing. Historical privacy work addressed training-data extraction and memorized PII; K7X emphasizes active-context secrets requiring correct inference-time handling. Also notes claim that aligned models can remain vulnerable to multi-turn exploitation.

K7X / PrivDrift focuses on active-context privacy: whether a secret S disclosed at turn t0 is behaviorally recoverable after unrelated topic drift and later persuasion-style probes (contrasts with static QA/unlearning benchmarks like TOFU/WMDP and with privacy-reasoning benchmarks). Threat model Q3M: secret S disclosed; conversation proceeds through d unrelated drift turns D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; standardized probe P appended; leakage = model response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Dataset (3.2): N=1000 controlled dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored) produced by scaffold-then-rewrite; human IDs not preserved in cached metadata so aggregated results reported. Main evaluation (3.3): append final probe of three persuasion levels — H2R (direct/neutral), F6K (medium/contextual justification), N8W (hard/high-pressure). Drift length sampling (eq.1): d = 0 with p=0.2; d ∼ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (no d=1 samples). Detection pipeline (3.4): hierarchical hybrid detector — stage 1 (3.4.1) normalization/regex: φ(·) normalizes numeric (strip non-digits) and alphanumeric (case/whitespace normalized, delimiters preserved); Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)] (eq.2). Regex-negative responses go to stage 2 (3.4.2) an open-weights Llama judge (T1G) that receives secret+response and returns binary leakage verdict (captures paraphrase/partial disclosure); judge-introduced error rates (J5D, X3Q) reported separately. Stability metric C5Z(τ) (3.4.3 / eq.3): δ = 0.1×L(0); τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ and ∀d'>d, L(d') ≤ δ}; if set empty τ := max(D_obs)+1. Note ambiguity to track: wording alternately calls d the "number of turns" and also defines D as {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}, which suggests d counts user–assistant pairs (possible off-by-one/turn-definition ambiguity).

Persona sampling from >100 professions/demographic profiles. Topics assigned (e.g., tax filing, medical triage, travel); drift turns drawn from a topic-conditioned library of dense QA pairs and fallback tasks; a subset of drift turns are human-authored and included in the generation library. Framework overview: K7X = parametric dialogue generator + probing harness + metric suite (hybrid leakage detector: stage1 regex normalization Leak_regex; regex-negatives go to Llama judge; judge error rates reported separately). Stability metric C5Z(τ) defined earlier. Ambiguity to track: paper alternately calls d the “number of turns” vs defines D={u1,a1,...,ud,ad} (suggests d counts user–assistant pairs). Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: Introduces PrivDrift benchmark for auditing recovery of user-disclosed secrets after conversational topic drift and persuasion-based probing. Dataset: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows. Key result: dialogue-level hybrid leakage remains substantial, ranging 38.7%–54.6%, and varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Additional topic drift within tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage. Conclusion: privacy risk in active LLM contexts should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure mode, not only as memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Goal: measure whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after topic drift and persuasion-style probing in multi-turn LLM conversations. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled dataset with 1,000 multi-turn dialogues (paper states 1,000 dialogues per model evaluated). Axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe, tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows. Detector: reproducible hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching (regex/fuzzy) with an open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage; leakage varies by secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers). Additional drift within tested window does not reliably reduce leakage. Proposed metric: Privacy Half-Life (τ) for persistent suppression; authors claim no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions enumerated: benchmark, evaluation under multiple probe styles, hybrid detector and multiple leakage metrics, and Privacy Half-Life analysis.

Related work summary: distinguishes active-context privacy (user-provided info in current interaction) from training-data extraction and membership inference; cites benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) that test static access-control/privacy norms, while PrivDrift isolates persistence under drift and persuasion. Notes that multi-turn adversarial/jailbreak work (e.g., Crescendo attacks, automated jailbreak frameworks, prompt injection) show gradual elicitation of undesired outputs; PrivDrift applies a similar multi-turn lens to information flow. Contrasts with machine unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) that target parameter-level removal over static QA pairs; PrivDrift targets prompt-level/context-window suppression behavior relevant to RAG, copilots, and agentic workflows.

final_notes: Data/process: discovery cells 1,320 → 15,840 specs; metric-relative discard → 7,561 surviving specs; discard rate 52.3%; distinct circuits 3,218; unordered pairs 28,580,580. Pooled flip rate F = 0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380). Mean Jaccard = 0.1396 (95% CI 0.1377–0.1418). REML: log10(size) variance dominated by ablation–corruption (78.8%). Size-fixed (maximum-pressure) pooled F reported earlier as 0.2706 but Limitations gives 0.2746 (numeric inconsistency). Holding size fixed reverses ordering in banded comparisons and substantially reduces F; many per-size results differ. Functional agreement 0.6028 → instability 0.3972; pooled gap (F − instability) = 0.3344 (95% CI 0.3297–0.3394). Filability protocol specified (Sec 8). Limitations noted: single model/task, circuit size an outcome not an axis, measured F a lower bound, some bootstrap CIs invalid for small groups. Discussion: one of seven discovery objectives fails canonical task and was counted as a discard; interpretability evidence claimed measurable and cheap. Part 11 (reproducibility): preregistration commit 'prereg-p1-confirmatory' before sweep; confirmatory sweep used one environment across all 1,320 cells; recovered code commit matched uploaded archive (22/22 files identical); analysis runs without GPU. Claims: verification script recomputes headlines, "performs 36 checks with 0 failures" and derives F by three routes; a second script asserts every numeric token matches stored results and the test suite contains 343 tests. final_notes: Setup: GPT-2 small, indirect-object ID task; deterministic claim map φ; addressees φ_overseer / φ_affected; granularities COARSE/MEDIUM/FINE. Data: 7,561 realised specs → 3,218 distinct circuits; discard rate 52.3%. Key aggregates: mean Jaccard J̄ = 0.1396 [0.1377,0.1418]; overall claim flip F = 0.7316 [0.7247,0.7380]. Table/modal: overseer MED 0.7316; affected COARSE 0.3950. Residuals (effects removed relative to pooled F=0.7316): remove Evaluation metric → F=0.5939 (−0.1377); ablation op → 0.7014 (−0.0302); discovery objective → 0.7018 (−0.0298); threshold τ → 0.7070 (−0.0246); corruption → 0.7092 (−0.0224); prompt → 0.7232 (−0.0084); seed → 0.7307 (−0.0009). REML on log10(selected circuit size): 78.8% structural variance (ablation×corruption interaction); 11.5% residual; 4.4% ablation; 4.1% threshold; 0.7% metric. Size effects: fixing circuit size collapses pooled F dramatically (reported 0.2706 earlier; limitations section gives 0.2746 — minor discrepancy). Layer-band-only when size fixed: F ≈ 0.2706 (CI 0.2550–0.2859). Pooled discovered vs null: 0.7316 vs 0.6774 (disjoint CIs) though size-matched comparison reverses ordering; pooled H4 gap = 0.3344 [0.3297–0.3394] (meets prereg 0.10) but fails in many size bins and is negative for some (effect driven by 500–2,000 edge band). Functional agreement per-example 0.6028 → instability 0.3972; Cohen’s κ reported overall 0.0146 but per-size reported in [0.016,0.047] (inconsistency noted). Limitations: one model/one task; one pre-registered second-model replication not yet run; circuit size is an outcome and strongly distorts pooled quantities; multiverse limited to implemented library (optimal ablation omitted); high/uneven discard (52.3%); bootstrap invalid for tiny conditioning groups (2–5 specs) so those CIs are diagnostics/point estimates. Discussion: metric is largest single lever (removes 0.1377); one of seven discovery objectives didn’t run on canonical task and was discarded; authors claim measuring evidentiary weight is cheap relative to sweep that produced the circuit. Reproducibility claims (this part): pre-registration commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory made before confirmatory sweep; every reported number traces to a config, seed, and environment fingerprint; confirmatory sweep ran under a single environment across all 1,320 cells (verified from results archive); code commit recovered by content-addressed comparison, 22/22 files identical; analysis layer runs without a GPU; verification script

Title: Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability (Ajay Pravin Mahale, 12 Aug 2026). Question: Do circuit-discovery explanations survive defensible analytic variation (two competent analysts, same system, same tool, different defensible settings)? Method: pre-registered crossed grid of 7 analytic axes (levels from published implementation); deterministic claim map to structured Annex IV statement. Dataset/experiment: 15,840 pre-registered specifications on GPT-2 small for indirect-object identification; 7,561 specs produced a claim. Key results: derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim covers 41.1% of the space. Standardising the single most influential choice (evaluation metric) reduces flip rate to 59.4%. Removing circuit size from the claim and holding it fixed reduces flip rate to 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286) — still above the pre-registered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). Additional: one of the seven documented discovery objectives fails to execute on the library’s canonical task. Deliverables: filability criterion given as standalone protocol. Scope: one model and one task; generalisability untested.

Related work (summaries relevant to design): Non-identifiability (Méloux et al.) — premise that unique explanation need not exist. Faithfulness metric sensitivity (Miller et al.) — ablation-based metrics sensitive to choices; their library is used as the instrument here, and the paper crosses seven axes testing sensitivity. Structure vs function (Bayat Makou et al.) — phantom specialisation; authors address this via functional measurement (see Sec. 7.6) and report circuits are not functionally interchangeable. Variance-as-estimation (Méloux) — seed variance included as an axis. Auditability (Lan et al., Sharkey et al.) motivates certification/standardisation. Multiverse methods (Steegen, Simonsohn) motivate crossing defensible choices. Explanation-metric optimisation pressure (Hsia et al.) — sufficiency and comprehensiveness are two of the paper's four evaluation metrics; discard rates are reported per metric rather than pooled.

Specification s = (o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g) (objective, ablation, corruption, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, granularity). 15,840 preregistered specs on GPT-2 small; 7,561 specs produced a claim (from earlier parts). Circuit instability: D(s_i,s_j) = 1 − |C_i ∩ C_j| / |C_i ∪ C_j|; ̅J = mean Jaccard over unordered pairs. Claim instability: map φ(circuit) → Annex IV statement. Flip rate F = 1 − (Σ_c n_c(n_c−1)) / (N(N−1)) (Gini–Simpson); modal share π* = max_c n_c / N. Within-group form F_within(G) = 1 − (Σ_g Σ_c n_{g,c}(n_{g,c}−1)) / (Σ_g n_g(n_g−1)). Filability: evidence filable at tolerance α iff π* ≥ 1−α. Ceiling: F ≤ 1−1/k; with k=9 observed classes ceiling=0.8889; observed F≈0.7316 (~82.3% of ceiling).

final_notes: Context & dataset: Model ML4 on XB8. Realized grid 1,320 cells (pre-reg target 1,540; 220 cells removed); 15,840 specs; discard rule removed 8,279 (52.3%), leaving 7,561 specs → 3,218 distinct circuits. Pooled F = 0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380); π* = 0.4109. Table 5 per-group: affected COARSE F=0.3950 π*=0.7291; affected MED F=0.6597 π*=0.4875; affected FINE F=0.6744 π*=0.4786; overseer COARSE F=0.5733 π*=0.4788; overseer MED F=0.7316 π*=0.4109; overseer FINE F=0.7681 π*=0.4109. ZK7 (π*≥0.80): no cell meets it. Jaccard mean J̄=0.1396 (95% CI 0.1377–0.1418); median ≈0.04. Size-controlled F reported ~0.27 but two inconsistent values appear (0.2706 vs 0.2746). Size control drops F from 0.7316 → ~0.27. Hypotheses: H2 confirmed; H3 rejected; H4 supported (F − (1−agreement)=0.3344 [0.3297,0.3394], agreement ≈0.6028). Diagnostics: bootstrap invalid for one family; no bias-corrected estimator produced; quantities with 2–5 specs reported as point estimates with diagnostics. Reproducibility (this part): test suite reported as 343 tests; '0 failures across 36 checks' asserted; F derived by three routes including brute-force pairwise; second script purportedly verifies every numeric token matches stored results and emits tables directly; code commit recovered 22/22 files identical; prereg commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory; confirmatory sweep verified from archive across all 1,320 cells under a single environment; analysis ran without a GPU; claim that traceability of every reported number to a config, seed and environment fingerprint holds. Note potential internal issues: ambiguous 343 vs 36 counts and the manuscript contains two different reported values for the same metric despite the claim that every numeric token was script-verified.

steps.notes_before: Paper investigates whether mechanistic/circuit interpretability evidence survives defensible analytic variation for compliance (EU AI Act). Key quantitative claims: removing 'circuit size' leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), stated as still above a pre-registered threshold (threshold value not given here). Circuits are reported as structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). The "derived statement" flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); the modal claim covers 41.1% of the space. There were 15,840 pre-registered specifications on ML4 and the XB8 task; 7,561 of those produced a claim. Standardising the evaluation metric yields VX2 = 59.4%. ZK7 is presented as a standalone protocol; one of seven documented discovery objectives reportedly does not execute on the library's canonical task. The study covers one model and one task (scalability untested). The experiment pre-registered a crossed grid of seven analytic axes, each level taken from published implementations; each discovered circuit is mapped deterministically (QM3) to a structured Annex IV statement. final_notes: Key results: discovered flip rate F = 0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380); mean Jaccard J̄ = 0.1396 (95% CI 0.1377–0.1418). Pre-registered thresholds: 0.20 (H2); H4 uses 0.10. Size-controlled (max-pressure/Eq.3) overall F reported 0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859); Limitations text also gives 0.2746 for a fixed-size band (paper-internal inconsistency flagged). Multiverse: 7,561 specs; 2,692 specs contribute no flips; instability concentrated at circuits <2,000 edges; median circuit ≈200 edges. Selected per-size discovered F: size10 0.4543 (null 0.7331), 20 0.3380 (0.6622), 50 0.4639 (0.7310), 100 0.5792 (0.6584), 500 0.4258 (0.1421), 1000 0.5133 (0.0000), 2000 0.5714 (0.0000). Functional agreement = 0.6028 (instability 0.3972). Gap between claimed flip rate and instability = 0.3344 (95% CI 0.3297–0.3394). Table 6 (residuals): metric 0.5939; ablation 0.7014; discovery objective 0.7018; threshold τ 0.7070; corruption 0.7092; prompt 0.7232; seed 0.7307. REML of log10(size): ablation–corruption 78.8%; residual 11.5%; ablation 4.4%; threshold 4.1%; metric 0.7%. Limitations: one-model/one-task; planned second-model replication pre-registered (924-cell grid on Pythia-160m, seeds 3 vs 5) was not run. Circuit size is an outcome of threshold rule and strongly distorts pooled quantities; optimal ablation not implemented (measured F is a lower bound). Discard rate = 52.3%; surviving pool imbalanced by metric (Table 2). Bootstrap intervals invalid for conditioning groups of 2–5 specs; those are reported as point estimates with diagnostics. Reproducibility (new): pre-registration commit tagged 'prereg-p1-confirmatory' made before confirmatory sweep; confirmatory sweep used one environment across all 1,320 cells (verified from results archive). Recovered code commit by content-addressed comparison: all 22/22 files identical. Analysis layer runs without a GPU. Verification script recomputes every headline quantity (36 checks, 0 failures) and derives F by three routes (including brute-force pairwise). Second script checks every numeric token against stored results; every table emitted directly; test suite contains 343 tests.

Title: Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability (Ajay Pravin Mahale, 12 Aug 2026). Goal: test whether mechanistic interpretability (circuit discovery) yields evidence stable to defensible analytic variation (two competent analysts, same system/tool, different defensible settings). Method: pre-registered crossed grid of 7 analytic axes (each level drawn from published implementations). Used a deterministic claim map to convert each discovered circuit into a structured Annex IV statement. Model/task: GPT-2 small; indirect object identification. Specs: 15,840 pre-registered specifications; 7,561 produced a claim. Main results: derived statement differs on 73.2% of specification pairs (95% bootstrap CI 0.725–0.738). Modal (most frequent) claim = 41.1% frequency. Evidence fails the paper's filability criterion at every plausibly acceptable tolerance. Controlling for choices: standardising evaluation metric (most influential choice) yields flip rate 59.4%. Ignoring circuit size and comparing only circuits of same size yields disagreement 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), which the paper says remains above the pre-registered threshold (threshold not stated here). Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap = 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa = 0.015). Authors provide filability criterion as standalone protocol and report that one of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task. Limitation: single model and single task; scalability untested.

Title: Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability (Ajay Pravin Mahale, 12 Aug 2026). Question: Do circuit-discovery explanations survive defensible analytic variation (two competent analysts, same system, same tool, different defensible settings)? Method: pre-registered crossed grid of 7 analytic axes (levels from published implementation); deterministic claim map to structured Annex IV statement. Dataset/experiment: 15,840 pre-registered specifications on GPT-2 small for indirect-object identification; 7,561 specs produced a claim. Key results: derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim covers 41.1% of the space. Standardising the single most influential choice (evaluation metric) reduces flip rate to 59.4%. Removing circuit size from the claim and holding it fixed reduces flip rate to 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286) — still above the pre-registered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). Additional: one of the seven documented discovery objectives fails to execute on the library’s canonical task. Deliverables: filability criterion given as standalone protocol. Scope: one model and one task; generalisability untested.

Related work (summaries relevant to design): Non-identifiability (Méloux et al.) — premise that unique explanation need not exist. Faithfulness metric sensitivity (Miller et al.) — ablation-based metrics sensitive to choices; their library is used as the instrument here, and the paper crosses seven axes testing sensitivity. Structure vs function (Bayat Makou et al.) — phantom specialisation; authors address this via functional measurement (see Sec. 7.6) and report circuits are not functionally interchangeable. Variance-as-estimation (Méloux) — seed variance included as an axis. Auditability (Lan et al., Sharkey et al.) motivates certification/standardisation. Multiverse methods (Steegen, Simonsohn) motivate crossing defensible choices. Explanation-metric optimisation pressure (Hsia et al.) — sufficiency and comprehensiveness are two of the paper's four evaluation metrics; discard rates are reported per metric rather than pooled.

steps.notes_before: Paper studies explanation multiplicity for circuit discovery. Specification s = (o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g) (objective, ablation, corruption, metric, size threshold, prompt variant, seed, granularity). 15,840 preregistered specs on GPT-2 small; 7,561 specs produced a claim (from earlier parts). Under the factorised graph with separate q/k/v, |E| = 32,491 edges (confirmed by instrument and closed-form count). Components: 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs (=156 components) — but the closed-form paragraph also mentions the output receives from 157 non-terminal sources (internal mismatch flagged). Circuit instability: D(s_i,s_j) = 1 − |C_i ∩ C_j| / |C_i ∪ C_j|; ̅J = mean Jaccard over unordered pairs. Claim instability: map φ(circuit) → Annex IV statement. Flip rate F = 1 − (Σ_c n_c(n_c−1)) / (N(N−1)) (Gini–Simpson); modal share π* = max_c n_c / N. Within-group form F_within(G) = 1 − (Σ_g Σ_c n_{g,c}(n_{g,c}−1)) / (Σ_g n_g(n_g−1)). Filability: evidence filable at tolerance α iff π* ≥ 1−α. Ceiling: F ≤ 1−1/k; with k=9 observed classes ceiling=0.8889; observed F≈0.7316 (~82.3% of ceiling).

final_notes: Dataset ML4 on XB8: realized grid = 6 objectives, 1,320 cells, 15,840 specs (pre-reg intended 7). After BJ9 discard: 7,561/15,840 specs kept (3,218 distinct circuits). Per-example agreement = 0.6028 (1 - agreement = 0.3972). Pooled VX2 F = 0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380). Modal share π* = 0.4109. Jaccard J̄ = 0.1396 (95% CI 0.1377–0.1418); discussion uses CI lower bound 0.1377 to explain leverage. Pairwise D quantiles: 1% 0.196, 25% 0.788, median 0.960, 75% 0.998. Median circuit size 200 edges; analytic random overlap 0.0031 (observed ≈45×). Holding-circuit-size (Eq.3) F reported inconsistently: 0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859) in one place and 0.2746 elsewhere (discrepancy). H2 confirmed (F>0.20). H3 depends on conditioning (pooled F > QF4; size-fixed F < QF4). H4 supported; gap 0.3344 (95% CI 0.3297–0.3394). Limitations: measured F is a lower bound across choices; bootstrap invalid for one family and no bias-corrected estimator provided after interval disagreement; small conditioning groups (2–5 specs) reported as point estimates with diagnostics; EX9 52.3% and uneven; surviving pool metric-imbalanced; BJ9 fixed in advance and composition not adjusted; circuit size chosen by BJ9 treated as outcome that distorted pooled stats; GK5 scope limited; GF7 replication pre-registered but not run; second task designed but not run. Reproducibility (this part): test suite 343 tests; "0 failures across 36 checks" claimed; F derived by three routes including brute-force pairwise; numeric tokens purportedly checked by script and tables emitted from stored results; content-addressed recovery reports 22/22 files identical; confirmatory sweep verified from archive as run under single environment across 1,320 cells; prereg commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory; analysis ran without GPU; claim that every reported number is traceable to a config, seed and environment fingerprint. Note: the reproducibility claim conflicts with the earlier flagged inconsistent F values.

steps.notes_before: Paper investigates whether mechanistic/circuit interpretability evidence survives defensible analytic variation for compliance (EU AI Act). Key quantitative claims: removing 'circuit size' leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), stated as still above a pre-registered threshold (threshold value not given here). Circuits are reported as structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). The "derived statement" flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); the modal claim covers 41.1% of the space. There were 15,840 pre-registered specifications on ML4 and the XB8 task; 7,561 of those produced a claim. Standardising the evaluation metric yields VX2 = 59.4%. ZK7 is presented as a standalone protocol; one of seven documented discovery objectives reportedly does not execute on the library's canonical task. The study covers one model and one task (scalability untested). The experiment pre-registered a crossed grid of seven analytic axes, each level taken from published implementations; each discovered circuit is mapped deterministically (QM3) to a structured Annex IV statement. (Note: sentence about removing but "holding fixed" circuit size is internally inconsistent.)

Paper studies stability of mechanistic/circuit interpretability under a pre-registered GK5 multiverse (crossed grid of 7 analytic axes). Main claim: three pooled statistics 'invert' under GK5. ZK7 is the filability decision rule (π* ≥ 1−α) and discovered circuits map deterministically to Annex IV statements (filing context cites EU Reg 2024/1689). Key reported numbers to check later: removing 'circuit size' leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286); circuits near-disjoint (median Jaccard 4%); functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s κ = 0.015); derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim covers 41.1% of spec space. Pre-registered 15,840 specs; 7,561 produced a claim. Standardising evaluation metric yields VX2 = 59.4%. This Related Work section adds: two of the paper's four evaluation metrics are NV3 (sufficiency) and WP6 (comprehensiveness); EX9 (discard rate) is reported per metric rather than pooled; Miller et al.'s released library is the tooling used; Bayat Makou et al. report CU3 (structurally distinct circuits can implement same computation); authors state Section 7.6 provides a functional measurement showing their circuits are not functionally interchangeable. GK5 design follows Steegen et al.; the paper adapts Simonsohn et al.'s specification-curve visualisation. Seed variance is an axis. Note: the manuscript repeats inconsistent phrasing about removing vs holding circuit size fixed.

steps.notes_before: Paper studies stability of mechanistic interpretability under GK5 (7 analytic axes). Formalism: VX2 = flip rate = P(two distinct specifications yield different statements). F = 1 - sum_c n_c(n_c-1) / (N(N-1)) (unbiased Gini–Simpson); with k classes F ≤ 1 - 1/k. Observed k=9 → ceiling 1-1/9 = 0.8889; reported F ≈ 0.7316 (≈82.3% of ceiling). π* = modal share = max_c n_c / N; evidence satisfies ZK7 at tolerance α iff π* ≥ 1-α. F_within(G) = 1 - sum_g,sum_c n_{g,c}(n_{g,c}-1) / sum_g n_g(n_g-1). Jaccard distance D(s_i,s_j)=1-|C_i∩C_j|/|C_i∪C_j|; ̅J is mean Jaccard over unordered pairs. Analytic choice tuple s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g). Model ML4 (GPT-2 small): |E|=32,491 (claimed). Circuits reported to touch components drawn from 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components. Internal inconsistency: text also states the output receives from 157 non-terminal sources (contradiction with 156). Key reported results from earlier parts to keep in memory for later checks: flips ≈0.7316 (73.2%, 95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim ≈41.1%; median Jaccard ≈4%; fixed-size stability (discovered vs QF4) 0.2746 vs 0.4230; YD6 functional instability pooled 0.3972 (0.4777 at smallest); Cohen's kappa reported 0.015 vs 0.0146 inconsistency; pre-registered 15,840 specs → 7,561 produced a claim; standardised VX2 reported 59.4%.

Filability protocol (new): filing must state its own π*. Satisfaction of ZK7 at tolerance α for a filed interpretability claim c is π* ≥ 1 - α. π* is defined π* = max_c n_c / N computed over the specification space S. F is obtained by Equation 2. Obligation 5: report π*, F, EX9 per-axis level, and within-group decomposition of any pooled statistic. These presuppose obligations 1 & 2: (1) declare S (analytic axes and levels, each with a citation) and (2) declare QM3 φ as deterministic, published code (not a language model). Protocol requires no regulator adjudication of analytic choices—only that the filer declare the space and report how much of it agrees.

final_notes: Pre-registered 15,840 specs → 7,561 survivors → 3,218 distinct circuits; median circuit size 200 edges. Analytic random overlap k/(2|E|-k)=0.0031 (|E|=32,491). Pooled claim‑flip F = 0.7316 [0.7247,0.7380]. Pooled per‑example agreement = 0.6028 (instability = 0.3972). Pooled functional gap = 0.3344 [0.3297,0.3394] (pre‑registered threshold 0.10 met on pooled). REML on log10(size): ablation–corruption interaction explains 78.8% variance; residual 11.5%; ablation 4.4%; threshold 4.1%; metric 0.7%. Controlling for size drops pooled F to ≈0.2706–0.2746 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859). Median circuit size and per‑size results heterogeneous. Confirmatory sweep: preregistered commit prereg-p1-confirmatory made before sweep; confirmatory sweep ran under a single environment across 1,320 cells; commit recovered by content-addressed comparison (22/22 files identical). Analysis layer runs without a GPU. Verification: a script recomputed headline quantities (36 checks, 0 failures; F derived by three routes including brute-force pairwise); a second script verified every numeric token in the manuscript; every table emitted from results; test suite = 343 tests. Limitations: second‑model replication was pre‑registered but not run (924‑cell Pythia‑160m grid; seed axis levels changed); circuit size is an outcome (threshold‑selected) and biases pooled quantities; multiverse may omit optimal ablations so measured F is a lower bound; discard rate ≈52.3%; metric imbalance; bootstrap invalid for at least one reported family when conditioning groups have only 2–5 specs (those reported as point estimates); one exported discovery objective failed to run and was reported as a discard. Discussion emphasizes limited gains from single‑axis standardisation and that measuring evidentiary weight is cheap relative to original sweep.

Title: Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability (Ajay Pravin Mahale, 12 Aug 2026). Question: Do circuit-discovery explanations survive defensible analytic variation (two competent analysts, same system, same tool, different defensible settings)? Method: pre-registered crossed grid of 7 analytic axes (levels from published implementation); deterministic claim map to structured Annex IV statement. Dataset/experiment: 15,840 pre-registered specifications on GPT-2 small for indirect-object identification; 7,561 specs produced a claim. Key results: derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim covers 41.1% of the space. Standardising the single most influential choice (evaluation metric) reduces flip rate to 59.4%. Removing circuit size from the claim and holding it fixed reduces flip rate to 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286) — still above the pre-registered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). Additional: one of the seven documented discovery objectives fails to execute on the library’s canonical task. Deliverables: filability criterion given as standalone protocol. Scope: one model and one task; generalisability untested.

Related work (summaries relevant to design): Non-identifiability (Méloux et al.) — premise that unique explanation need not exist. Faithfulness metric sensitivity (Miller et al.) — ablation-based metrics sensitive to choices; their library is used as the instrument here, and the paper crosses seven axes testing sensitivity. Structure vs function (Bayat Makou et al.) — phantom specialisation; authors address this via functional measurement (see Sec. 7.6) and report circuits are not functionally interchangeable. Variance-as-estimation (Méloux) — seed variance included as an axis. Auditability (Lan et al., Sharkey et al.) motivates certification/standardisation. Multiverse methods (Steegen, Simonsohn) motivate crossing defensible choices. Explanation-metric optimisation pressure (Hsia et al.) — sufficiency and comprehensiveness are two of the paper's four evaluation metrics; discard rates are reported per metric rather than pooled.
