F = 1 − Σ_c n_c(n_c−1)/(N(N−1)) (unbiased Gini–Simpson). F_within(G) = 1 − Σ_g Σ_c n_{g,c}(n_{g,c}−1)/Σ_g n_g(n_g−1) (weights pairs equally; equals global F for trivial grouping). D(s_i,s_j) = 1 − |C_i ∩ C_j|/|C_i ∪ C_j| (Jaccard distance); J̄ = RW5 over unordered pairs. Specification tuple s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g). C(s) ⊆ E with |E|=32,491 for ML4 (GPT-2 small, factorised q/k/v). Architecture counts: block-b attention uses 1+13b sources; output takes 157 non-terminal sources; circuits draw on 156 components (144 heads + 12 MLPs).

This gives 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications."
errors.explanation: Given the stated factors, discovery cells should be 7 × (5 operators × 4 corruption levels + 2 operators × 1) = 154, not 1,540. The total specifications count 154 × (4 metrics × 3 thresholds × 2 prompts × 5 seeds) = 18,480, so 18,480 is consistent but 1,540 is off by a factor of 10.

errors.explanation: Per the stated design each objective contributes 22 discovery cells (5×4 + 2 = 22). Thus the failing objective should have 22 failing cells (not 220), and removing it yields 154−22 = 132 discovery cells (not 1,320). 132 × 120 (metrics×thresholds×prompts×seeds) = 15,840, which matches the reported specs, showing the cell counts have a factor-of-ten error.

Reproducibility: confirmatory sweep used one environment across all 1,320 cells; analysis layer runs without GPU. Verification: a verification script recomputes every headline quantity (36 checks, 0 failures) and derives F by three routes including brute-force pairwise; a second script checks every numeric token in the manuscript against stored results; every table emitted from results; test suite contains 343 tests. Key outcomes: confirmatory set = 7,561 retained specs (3,218 distinct circuits); pairwise pairs = 28,580,580. Pooled F = 0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380); pooled null = 0.6774. Mean Jaccard = 0.1396 (95% CI 0.1377–0.1418). Median circuit size = 200 edges. Holding size fixed F = 0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859); per-size values include medium 0.2746, coarse 0.2706. Functional agreement = 0.6028 (instability 0.3972). Gap = 0.3344 (95% CI 0.3297–0.3394). REML (log10 size) decomposition: ablation–corruption interaction 78.8%, residual 11.5%, ablation 4.4%, threshold 4.1%, metric 0.7%. Cohen's kappa pooled 0.0146 (paper also reports per-size 0.016–0.047 — noted earlier as inconsistent). Raw agreement per-size rises 0.52→0.92; accuracy 0.51→0.95. Pooled gap driven by 500–2,000 edge band; gap fails 0.10 at 6/10 sizes and is negative at 5 sizes. Limitations: one-model/one-task; second-model replication pre-registered on Pythia-160m (924-cell grid); seed axis 3 vs 5 levels; circuit size is outcome not axis; multiverse limited by library (optimal ablation omitted); discard rate 52.3%; bootstrap invalid for small conditioning groups (no bias-corrected estimator adopted).

Paper tests stability of mechanistic circuit discovery across a pre-registered multiverse (15,840 specs; 7,561 produced a claim). Main results: statement differs on 73.2% of specification pairs (95% boot CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim frequency 41.1%; evidence fails filability at all plausibly acceptable tolerances. Key controlled analyses: standardising the evaluation metric (most influential axis) yields flip rate 59.4%; restricting comparisons to circuits of the same size yields disagreement 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286). At fixed circuit size, discovered circuits flip less than a size-matched random null (flip rates 0.2746 vs 0.4230). Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap ≈4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa ≈0.0146–0.015). Functional instability (probability circuits disagree about individual examples) = 0.3972 pooled, 0.4777 at smallest circuits. Authors emphasise what they are not claiming: circuits are not “no better than random”; filings do not differ where mechanisms do not (mechanisms differ substantially); discovery is not just sampling one mechanism described differently (kappa shows lack of correlation); random seeds here index evaluation-set variability (seed picks prompts), not nondeterminism; and no claims about scale (single model GPT-2-small, single task indirect-object identification). Paper notes pooled-statistic reversal effects and reports related limitations and relevant prior work.

Formalism: a specification s = (o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g). Circuit discovery returns C(s) ⊆ E (edges of model). For GPT-2 small the factorised graph has |E| = 32,491 edges (confirmed instrument + closed-form). For block index b, attention receives from 1+13b sources at three input slots for each of 12 attention heads. Each MLP in block b receives from those sources plus its own block's heads. The output receives from all 157 non-terminal sources. Circuits touch components drawn from 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components total. Definitions: circuit distance D(s_i,s_j) = 1 − |C_i ∩ C_j| / |C_i ∪ C_j| (one minus Jaccard); ¯J denotes mean Jaccard over unordered pairs. Claim map φ converts a circuit into a structured statement. Flip rate F = 1 − (Σ_c n_c(n_c−1)) / (N(N−1)) (unbiased Gini–Simpson; probability two draws without replacement differ); modal share π* = max_c n_c / N. Within-group flip rate F_within(G) = 1 − (Σ_g Σ_c n_{g,c}(n_{g,c}−1)) / (Σ_g n_g(n_g−1)); reduces to Eq.2 when G empty. Filability: evidence filable at tolerance α iff π* ≥ 1−α. F has ceiling 1 − 1/k; with k=9 observed ceiling = 8/9 ≈ 0.8889; reported observed F = 0.7316 (≈82.3% of ceiling). Note: N is the count of specifications used in the claim analysis (earlier parts reported 15,840 specs, 7,561 produced a claim).

Title: Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability (Ajay Pravin Mahale, 12 Aug 2026). Question: Do circuit-discovery explanations survive defensible analytic variation (two competent analysts, same system, same tool, different defensible settings)? Method: pre-registered crossed grid of 7 analytic axes (levels from published implementation); deterministic claim map to structured Annex IV statement. Dataset/experiment: 15,840 pre-registered specifications on GPT-2 small for indirect-object identification; 7,561 specs produced a claim. Key results: derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim covers 41.1% of the space. Standardising the single most influential choice (evaluation metric) reduces flip rate to 59.4%. Removing circuit size from the claim and holding it fixed reduces flip rate to 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286) — still above the pre-registered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). Additional: one of the seven documented discovery objectives fails to execute on the library’s canonical task. Deliverables: filability criterion given as standalone protocol. Scope: one model and one task; generalisability untested.

Experiment & pre-registered grid: GPT-2 small, indirect-object identification. Pre-reg: 7 discovery objectives; 5 operators that read corruption distributions (5×4 + 2×1 = 22 operator+corruption combos per objective); 7 ablation operators total; 4 metrics; 3 thresholds; 2 prompt (addressee) variants; 5 seeds → 120 specs per cell. Key results (Section 7): P0: mean Jaccard J̄ = 0.1396 (95% CI [0.1377, 0.1418]), computed exactly over all C(7,561,2) = 28,580,580 specification pairs; the 7,561 specs map to 3,218 distinct circuits. Median circuit size ≈200 edges; analytic random expected Jaccard ≈0.0031 → mean observed J ≈0.1396 ≈45× random.

final_notes: Dataset/design: 1,320 cells, 15,840 specs; 7,561 specs retained. Bootstrap B=10,000. Overlap mean J = 0.1396 [0.1377,0.1418]; pairwise D quantiles 1%=0.196,25%=0.788,median=0.960,75%=0.998 (median J≈4%). Analytic random-overlap at median size ≈0.0031 (observed ≈45× chance). Main pooled F = 0.7316 [0.7247,0.7380]. Size-controlled F reported as 0.2706 [0.2550,0.2859] but elsewhere 0.2746 appears (internal numeric disagreement). H3 pre-reg decision conflicted; H4 supported: F-(1-agreement)=0.3344 [0.3297,0.3394]. Modal step width π* = 0.4109 (fails prereg π*≥0.80); seed effect on F ≈0.0009. Table 4: nine claim classes sum to 7,561; layer attribution early 47.9%, late 43.6%, middle 8.5% (COARSE TN4=0.4788). Filability protocol requires declaring S and deterministic QM3, reporting π*, F, EX9 and within-group decompositions. Limitations: measured F is a lower bound over defensible choices; bootstrap invalid for one reported family; no bias-corrected estimator; small-conditioning groups (2–5 specs) reported as point estimates with diagnostics; EX9 high/uneven (52.3%); circuit size treated as outcome distorting pooled F/QF4/functional-gap sign; GK5 spans library not literature. Reproducibility (this part): test suite 343 tests; "0 failures across 36 checks" for headline-quantity assertions; every table emitted from stored results by script; code commit recovery 22/22 files identical; sweep verified as run in single environment across 1,320 cells; analysis ran without GPU; traceability of every reported number to config/seed/environment is claimed; F derived by three routes including brute-force pairwise. Flag: numeric inconsistency for size-controlled F contradicts the claim that all manuscript numeric tokens match stored results.

steps.notes_before: Formalism: VX2 = flip rate (probability two distinct specifications yield different Annex-IV statements); TN4 = modal share π* = max_c n_c / N. Paper notes F = 1 - sum_c n_c(n_c-1) / [N(N-1)] (Eq.2, unbiased Gini–Simpson), and F_within(G) = 1 - sum_g sum_c n_{g,c}(n_{g,c}-1) / sum_g n_g(n_g-1) (Eq.3). Jaccard-based circuit distance D(s_i,s_j)=1-|C_i∩C_j|/|C_i∪C_j| (Eq.1); ̄J is mean Jaccard over unordered pairs. For GPT-2 small (ML4) |E|=32,491; circuits touch 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components; output receives from 157 non-terminal sources. ZK7 decision rule: evidence satisfies ZK7 at tolerance α iff π* ≥ 1−α. s is listed here as (o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g) — eight axes — but earlier description stated a pre-registered crossed grid of seven analytic axes (inconsistency flagged). Paper here reports VX2 observed = 0.7316 (82.3% of 0.8889 ceiling for k=9 classes); earlier parts/notes recorded VX2 ≈ 0.594 after standardising the evaluation metric (contradiction flagged). Keep track: pre-registered 15,840 specs; 7,561 produced a claim (from earlier parts).

Title: Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability. Author/date: Ajay Pravin Mahale, 12 Aug 2026. Context: EU AI Act Annex IV requires technical documentation; mechanistic interpretability (circuit discovery) proposed as source. Method: Pre-registered crossed grid of 7 analytic axes (each level from published implementations). Deterministic claim map used to turn each discovered circuit into structured statement. Model/task: GPT-2 small on indirect-object identification. Specifications: 15,840 pre-registered specifications; 7,561 produced a claim. Main results: derived statement differs on 73.2% of specification pairs (95% bootstrap CI 0.725–0.738). Modal claim accounts for 41.1% of the space. Evidence fails filability criterion at every plausibly acceptable tolerance. Standardising evaluation metric (most influential choice) yields flip rate 59.4%. Removing circuit size from the claim across full retained specification space yields 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286), still above pre-registered threshold. Circuits are structurally near-disjoint: median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%. Functionally uncorrelated: Cohen's kappa = 0.015. Additional notes: filability criterion provided as standalone protocol; one of seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library's canonical task. Scope limitation: single model, single task; scalability untested.

Title: Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability. Author/date: Ajay Pravin Mahale, 12 Aug 2026. Goal: assess whether circuit-level mechanistic explanations are "filable" under EU AI Act (cites Reg (EU) 2024/1689 as amended by 2026/1744). Definition used: an audit succeeds if two auditors reach the same conclusion. Method: pre-registered multiverse across 7 analytic axes of circuit discovery (each level drawn from published implementations). Deterministic map converts discovered circuits into structured Annex IV statements. Specs: 15,840 pre-registered specifications; 7,561 produced a claim. Filability criterion: π* ≥ 1−α, where π* is the share of specifications producing the most frequent (modal) claim; α is tolerated share outside that claim. Key results (canonical task: GPT-2 small on indirect-object identification): derived statement differs on 73.2% of specification pairs (95% bootstrap CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim covers 41.1% of specifications; evidence fails filability at all plausibly acceptable tolerances. Stability checks: standardising the evaluation metric (most influential axis) yields flip rate 59.4%; removing circuit size from claims yields 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286) and still fails threshold; holding size fixed also insufficient. Circuits are near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen's kappa 0.015). One of seven discovery objectives does not execute on the canonical library task. Scope: single model, single task; scalability untested. Also contributions: multiverse, filability criterion + measured value, robustness analyses, and methodological note on pooled-statistic reversals.

Related work: paper situates itself against non-identifiability (Méloux et al.); authors adopt premise and measure downstream cost to filing. They rely on Miller et al.'s ablation/faithfulness library and note Miller found high sensitivity (one axis matters); this paper crosses seven analytic axes and stress-tests that tooling. Bayat Makou et al.'s ‘phantom specialisation’ (structure can vary while function stays same) is acknowledged as the strongest objection; authors claim to address it with a functional measurement reported in Section 7.6 and assert their discovered circuits are not functionally interchangeable. Méloux et al. (other work) frame interpretability as statistical estimation; seed variance is one axis (seed controls prompt sampling). Auditability literature (Lan et al., Sharkey et al., Mueller et al.) motivates measurement + filability criterion (authors provide a measurement and criterion rather than prescriptive standards). Methodologically, they follow multiverse/specification-curve approaches (Steegen, Simonsohn) and warn about undisclosed analytic flexibility (Simmons). Two of four evaluation metrics are sufficiency and comprehensiveness (Hsia et al. show these can be gamed); authors report discard rates separately by metric rather than pooling. Retain: pre-registered multiverse across 7 axes, use of Miller's released library, functional check in Sec 7.6, four evaluation metrics with sufficiency/comprehensiveness included, and separate reporting by metric.

Paper frames interpretability as estimation; situates vs non-identifiability (Méloux) and phantom specialisation (Bayat Makou). Uses Miller et al.'s ablation/faithfulness library, pre-registered multiverse across 7 analytic axes, and reports four evaluation metrics (including sufficiency and comprehensiveness) with discard rates reported separately by metric. Authors say they addressed phantom specialisation with a functional check in Sec 7.6. New quantitative claims: discovered circuits are better than size-matched random nulls by flip rate (0.2746 vs 0.4230; Sec 7.5) so carry information; functional instability (rate circuits disagree on whether examples are correct) is 0.3972 pooled and 0.4777 at smallest circuits (Sec 7.6); Cohen's kappa = 0.0146 indicating circuits are functionally uncorrelated (Sec 7.6). Random-seed axis controls which prompts are sampled (measures evaluation-set variability, not nondeterminism). Authors explicitly do not claim results generalize by scale (one model, one task). They also note they themselves initially believed two of the excluded readings before decomposition.

steps.notes_before: Formalism: specification s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g) (g = granularity). Circuit discovery returns C(s) ⊆ E (edges); for GPT-2 small authors use a factorised q/k/v graph with |E| = 32,491 edges (confirmed instrumentally and by closed-form). For blocks: attention receives from 1+13b sources at three input slots for each of 12 heads; MLPs receive from those sources plus their block’s heads; output receives from 157 non-terminal sources. Circuits touch 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components. Circuit instability D(s_i,s_j)=1 - |C_i ∩ C_j| / |C_i ∪ C_j| (Jaccard distance); \bar{J} is mean Jaccard similarity over unordered pairs. Claim map φ maps circuits → claim classes. Flip rate (Eq.2): F = 1 - Σ_c n_c(n_c-1) / [N(N-1)] (Gini–Simpson without replacement); modal share π* = max_c n_c / N. Within-group flip rate F_within(G) = 1 - [Σ_g Σ_c n_{g,c}(n_{g,c}-1)] / [Σ_g n_g(n_g-1)]; when G empty reduces to Eq.2. Filability: evidence filable at tolerance α iff π* ≥ 1-α. Note: the paper claims F ≤ 1 - 1/k (giving 0.8889 for k=9), but that bound is incorrect for the finite-sample F defined in Eq.2 (actual upper bound depends on N: F = (N/(N-1))*(1 - Σ p_c^2), so F can exceed 1 - 1/k and can reach 1 in some finite-N cases). The authors unit-test Eq.2 against brute-force pairing.

Section 7 reports confirmatory results. Key confirmed numbers: premise P0 mean Jaccard J̄ = 0.1396 (95% CI [0.1377,0.1418]); flip rate F = 0.7316 (95% CI [0.7247,0.7380]) (H2 threshold 0.20: confirmed); H3 (hypothesis: not separated from random null) was rejected — intervals disjoint, i.e. separated from null; H4: F - (1 - agreement) = 0.3344 [0.3297,0.3394] (supported). The realized set has 7,561 kept specifications (consistent with prior method note) which map to 3,218 distinct circuits; all 7,561 choose 2 = 28,580,580 specification pairs were evaluated exactly (distinct-circuit reuse used to make this tractable). Pairwise distance D = 1 - J quantiles: 1% = 0.196, 25% = 0.788, median = 0.960, 75% = 0.998 — so median J ≈ 0.04 (median pair shares ~4% of edges); only 1% of pairs exceed J > 0.8. Median circuit size k = 200 edges gives random-overlap baseline k/(2|E|-k)=0.0031 (|E|=32,491), so observed overlap ~45× chance (mean J vs baseline). Modal share π* = 0.4109 (overall). final_notes: Key dataset/results: discovery grid → 7,561 surviving specs mapping to 3,218 distinct circuits. Pooled flip F = 0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380), π* = 0.4109. J̄ = 0.1396 (95% CI 0.1377–0.1418) over 28,580,580 spec pairs. Pairwise D median 0.960 (median pair shares ≈4% edges). Table 6 (axis-standardised residuals for flip rate) — metric: 0.5939 (removes 0.1377), ablation: 0.7014 (removes 0.0302), discovery objective: 0.7018 (removes 0.0298), threshold: 0.7070 (0.0246), corruption: 0.7092 (0.0224), prompt: 0.7232 (0.0084), seed: 0.7307 (0.0009). REML on log10(selected circuit size): 78.8% variance → ablation–corruption interaction; 11.5% residual; 4.4% ablation; 4.1% threshold; 0.7% metric. Holding circuit size fixed yields F ≈ 0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859). Sect.7.5: pooled discovered 0.7316 vs null 0.6774; with size fixed discovered ≈0.2746 vs null 0.4230 (medium) and 0.2706 vs null 0.3822 (coarse). Table 7: flip rate by circuit size (n sums to 7,561); discovered F = 0 at sizes 5,000 and 10,000 (n = 2,692 specs with zero flips). Authors' conclusion re H4: supported on pre-registered pooled quantity but gap disappears when holding size fixed; pooled effect concentrated in 500–2,000 edge band. Filability protocol (Sec.8): declare spec space S, deterministic claim map φ (published code), compute π* and F; filable iff π* ≥ 1−α; report π*, F, discard rates, within-group decomposition. Limitations: one model/task; second-model replication pre-registered (924-cell grid on Pythia-160m); circuit size chosen by threshold (fixing it greatly reduces F); multiverse limited by library (optimal ablation not implemented → measured F a lower bound); discard rate high (52.3%) and metric-imbalanced surviving pool; bootstrap invalid for conditioning groups of 2–5 (CIs reported only where valid). Reproducibility (new): pre-registration commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory; confirmatory sweep ran under a single environment across 1,320 cells (analysis layer runs without GPU); content-addressed check recovered code commit (22/22 files identical). Verification: script recomputes headline quantities (36 checks, 0 failures), F derived by three routes including brute-force pairwise; second script checks every numeric token in manuscript against stored results; every table emitted directly from results; test suite = 343 tests.

final_notes: Key results: pooled F = 0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380). J̄ = 0.1396 (28,580,580 spec pairs; 7,561 specs → 3,218 circuits). Modal class share π* = 0.4109 (3,107/7,561). COARSE TN4 class shares: early 47.9%, late 43.6%, middle 8.5% (COARSE F summary 0.4788). Table 5: all six addressee×granularity cells reject ZK7 (examples: affected COARSE F=0.3950, π*=0.7291; overseer MEDIUM F=0.7316, π*=0.4109). Pairwise D (J) quantiles; median J small. Per-example functional agreement 0.6028 (flip ≈0.3972); Cohen's kappa 0.0146. Within-size F reported as 0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859) but another part reports fixing circuit size reduces F to 0.2746 (numeric inconsistency noted). REML variance decomposition: ablation×corruption 78.8%, residual 11.5%, ablation 4.4%, threshold 4.1%, metric 0.7% (paper elsewhere mislabels 'metric'). Axis-standardisation effects: evaluation metric reduces pooled F by 0.1377; seed effect 0.0009. Discussion: metric is largest lever but no single knob suffices. Seven exported objectives: one discarded (EX9 reported earlier as 52.3%). Limitations: measured F treated as a lower bound; bootstrap invalid for one reported family and no bias-corrected estimator produced after discrepant naive intervals; quantities conditioned on 2–5 specs reported as point estimates with diagnostics; surviving-pool metric imbalanced; BJ9 fixed but composition unadjusted; circuit size treated as outcome and distorts pooled stats; GK5/library coverage limits; single model/task; planned GF7 replication (Pythia-160m, 924 cells) not run. Reproducibility claims (this part): test suite = 343 tests; "0 failures across 36 checks" for headline quantities; second script checks that every numeric token matches stored results and emits all tables directly; code commit recovery 22/22 identical; confirmatory sweep run under single environment across 1,320 cells verified from archive; prereg commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory; analysis layer ran without a GPU; traceability of reported numbers to config, seed and environment fingerprint asserted.

Key results: pooled F = 0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380). Exact J̄ = 0.1396 (28,580,580 spec pairs; 7,561 specs → 3,218 circuits). Modal class share π* = 0.4109 (3,107/7,561). Discussion claims: interpretability evidence's evidentiary weight is measurable and measurement is cheap relative to the original sweep; the metric is the biggest lever, removing 0.1377 from the 0.7316 pooled F, but there is no single knob—standardising one axis is insufficient. final_notes: Dataset |E|=32,491. Specs 15,840; BJ9 had no circuit for 8,279 specs (discarded), kept 7,561. 2,692 specs produce no flips; group sizes 1,512–2,520. Pooled vs size-matched null: discovered F=0.7316 vs null=0.6774. Holding size fixed dramatically reduces discovered F (examples: medium 0.2746 vs null 0.4230; coarse 0.2706 vs null 0.3822); fixing size reported to reduce F from 0.7316→0.2746 (Sec.7.5). Per-size table (edges: n F null classes): 10:2492 0.4543 0.7331 3; 20:489 0.3380 0.6622 4; 50:519 0.4639 0.7310 3; 100:242 0.5792 0.6584 3; 200:199 0.5122 0.6366 4; 500:236 0.4258 0.1421 3; 1,000:380 0.5133 0.0000 3; 2,000:312 0.5714 0.0000 3; 5,000:625 0.0000 0.0000 1; 10,000:2,067 0.0000 0.0000 1. Gap (F − instability) = 0.3344 (95% CI 0.3297–0.3394) — pooled gap > preregistered 0.10 but fails size-fixed check (effect concentrated in 500–2,000 edge band). Limitations/new: one model only; second-model replication pre-registered (Pythia-160m) not run; multiverse limited by library (optimal ablation not included → F is a lower bound); discard rate 52.3% and surviving pool metric-imbalanced; bootstrap invalid for small conditioning groups so reported only as point estimates. Reproducibility (new): preregistration is a timestamped commit tagged 'prereg-p1-confirmatory' made before confirmatory sweep. Every reported number traces to a configuration, seed, and environment fingerprint; confirmatory sweep used one environment across all 1,320 cells (verified from results archive). Recovered code commit by content-addressed comparison: all 22/22 files identical. Analysis layer runs without a GPU. Verification script recomputes headline quantities (36 checks, 0 failures) and derives F by three routes (incl. brute-force pairwise). A second script checks every numeric token against stored results; every table is emitted from results; test suite contains 343 tests. Note: Part 13's asserted claim "The metric is the biggest lever (removes 0.1377)" remains in the paper and conflicts conceptually with the reported size-effect (0.7316→0.2746).

Paper studies stability of circuit discovery evidence for EU AI Act Annex IV. Setup: mechanistic interpretability / circuit discovery on GPT-2 small, task = indirect object identification. They pre-registered a crossed grid of 7 analytic axes (each level taken from published implementations); total pre-registered specifications = 15,840. A deterministic claim map (no randomness or LM output) converts each discovered circuit into a structured Annex IV statement. Main results: across all 15,840 specs, derived statement pairs disagree on 73.2% of specification pairs (95% bootstrap CI 0.725–0.738). The modal claim occurs in 41.1% of specifications. They report the evidence fails a filability criterion (rule for whether evidence is stable enough to file) at every tolerance a conformity assessment body would plausibly accept. Sensitivity analyses: standardising the most influential choice (the evaluation metric) yields flip rate 59.4%; removing circuit size from claims and restricting to circuits of same size yields 27.1% flip (95% CI 0.255–0.286), which they say remains above their pre-registered threshold (threshold value not stated here). Circuits are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard overlap = 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa = 0.015). They provide the filability criterion as a standalone protocol and report one of the seven documented discovery objectives does not execute on the library’s canonical task. Study scope: one model, one task; generalisability untested.

errors.explanation: Given the reported 15,840 specifications and the listed axes (4×3×2×5 = 120), the number of cells must be 132, not 1,320; again the paper's 'cells' count appears to have an extra zero.

errors.claim: "Cohen's kappa is 0.0146" and later "kappa staying between 0.016 and 0.047 at every circuit size"
errors.evidence: "Cohen's kappa is 0.0146"; later: "kappa staying between 0.016 and 0.047 at every circuit size while raw agreement climbs from 0.52 to 0.92..."
errors.explanation: If every per-size kappa is at least 0.016, the overall (dataset-wide) kappa cannot be 0.0146 because the overall value must lie within the convex hull (min–max) of per-group values when groups have positive weight. The two numeric claims are therefore inconsistent.

final_notes: Key reported metrics: pooled 'discovered' F (overseer, MEDIUM)=0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380). Pairwise overlap mean J̄=0.1396 (95% CI 0.1377–0.1418) over 28,580,580 spec pairs (7,561 specs, 3,218 circuits). Standardising metric F reported 0.5939 (95% CI 0.5803–0.6063) but arithmetic implies 0.5920 (0.7316−0.1396), and paper subtracts 0.1377, creating ambiguity. Size-controlled F reported 0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859) but Limitations lists 0.2746 (inconsistency). Seed effect ≈0.0009. Modal/top-share π*=0.4109 (overseer, MEDIUM). Layer shares: early ~47.9%, late ~43.6%, middle ~8.5%. Table 5: ZK7 = no for all six rows. Median circuit shares ≈4% edges; ≈1% spec pairs J>0.8. Cohen's κ reported inconsistently (0.0146 vs per-size 0.016–0.047). Per-example agreement 0.6028 ⇒ (1−agreement)=0.3972. H3 rejected; H4 supported: F−(1−agreement)=0.3344 (95% CI 0.3297–0.3394). Filability requirements listed. Limitations: measured F is a lower bound; bootstrap invalid for one family; no bias-corrected estimator; small conditioning groups (2–5 specs) produced unusable intervals (reported as point estimates); EX9 high/uneven (52.3%); surviving pool metric-imbalanced; circuit size treated as outcome distorts some results; single-model/task confinement; planned replication unrun. Reproducibility claims (this part): 343 tests, 36 checks, "0 failures"; F derived by three routes including brute-force pairwise; every numeric token asserted to match stored results and every table emitted directly from stored results; code commit recovery 22/22 files identical; confirmatory sweep purportedly run under single environment across 1,320 cells with prereg commit tagged prereg-p1-confirmatory; analysis layer run without GPU; traceability claimed for every reported number to config, seed and environment fingerprint.

Related work situates this study in literature on robustness of mechanistic explanations and multiverse analyses. Two of the paper’s four evaluation metrics are NV3 (sufficiency) and WP6 (comprehensiveness); EX9 (discard rate) is reported per metric rather than silently pooled, and those per-metric results feed a regulatory statement after the seven analytic axes (GK5) are crossed. The study uses Miller et al.’s released library as the tooling/instrument, making the work a stress test of that tooling. Bayat Makou et al. report CU3 (structurally distinct circuits implementing the same computation) via varying input statistics while holding task fixed; the paper anticipates this objection and says Section 7.6 shows the paper’s circuits are not functionally interchangeable by a functional measurement. Méloux et al. provide the framing that mechanistic interpretability can lack a unique explanation and treat it as a statistical-estimation problem (seed variance is one axis). GK5 pre-registration follows Steegen et al.; the paper adapts Simonsohn et al.’s KY6 (specification curve) and cites Simmons et al. on researcher degrees of freedom. Keep earlier quantitative summaries and open checks: pre-registered GK5 over seven axes; deterministic mapping (QM3) from discovered circuits to Annex IV statements; ZK7 filability criterion (π* ≥ 1 − α) and the unknown pre-registered threshold; dataset/task restricted to one model and one task; 15,840 pre-registered specifications on ML4 and XB8. steps.notes_before: Formalism: Flip rate VX2 equals F, the Gini–Simpson (Eq.2) F = 1 - sum_c n_c(n_c-1)/[N(N-1)] (probability two draws without replacement differ); within-group form Eq.3 given. For k=9 claim classes ceiling 1-1/k=0.8889; observed VX2=0.7316 (~73.2%), which is ~82.3% of ceiling. Filability criterion ZK7: evidence satisfies iff π* ≥ 1-α, where π* = max_c n_c/N (TN4, modal share). Circuit instability D(si,sj)=1 - |Ci∩Cj|/|Ci∪Cj| (PD8); mean Jaccard ̄J (RW5) over unordered pairs. Circuit discovery returns C(s) ⊆ E. For GPT-2 small (ML4), |E| reported 32,491 (instrument + closed-form); description: attention block b receives from 1+13b sources at three input slots for each of 12 heads, MLP b receives from those sources plus its block's heads, output receives from all 157 non-terminal sources. Circuits touch components from 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components. Analytic-choice tuple s listed here as (o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g) (eight axes) — conflicts with earlier statement of seven pre-registered axes. Other remembered results: median pairwise Jaccard ≈4%; Cohen's kappa ≈0.0146; derived-statement flips ≈0.732 (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim ≈41.1% of specs (removing circuit size ~27.1%, 95% CI 0.255–0.286); reported discovered-circuit stability vs size-matched null earlier noted as numerically ambiguous; functional instability pooled 0.3972 and 0.4777 at smallest circuits.

final_notes:
Reproducibility claims (this part): 343 tests run; no GPU required; 36 verification checks reported with 0 failures; F established by three routes (brute force included); authors state "from stored results every manuscript number and table derives"; single-environment verification across 1,320 cells; code commit recovered by content-addressing (22/22 files); prereg tag prereg-p1-confirmatory.
Key results and flagged internal conflicts: pooled VX2 F=0.7316 (H2 pooled 0.7316 [0.7247,0.7380]) — pooled direction attributed to a size artefact. Fixed-size (within-size) contrasts: MEDIUM 0.2746 vs 0.4230; COARSE 0.2706 vs 0.3822. Main size-fixed value also reported as F=0.2706 (CI 0.2550–0.2859) but elsewhere (Part 11) given as 0.2746 (numeric inconsistency). Part 12 claims standardising one axis removes 0.1377 of 0.7316 (leaving ~0.5939), which conflicts with fixed-size reductions (~0.27–0.42) and with the authors' size-artefact attribution. Other flags: VX2 presented as a lower bound (optimal ablation unimplemented, GK5 coverage limited); EX9 uneven-family bootstrap invalid for small groups; Table 7: 7,561 specs, 2,692 produce no flips, per-example agreement 0.6028, κ 0.016–0.047, raw agreement climbs 0.52→0.92, circuits/spec-pairs counts. Verification claims in this part conflict with the manuscript's internal numeric inconsistencies.

Key quantitative results (from earlier parts): VX2 (flip rate) appears on 73.2% of pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); TN4 (modal share) = 41.1%; median pairwise Jaccard = 4%; Cohen's κ = 0.015. Standardising the metric yields 59.4%. Removing size from the claim and fixing it yields 27.1% (CI 0.255–0.286). Purpose/design: pre-registered crossed grid of seven analytic axes (GK5 = seven-axis multiverse) producing a deterministic QM3 / circuit→Annex IV mapping; test of claim instability (whether two competent analysts using same tool with different defensible settings produce stable circuit-discovery evidence). Contributions: (i) pre-registered seven-axis GK5 & deterministic circuit→Annex IV map; (ii) measured ZK7 filability criterion with π* ≥ 1−α. Part 3 (Related work) adds: §7.6 addresses non-interchangeability of circuits as response to CU3 (phantom specialisation — structurally distinct circuits implementing same computation); VX2 is interpreted as measuring which equivalence-class member was sampled. Ablation-based faithfulness is highly sensitive to minor choices; that sensitivity is counted as one of the seven axes. The authors treat an external library as their instrument (a stress test). They report per-metric EX9 (discard rate) because NV3 (sufficiency) and WP6 (comprehensiveness) — two of their four metrics — can be inflated without changing predictions; a unique explanation need not exist and its filing incurs a measured cost. Certification requires standardised specification; GK5 and KY6 (specification curve) are used; MI (statistical estimation) and seed variance are among the axes.

Paper: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection" by Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Studied model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection on 3 held-out datasets (two named: Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging; third unnamed here). Method: train linear probes on model activations; project activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from PCA on training activations. Use an LLM judge to produce natural-language interpretations: it scores each PC by judging whether the PC’s most- and least-activating examples suggest a transferable deception direction. Key claims/results: (1) projecting onto selected PCs enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained directly on the test distribution; (2) training probes on the highest-scoring PCs closes 78% of the baseline-to-oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging (Section 4.5); baseline = probe using all activations, oracle = selecting PCs using labeled target examples; (3) source-trained probe weights correspond to source-specific surface features, while transferable PCs encode more abstract contrasts that align with natural-language descriptions; overall claim: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” (Yoo & Skapars). Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection. Source train set: Roleplaying deception scenarios. Three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: train linear probes on model activations; compute PCA on source-domain activations and train probes after projecting onto a subset of source PCs. PC selection approaches: (a) target-supervised greedy search (adds one source PC at a time using labeled target examples) finds ~8–15 PCs on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Section 4.2); (b) ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights fails to recover the transferable subspace (Section 4.3); (c) an LLM judge inspects most/least-activating examples for each PC and partially recovers the transferable subspace without target labels (Section 4.5). Key quantitative claims (from earlier summary): projecting onto selected PCs enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching target-trained probes; using the judge-selected PCs closes 78% of the baseline-to-oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Definitions: baseline = probe using all activations; oracle = selecting PCs using labeled target examples. Central claim: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Task: deception detection; source training on roleplaying deception scenarios. Three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. PC selection approaches reported: (a) target-supervised greedy search (adds one source PC at a time using labeled target examples) finds ~8–15 PCs on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Section 4.2); (b) ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights fails to recover the transferable subspace (Section 4.3); (c) an LLM judge inspects most/least-activating examples per PC and partially recovers transferable subspace without target labels (Section 4.5). Definitions: baseline = probe using all activations; oracle = selecting PCs using labeled target examples. Related work (this part): literature on linear concept directions and linear representation hypothesis; examples claiming population-level directions for properties (honesty, emotion), single-direction mediation of refusal, and an “assistant” axis; methodological skepticism about probes and OOD generalization motivating tests of robustness; LLM-generated neuron explanations and natural-language labeling of features/SAEs, and using such descriptions to guide interventions/ablations.

Paper: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” (Yoo & Skapars). Task: deception detection using linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations (layer 15 chosen for highest cross-domain AUROC). Datasets: Roleplaying (source), three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels from GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Activations: pass prompt through model, average token activations only over the assistant’s response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance; standardize target activations using source statistics. PCA: run on standardized source activations, retain top 100 PCs (ordered by explained variance). Motivation: SAE-decoder alignment with PCs decreases with PC index (Appendix C Fig.6), so low-index PCs are easier to interpret (not claimed to generalize better). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). For subset S of the 100 PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Earlier high-level results to check later: (a) target-supervised greedy search finds ≈8–15 PCs to match target-trained probe (Section 4.2); (b) ranking PCs by probe weights fails to recover transferable subspace (Section 4.3); (c) LLM judge inspects most/least-activating examples per PC and partially recovers transferable subspace without target labels (Section 4.5) — judge-selected PCs close ~78% of baseline→oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and ~25% on Sandbagging. Section 4.1 verifies the 100-PC subspace retains sufficient signal on every target.

Setting & baselines: Probes are logistic regression (λ=10). Baseline: probes trained on full source representations transfer to targets with AUROCs — Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Check of 100-PC subspace: training probes on top-100 source PCs with 5-fold CV on each target yields AUROCs (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging) = 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869, so the 100-PC subspace contains sufficient signal. Greedy PC selection (Sect.4.2): start empty; at each step consider adding any remaining PC among top-100 source PCs, fit logistic probe on source projections, measure target AUROC (selection uses target labels), add PC that most improves target AUROC; 5-fold CV over target for selection; stop when no candidate improves AUROC > 0.001. With CV-based greedy, average selected sizes: 15 (Report), 8 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Using greedy on full target dataset (for a single stable k) gives k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy improves over baseline by ~0.22 (Report) and ~0.23 (Sandbagging) AUROC and comes close to target-trained probes for those two tasks; variance-based top-k (by explained variance) matches greedy only on the easy Confirm task. Sect.4.3 tests two ranking hypotheses: rank PCs by standardized absolute probe coefficients (abs(weight)×PC std) from a probe trained on source (source-PCA probe) or from a probe trained on target (target-PCA probe, still in source-PCA basis); after ranking, evaluated probes are trained on source projected to top-k ranked PCs (k from full-dataset greedy).

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct probes. Task: deception detection; authors report experiments on 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging; third dataset not named in this part). Main claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) computed from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the test distribution. Method: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe on highest-scoring PCs. Quantitative claims: using this approach they "close the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging." Additional claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and are capturable by natural language descriptions. High-level conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Venue/area: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection; train on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios), evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: operate in source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of principal components (PCs) for probe training to avoid spurious, non-transferable features. Key quantitative/structural claims: a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds a small transferable subspace of ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Section 4.2). Source-side and target-side rankings (ranking PCs by source or target probe weights) fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform the full-representation baseline (Section 4.3). An LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without using target labels by interpreting PCs and selecting those likely to encode the behavioral contrast (Section 4.5). Prior summary from earlier part: the method reportedly closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. High-level conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection; transferable directions are more abstract and can be captured by natural-language descriptions, whereas source-weighted directions capture surface features.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection; train on one source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios), evaluate on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Core idea: work in source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of principal components (PCs) for probe training to avoid spurious, non-transferable features. Key quantitative/structural claims: a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds a small transferable subspace of ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Section 4.2). Source-side and target-side rankings (ranking PCs by source or target probe weights) fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform the full-representation baseline (Section 4.3). An LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without using target labels by interpreting PCs and selecting those likely to encode the behavioral contrast (Section 4.5). Reported effect sizes: method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Related work: evidence for linear/low-dimensional concept directions (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024; Zou et al. 2025); examples of single-direction behaviors (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); longstanding skepticism about probes and OOD generalization (Hewitt & Liang 2019; Ravichander et al. 2021; recent work on uneven OOD probe performance). LLMs have been used to generate natural-language explanations of neurons/features and to label/ablate concepts for intervention (Bills et al. 2023; Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023; Casademunt et al. 2025).

Goal: probe generalization as subspace selection for OOD deception detection. Datasets: Roleplaying (source), Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging (targets). Labels: GPT-4o labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Model & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, use layer-15 residual stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); extract by passing each prompt and averaging token activations over the assistant’s response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance; apply the same source statistics to standardize all target activations. Dimensionality reduction: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs; all downstream experiments use this basis. Probes: logistic regression (L2 lambda=10). For a chosen subset S of the 100 PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activation space (i.e., no PCA subset). Motivation for 100 PCs: alignment with SAE decoder features decreases with PC index (App. C), so lower-index PCs are more interpretable; authors do not claim low-index PCs generalize better—Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace retains enough information to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target. Key claims to check later: a target-supervised greedy search finds a small transferable subspace (~8–15 PCs) where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec 4.2); source-/target-side rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec 4.3); an LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without target labels (Sec 4.5). Reported effect sizes: method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

steps.notes_before: Experiments: evaluate transfer of logistic-regression probes (L2) from source (Roleplaying) to three targets: Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Baselines: source-trained on full representations (blue) and on top-100 PCs (orange). Target-trained probes (5-fold CV) on top-100 source PCs provide oracle performance. Baseline (source→target, full reps) AUROCs: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained (within 100 PCs) AUROCs: 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (mapped to Confirm / Report / Sandbagging). Conclusion 4.1: 100-PC subspace retains sufficient info; poor transfer stems from source probe direction. Greedy PC selection (oracle, uses labeled target folds for subset selection with 5-fold CV, stop if AUROC improvement ≤0.001) iteratively adds PCs to maximize AUROC on held-out fold; probe weights always fit on source data. Greedy converges to small subsets (avg sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14). Greedy improves baseline by +0.22 AUROC (Report) and +0.23 AUROC (Sandbagging), coming close to target-trained probe. Top-k-by-variance baseline (k matched to greedy) matches greedy only for Confirm; falls short for Report and Sandbagging. 4.3 tests two hypotheses for transferable PCs: (a) PCs that individually separate target classes, (b) PCs the source probe heavily weights. They compare rankings by target-probe and source-probe standardized coefficients (|coef| * stddev of PC).

steps.notes_before: Experiments transfer LR probes from a source (Roleplaying) to three targets: Insider Trading Confirm, Report, Sandbagging. Baselines: source-trained on full representations and on top-100 source PCs. Target-trained probes on top-100 PCs give oracle performance (AUROCs reported earlier). Greedy PC selection (previously run per-fold) produced small subsets (avg sizes: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14) and improved source→target AUROC substantially (+0.22 Report, +0.23 Sandbagging), approaching target-trained probes. In this part, greedy run on the full target datasets yields k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging) — numbers differ slightly from CV. Two hypotheses tested: source-PCA probe (rank PCs by source-probe weights) and target-PCA probe (rank by target-probe weights). Both fail: source-PCA matches full-representation baseline (poor transfer); target-PCA does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below-random on Sandbagging. Interpretability: for each top-100 source PC, take 8 most/8 least activating source examples, prompt an LLM to describe poles and rate generalizability (OOD). The paper inconsistently reports the judge's scale (claims 1–5, later references 1–10 and treating 6 as max). They retained PCs that received the maximum observed OOD score in both runs, yielding 19 "interp-selected" PCs. Five PCs appeared in greedy selections for more than one target; 3 of those 5 had the maximum OOD score. Interp-selected 19 PCs are evaluated vs controls (full rep, top-19 by variance, remaining 81 ablated).

Setup: transfer linear-probe (LR) classifiers from source (Roleplaying) to 3 targets: Insider Trading {Confirm, Report} and Sandbagging. Baselines: source-trained on full representations and on top-100 source PCs; oracle = target-trained probes on top-100 PCs. Greedy PC selection (per-fold) produced small subsets (avg sizes: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14) and boosted source→target AUROC substantially (+0.22 Report, +0.23 Sandbagging), approaching oracle. Greedy run on full targets: k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Source-PCA ranking (by source-probe weights) failed (matches poor baseline); target-PCA ranking failed on Sandbagging (below random), mixed on others. Interpretability selection: for each top-100 source PC, take most/least activating source examples, ask LLM to describe poles and rate OOD generalizability (judge-scale reported inconsistently earlier). They retained PCs that received the maximum observed OOD score in both runs, yielding 19 "interp-selected" PCs; 5 PCs overlapped with greedy selections for multiple targets (3 of those 5 had max OOD). Controls: full rep, top-19 by variance (source-variance), remaining 81 ablated. Results (this part): interp-selected 19-PC probe outperforms baseline on all 3 targets, outperforms source-variance-selected control ("wide margins" on Report and Sandbagging), and outperforms interp-ablated. Recovery varies by dataset: Report: interp closes 78% of gap between baseline (0.706) and greedy oracle (0.929) (interp ≈0.880). Confirm: baseline near ceiling; little headroom — most selection methods (except interp-ablated) perform similarly. Sandbagging: interp closes 25% of gap to greedy oracle (0.832) (implies interp ≈0.66 if baseline ≈0.602). Conclusion: selecting PCs via NL descriptions (no target data) yields meaningful improvement over baseline.

Setup: Transfer linear probes (PCA projection → logistic regression) from a source dataset (Roleplaying) to three targets: Insider Trading (Confirm, Report) and Sandbagging. Baselines: source-trained on full representations and on top-100 source PCs; oracle = target-trained probes on top-100 PCs. Greedy PC selection (per-fold) found small subsets (avg sizes: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14) and substantially improved source→target AUROC (+0.22 Report, +0.23 Sandbagging), approaching oracle. Greedy run on full targets selected k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Source-PCA ranking (by source-probe weights) failed; target-PCA ranking failed on Sandbagging. Interpretability selection: for each top-100 source PC, collect most/least activating source examples, ask an LLM to describe poles and rate out-of-distribution generalizability; retain PCs receiving maximal OOD score in both runs → 19 interp-selected PCs. Five PCs overlapped with greedy selections across targets (3 of those had max OOD). Controls: full representation, top-19-by-variance (source-variance), and an interp-ablated set (remaining 81 PCs removed). Results: interp-selected 19-PC probe outperforms baseline on all three targets, outperforms source-variance control and interp-ablated. Recovery by target: Report baseline 0.706 → interp 0.881 (closes ~78% of gap to greedy at 0.929); Confirm baseline ≈0.874 (near ceiling) so little headroom and selection methods perform similarly; Sandbagging baseline 0.606 → interp 0.662 (recovers ~25% of gap to greedy at 0.832). Limitations: single model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) and single source dataset; Sandbagging improvement small (likely OOD); fully linear probe pipeline may limit generality; no causal validation (no intervention/ablation to prove PCs carry contrasts).

Setup: Transfer linear probes (PCA projection → logistic regression) from a Roleplaying source to three targets: Insider Trading (Confirm, Report) and Sandbagging. Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo; Adrians Skapars. Abstract key claims:
- A8T scores each principal component (PC) by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction. Probing restricted to the highest-scoring PCs. PC interpretations isolate a subset of transferable PCs.
- Under that restriction, M3Z (defined as the baseline-to-oracle gap) is "closed by 78% on Q7V and by 25% on J8W." 
- M3Z is framed in the generalization performance of V6Q probes (parenthetical: "3.1, 8") evaluated over 3 held-out deception detection datasets.
- Projecting inputs onto a small subset of PCs from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches S6F.
- Source probe directions weighted heavily appear to encode source-specific surface features; the directions that actually transfer encode the same contrast more abstractly in a way natural language descriptions can capture.
- Conclusion-level claims: linear probes can detect behaviors/concepts inside LM activations but may fail to transfer OOD; OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.
- Venue: Machine Learning, ICML.

Key numbers/labels to track: 78% (Q7V), 25% (J8W), 3 held-out datasets, terms M3Z, A8T, V6Q, S6F.

steps.notes_before: Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo; Adrians Skapars. Main claims (abstract/introduction): A8T scores PCs by whether most/least-activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs yields transfer. Target-supervised greedy search over source-domain PCs recovers a small transferable subspace of ~8–15 PCs on which a source-trained probe nearly matches the S6F (Section 4.2). Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights fails to produce a basis that transfers better than the V9D (Section 4.3). A8T can partially recover the subspace without target data by interpreting/selecting PCs encoding transferable contrast (Section 4.5). Experimental setup: probes trained on a single source dataset (Z4K: Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on three held-out target datasets (Q7V: Insider Trading Report; P3Y: Insider Trading Confirm; J8W: Sandbagging). Baselines: S6F = target-trained probe; V9D = full-representation baseline; A8T = LLM judge. Paper repeatedly references V6Q but inconsistently: one place labels V6Q as the dataset/testbed (citing Grattafiori et al., 2024) and another labels V6Q as the model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct)—this ambiguity needs resolution. Key numbers from abstract to verify later: M3Z gap closed by 78% (Q7V) and 25% (J8W).

Setup: R2F = top 100 PCs from PCA on standardized source activations; same source scaling applied to targets. Datasets: source Z4K; targets Q7V, P3Y, J8W. steps.notes_before: Part 6 summary: Figures 4 and 3 test whether K9U's transferable PC subset can be predicted from source-only signals via two hypotheses: Z1M = ranking by source-trained probe weights; H5X = ranking by target-trained probe weights. U1L = |probe coefficient| * stddev(PC) on activations projected to the source-PCA basis. Evaluation protocol: for each ranking, select top-k PCs, train logistic regression probes on source data projected onto those PCs, evaluate E3K on target. K9U greedy selection (per-fold H6Q) stops when no PC improves E3K by >0.001 and converges on average k: Q7V=15, P3Y=8, J8W=14. When K9U is run on the full target dataset it yields k=13 (Q7V), 7 (P3Y), 14 (J8W) — numbers differ because full-data vs per-fold. Results: both hypotheses fail: Z1M transfers about as well as V9D (so source-probe PCs do not generalize); H5X helps on Q7V but is worse than K9U on P3Y and below-random on J8W. Fig3: K9U improves over V9D by 0.22 (Q7V) and 0.23 (J8W); W4J (top-k variance, k matched to K9U) only matches K9U on the easy case P3Y. Note: text is ambiguous/contradictory about whether H5X is derived from a probe trained on target data versus the later statement that "in both cases" the probes are trained on source data when evaluating top-k subsets.

Evaluation protocol: rank PCs (by hypotheses Z1M: source-trained probe weights; H5X: target-trained probe weights per earlier ambiguity), select top-k, train logistic probes on source data projected to source-PCA basis, evaluate E3K on target. K9U greedy selection (per-fold stop when no PC improves E3K >0.001) avg k: Q7V=15, P3Y=8, J8W=14; K9U on full target: k=13 (Q7V), 7 (P3Y), 14 (J8W). Main results: both predictive hypotheses fail overall — Z1M ~ V9D (source-probe PCs do not generalize); H5X helps on Q7V but is worse than K9U on P3Y and below-random on J8W. K9U improves over V9D by ~0.22 (Q7V) and ~0.23 (J8W). From Limitations (Part 7): J8W: E3K raised 0.606 -> 0.662 by selection (Q8B), which recovers ~25% of gap to K9U upper bound 0.832; Q7V: 0.706 -> 0.881, closing ~78% of gap to K9U 0.929. P3Y baseline transfer already high (0.874), making P3Y results less informative. Limitations listed: structural "encoding" claims are descriptive (no causal ablations); probe pipeline is fully linear (PCA + logistic regression) — extension to nonlinear probes/readout locations open; all experiments used single model V6Q (3.1-series, 8B, layer 15) and single source dataset Z4K, so generalization to other models/datasets is unresolved. Note earlier ambiguity in paper about whether H5X probes are trained on target vs source when evaluating top-k subsets.

Paper: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection" by Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Studied model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection on 3 held-out datasets (two named: Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging; third unnamed here). Method: train linear probes on model activations; project activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from PCA on training activations. Use an LLM judge to produce natural-language interpretations: it scores each PC by judging whether the PC’s most- and least-activating examples suggest a transferable deception direction. Key claims/results: (1) projecting onto selected PCs enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained directly on the test distribution; (2) training probes on the highest-scoring PCs closes 78% of the baseline-to-oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging (Section 4.5); baseline = probe using all activations, oracle = selecting PCs using labeled target examples; (3) source-trained probe weights correspond to source-specific surface features, while transferable PCs encode more abstract contrasts that align with natural-language descriptions; overall claim: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” (Yoo & Skapars). Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection. Source train set: Roleplaying deception scenarios. Three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: train linear probes on model activations; compute PCA on source-domain activations and train probes after projecting onto a subset of source PCs. PC selection approaches: (a) target-supervised greedy search (adds one source PC at a time using labeled target examples) finds ~8–15 PCs on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Section 4.2); (b) ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights fails to recover the transferable subspace (Section 4.3); (c) an LLM judge inspects most/least-activating examples for each PC and partially recovers the transferable subspace without target labels (Section 4.5). Key quantitative claims (from earlier summary): projecting onto selected PCs enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching target-trained probes; using the judge-selected PCs closes 78% of the baseline-to-oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Definitions: baseline = probe using all activations; oracle = selecting PCs using labeled target examples. Central claim: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Task: deception detection; source training on roleplaying deception scenarios. Three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Related work (this part): literature on linear concept directions and linear representation hypothesis; examples claiming population-level directions for properties (honesty, emotion), single-direction mediation of refusal, and an “assistant” axis; methodological skepticism about probes and OOD generalization motivating tests of robustness; LLM-generated neuron explanations and natural-language labeling of features/SAEs, and using such descriptions to guide interventions/ablations.

Paper: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” (Yoo & Skapars). Task: deception detection using linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations (layer 15 chosen for highest cross-domain AUROC). Datasets: Roleplaying (source), three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels from GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Activations: pass prompt through model, average token activations only over the assistant’s response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance; standardize target activations using source statistics. PCA: run on standardized source activations, retain top 100 PCs (ordered by explained variance). Motivation: SAE-decoder alignment with PCs decreases with PC index (Appendix C Fig.6), so low-index PCs are easier to interpret (not claimed to generalize better). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). For subset S of the 100 PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Earlier high-level results to check later: (a) target-supervised greedy search finds ≈8–15 PCs to match target-trained probe (Section 4.2); (b) ranking PCs by probe weights fails to recover transferable subspace (Section 4.3); (c) LLM judge inspects most/least-activating examples per PC and partially recovers transferable subspace without target labels (Section 4.5) — judge-selected PCs close ~78% of baseline→oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and ~25% on Sandbagging. Section 4.1 verifies the 100-PC subspace retains sufficient signal on every target.

Setting & baselines: Probes are logistic regression (λ=10). Baseline: probes trained on full source representations transfer to targets with AUROCs — Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Check of 100-PC subspace: training probes on top-100 source PCs with 5-fold CV on each target yields AUROCs (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging) = 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869, so the 100-PC subspace contains sufficient signal. Greedy PC selection (Sect.4.2): start empty; at each step consider adding any remaining PC among top-100 source PCs, fit logistic probe on source projections, measure target AUROC (selection uses target labels), add PC that most improves target AUROC; 5-fold CV over target for selection; stop when no candidate improves AUROC > 0.001. With CV-based greedy, average selected sizes: 15 (Report), 8 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Using greedy on full target dataset (for a single stable k) gives k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy improves over baseline by ~0.22 (Report) and ~0.23 (Sandbagging) AUROC and comes close to target-trained probes for those two tasks; variance-based top-k (by explained variance) matches greedy only on the easy Confirm task. Sect.4.3 tests two ranking hypotheses: rank PCs by standardized absolute probe coefficients (abs(weight)×PC std) from a probe trained on source (source-PCA probe) or from a probe trained on target (target-PCA probe, still in source-PCA basis); after ranking, evaluated probes are trained on source projected to top-k ranked PCs (k from full-dataset greedy).

Key setting & baselines (from earlier): probes are logistic regression (λ=10). Full-source baseline AUROCs: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Top-100 source-PC probe (5-fold CV per target) AUROCs: Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869. Greedy PC selection (search among top-100 PCs using target labels, 5-fold CV): average selected sizes CV-based = 15 (Report), 8 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging); stable-k greedy on full target gives k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy improves over baseline by ~0.22 (Report) and ~0.23 (Sandbagging). Section 4.3 tested two ranking hypotheses (source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe); both fail differently: source-PCA probe transfers about as well as full-representation baseline but relies on PCs that do not generalize; target-PCA probe works on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and is below-random on Sandbagging. Section 4.4 (LLM-based interpretation): for each top-100 PC gather 8 most/least-activating examples and prompt an LLM to describe poles and contrast; judge rates OOD generalizability 1–10. Observed max score = 6; keeping PCs scoring the max in both independent runs yields 19 "interp-selected" PCs. Of 5 PCs greedy selected for >1 target, 3 (PC62, PC57, PC86) have max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA-ranked PCs (PC4) has max. Section 4.5: evaluate interp-selected (19 PCs) vs controls (full baseline, top-19 by variance, interp-ablated remaining 81). Interp-selected outperforms baseline on all three targets: Report AUROC 0.881 (closes 78% of gap from 0.706->0.929), Sandbagging AUROC 0.662 (closes 25% of gap to greedy 0.832); Confirm: baseline near ceiling and methods (except interp-ablated) perform roughly alike. Figures referenced: Figure 4 (PC generalization), Figure 5 (AUROC comparisons).

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct probes. Task: deception detection; authors report experiments on 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging; third dataset not named in this part). Main claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) computed from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the test distribution. Method: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe on highest-scoring PCs. Quantitative claims: using this approach they "close the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging." Additional claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and are capturable by natural language descriptions. High-level conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Venue/area: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection; train on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios), evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: operate in source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of principal components (PCs) for probe training to avoid spurious, non-transferable features. Key quantitative/structural claims: a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds a small transferable subspace of ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Section 4.2). Source-side and target-side rankings (ranking PCs by source or target probe weights) fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform the full-representation baseline (Section 4.3). An LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without using target labels by interpreting PCs and selecting those likely to encode the behavioral contrast (Section 4.5). Prior summary from earlier part: the method reportedly closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. High-level conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection; transferable directions are more abstract and can be captured by natural-language descriptions, whereas source-weighted directions capture surface features.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection; train on one source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios), evaluate on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Core idea: work in source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of principal components (PCs) for probe training to avoid spurious, non-transferable features. Key quantitative/structural claims: a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds a small transferable subspace of ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Section 4.2). Source-side and target-side rankings (ranking PCs by source or target probe weights) fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform the full-representation baseline (Section 4.3). An LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without using target labels by interpreting PCs and selecting those likely to encode the behavioral contrast (Section 4.5). Reported effect sizes: method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Related work: evidence for linear/low-dimensional concept directions (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024; Zou et al. 2025); examples of single-direction behaviors (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); longstanding skepticism about probes and OOD generalization (Hewitt & Liang 2019; Ravichander et al. 2021; recent work on uneven OOD probe performance). LLMs have been used to generate natural-language explanations of neurons/features and to label/ablate concepts for intervention (Bills et al. 2023; Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023; Casademunt et al. 2025).

Goal: probe generalization as subspace selection for OOD deception detection. Datasets: Roleplaying (source), Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging (targets). Labels: GPT-4o labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Model & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, use layer-15 residual stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); extract by passing each prompt and averaging token activations over the assistant’s response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance; apply the same source statistics to standardize all target activations. Dimensionality reduction: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs; all downstream experiments use this basis. Probes: logistic regression (L2 lambda=10). For a chosen subset S of the 100 PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activation space (i.e., no PCA subset). Motivation for 100 PCs: alignment with SAE decoder features decreases with PC index (App. C), so lower-index PCs are more interpretable; authors do not claim low-index PCs generalize better—Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace retains enough information to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target. Key claims to check later: a target-supervised greedy search finds a small transferable subspace (~8–15 PCs) where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec 4.2); source-/target-side rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec 4.3); an LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without target labels (Sec 4.5). Reported effect sizes: method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Experiments probe transfer of logistic-regression probes (L2) trained on source (Roleplaying) to three targets: Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Key AUROCs: source→target baseline: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained (oracle, 5-fold CV on top-100 source PCs): Confirm ~0.936, Report ~0.950, Sandbagging ~0.869. Interpretability selection: for each top-100 PC show top/bottom activating source examples, ask LLM judge OOD-generalizability 1–10. No PC scored >6; keeping PCs that scored the max (6) in both runs yields 19 interp-selected PCs. Of 5 PCs that appear in greedy selections for >1 target, 3 got max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA PCs got max OOD. The interp-selected (19 PC) probe outperforms baseline and the top-19-by-variance control on all 3 targets; beats interp-ablated. Experiments studied transfer of linear probes (PCA projection of top-100 source PCs + L2 logistic regression) trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying) from a single model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) to three OOD targets: Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo; Adrians Skapars. Abstract key claims:
- A8T scores each principal component (PC) by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction. Probing restricted to the highest-scoring PCs. PC interpretations isolate a subset of transferable PCs.
- Under that restriction, M3Z (defined as the baseline-to-oracle gap) is "closed by 78% on Q7V and by 25% on J8W." 
- M3Z is framed in the generalization performance of V6Q probes (parenthetical: "3.1, 8") evaluated over 3 held-out deception detection datasets.
- Projecting inputs onto a small subset of PCs from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches S6F.
- Source probe directions weighted heavily appear to encode source-specific surface features; the directions that actually transfer encode the same contrast more abstractly in a way natural language descriptions can capture.
- Conclusion-level claims: linear probes can detect behaviors/concepts inside LM activations but may fail to transfer OOD; OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.
- Venue: Machine Learning, ICML.

Key numbers/labels to track: 78% (Q7V), 25% (J8W), 3 held-out datasets, terms M3Z, A8T, V6Q, S6F.

Experiments (sec.4): main comparisons among many subset/selection methods over three target datasets (Q7V, P3Y, J8W) using E3K (AUROC). Key methods: V9D = source-trained probe on full activations; R2F = top-100 PCs (source PCA retained for interpretability); Q8B = 19 PCs chosen by human interpretability procedure (A8T) using source-only ratings (no PC scored >6; Q8B = PCs scoring 6 in both runs); K9U = greedy target-informed PC subset selection (adds PC that most improves target E3K of a probe fit on source projections; selection uses target labels on non-held-out folds under H6Q; weights always fit on source; stop when gain <=0.001).
