steps.notes_before: Paper: 'Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection' (Yoo & Skapars). Datasets: Roleplaying (source); targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels: GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; use layer-15 residual stream activations; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance); standardize targets using source stats. PCA: run on standardized source activations; retain top 100 PCs (by explained variance). Probes: logistic regression (regularization lambda=10). For subset S of the 100 PCs, project activations onto S before training/eval; baseline probes use full standardized activations. Paper claims justification for picking top-100: 'alignment with SAE decoder features increases with PC index' and also asserts 'lower-index PCs are therefore more amenable to natural-language interpretation' (internal contradiction noted). Section 4.1 will test whether the 100-PC subspace retains enough signal on targets. Keep prior-summary claims about PC-selection methods (target-supervised greedy finds ~8–15 PCs; probe-weight ranking fails; LLM judge partly recovers) for cross-checking later.

Experiments: baseline and PC-selection. Baselines: source-trained probes on full representations transfer to targets with AUROC — Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes trained within the top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) get AUROC 0.936 (Report) / 0.950 (Confirm) / 0.869 (Sandbagging), so authors conclude the top-100 PC subspace contains enough signal and transfer failures are due to learned source direction, not missing info. PCA/projection: top 100 PCs of standardized source activations are used. Greedy PC-selection: start empty, iteratively consider adding any remaining of the top-100, for each candidate train logistic probe on source data projected to that subset and evaluate on labeled target folds; add PC that most improves target AUROC; stop when no candidate improves AUROC > 0.001. Greedy selection uses 5-fold CV over target: within each fold, selection uses non-held-out target folds and eval on held-out fold. Average # PCs selected (Sec 4.2): Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy nearly matches target-trained probe on Report and Sandbagging, improving over the baseline by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging). Variance-based top-k control (k matched to greedy) matches greedy only on Confirm; falls far behind on Report and Sandbagging. For analyses in Sec 4.3, to set k authors run greedy on the full target dataset (not per-fold), yielding k=13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging) — noted as slightly different from fold-averaged numbers. Hypotheses tested: (1) transferable PCs individually separate target classes; (2) transferable PCs are those most used by source probe. Two ranking methods: source-PCA-probe weights and target-PCA-probe weights; standardized ranking uses abs(coef)*PC std. After ranking, probes for transfer are trained on source data projected onto top-k ranked PCs. Key procedural points to check later: which probe weights are fit on source vs target in each experiment, exact AUROC values for greedy and ranking methods (Figures 3/4), and cross-validation vs full-data k differences.

Experiments compare source-trained baseline vs PC-selection and interpretability-based selection. Baseline (source-trained on full reps) AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes (fit on target within top-100 source-PC subspace, 5-fold CV) AUROC: Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869. Greedy PC-selection (fold-averaged # PCs): Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; greedy run on full target to set k yields k=13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy nearly matches target-trained on Report and Sandbagging and substantially improves over baseline (+~0.22 Report, +~0.23 Sandbagging). Two ranking hypotheses (source-PCA-probe-weight ranking and target-PCA-probe-weight ranking) fail: source-PCA probe transfers about as well as full baseline and relies on PCs that do not generalize; target-PCA probe helps on Report, is worse than greedy on Confirm, and is below-random on Sandbagging. Interpretation: for top-100 source PCs, take 8 most/least activating examples, prompt an LLM to describe poles and rate OOD generalizability 1–10. No PC >6; keep PCs scoring the observed max (6) in both scoring runs -> 19 "interp-selected" PCs. Five PCs were chosen by greedy for >1 target; 3 of these (PC62, PC57, PC86) got max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA-ranked PCs got max (PC4). Interp-selected probe (19 PCs) vs controls: outperforms baseline and variance-top-19 control, especially on Report and Sandbagging, and outperforms interp-ablated (remaining 81) on all targets. Numbers: Report interp-selected AUROC 0.881 (closes 78% of gap from baseline 0.706 to greedy 0.929); Sandbagging AUROC 0.662 (closes 25% of gap from 0.606 to greedy 0.832). Confirm: baseline near ceiling, selection results similar across methods (uninformative). Appendices/figures cited for full breakdown.

Single model/dataset: experiments use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (layer 15) and one source dataset (Roleplaying). Targets: Insider Trading Report, Confirm, Sandbagging. Baseline (source-trained, full repr) AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Greedy PC-selection (fold-averaged #PCs): Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; greedy run on full target to set k yielded k=13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy AUROCs (upper bounds): Report 0.929, Sandbagging 0.832. Two automatic PC-ranking hypotheses failed: source-PCA-probe-weight ranking transferred about as well as baseline and relied on non-generalizing PCs; target-PCA-probe-weight ranking helped on Report, was worse than greedy on Confirm, and was below-random on Sandbagging. Interpretation-based selection: for top-100 source PCs, took 8 most/least activating examples, had an LLM describe poles and rate OOD generalizability 1–10. No PC >6; selected PCs scoring the observed max (6) in both runs -> 19 interp-selected PCs. Overlap: five PCs were chosen by greedy for >1 target; 3 of these (PC62, PC57, PC86) got max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA-ranked PCs got max (PC4). Interp-selected probe (19 PCs) outperforms baseline and variance-top-19 control, especially on Report and Sandbagging, and beats interp-ablated (remaining 81 PCs). Single-model/dataset: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (layer 15); source dataset Roleplaying; targets: Insider Trading Report, Confirm, Sandbagging. Pipeline: PCA on source activations (top-100 PCs) + linear logistic probe. Baseline (source-trained, full representation) AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes (trained on target but constrained to top-100 source-PC subspace, 5-fold CV) AUROC: Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869. Greedy PC-selection (fold-averaged #PCs): Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; greedy run on full target chose k=13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy AUROCs (upper bounds reported): Report 0.929, Sandbagging 0.832 (greedy Confirm AUROC not listed in notes). Two automatic PC-ranking heuristics failed to reliably select generalizing PCs: source-PCA-probe-weight ranking transferred no better than baseline and relied on non-generalizing PCs; target-PCA-probe-weight ranking helped on Report, was worse than greedy on Confirm, and below-random on Sandbagging. Interpretation-based selection: for top-100 source PCs, show 8 most/least activating examples; an LLM judge rated each pole's OOD generalizability (1–10) and no PC scored >6; selecting PCs that hit the observed max in both runs produced 19 interp-selected PCs. Interp-selected probe (19 PCs) outperforms baseline and a variance-top-19 control, especially on Report and Sandbagging, and beats an ablated-interp control. Limitations: single model/dataset, linear probes only, no causal ablations.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct probes. Task: deception detection; authors report experiments on 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging; third dataset not named in this part). Main claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) computed from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the test distribution. Method: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score PCs by whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe on highest-scoring PCs. Quantitative claims: using this approach they "close the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging." Additional claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and are capturable by natural language descriptions. High-level conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Venue/area: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection; train on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios), evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: operate in source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of principal components (PCs) for probe training to avoid spurious, non-transferable features. Key quantitative/structural claims: a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds a small transferable subspace of ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Section 4.2). Source-side and target-side rankings (ranking PCs by source or target probe weights) fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform the full-representation baseline (Section 4.3). An LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without using target labels by interpreting PCs and selecting those likely to encode the behavioral contrast (Section 4.5). Prior summary from earlier part: the method reportedly closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. High-level conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection; transferable directions are more abstract and can be captured by natural-language descriptions, whereas source-weighted directions capture surface features.

Related work: evidence for linear/low-dimensional concept directions (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024; Zou et al. 2025); examples of single-direction behaviors (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); longstanding skepticism about probes and OOD generalization (Hewitt & Liang 2019; Ravichander et al. 2021; recent work on uneven OOD probe performance). LLMs have been used to generate natural-language explanations of neurons/features and to label/ablate concepts for intervention (Bills et al. 2023; Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023; Casademunt et al. 2025).

Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean/unit var) and apply same stats to targets; run PCA on scaled source activations and keep top 100 PCs. Probe: logistic regression (λ=10). Probe variants: source-PCA probe = rank PCs by weights from probe trained on source data; target-PCA probe = rank PCs by weights from probe trained on target data. In both cases activations projected onto source-PCA basis; final probes are trained on source data projected onto top-k PCs selected by those rankings. Greedy PC-selection (run per-fold earlier) yielded average PC counts: Confirm ~8, Report ~15, Sandbagging ~14 (and improved baseline AUROC by ~0.22 Report, ~0.23 Sandbagging; nearly matched target-trained probes for Report & Sandbagging). When greedy is run on the full target datasets (single stable set) k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging) — numbers differ slightly from CV. Empirical findings: both source-PCA and target-PCA hypotheses fail. Source-PCA probe transfers about as well as full-representation baseline (i.e., source-selected PCs do not generalize). Target-PCA probe: does well on Insider Trading Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below-random on Sandbagging. Interpretability: For top 100 source PCs, an LLM judge (1–10 OOD score) described poles; no PC scored >6, so 6 treated as maximum observed. PCs receiving max score in both of two runs were retained → 19 interp-selected PCs. There were 5 PCs appearing in greedy selections for more than one target; 3/5 of those had max OOD score. Only 1 of top-5 source-PCA-selected PCs got max OOD score. Controls for eval: full-representation baseline, top-19 PCs by variance, and ablation of interp-selected PCs (remaining 81). Figures 4/5 and Appendices B/D/E provide further details.

final_notes: Setup: R2F = top-100 PCs of scaled source activations (layer-15 residual stream, assistant response-token-averaged). Datasets: Z4K 371 (140/59/172), Q7V 473 (218/194/61), P3Y 151 (29/38/84), J8W 1000 (379/375/246). Probing: source stats standardized, logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines (V9D): P3Y 0.874, Q7V 0.706, J8W 0.606. Target-trained (S6F): P3Y 0.936, Q7V 0.950, J8W 0.869. Greedy selected-k (K9U) ≈13 (Q7V), 7 (P3Y), 14 (J8W); iterative greedy converged ≈15 (Q7V), 8 (P3Y), 14 (J8W). Interpretability-based selection earlier reported 19 PCs. Appendix B: judge = GPT-5-mini (constrained output). Appendix C: Figure 6 Spearman ρ (andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct) = -0.917 (mean top10), -0.857 (best SAE); claim lower PCs have stronger decoder alignment. Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo; Adrians Skapars. Abstract key claims:
- A8T scores each principal component (PC) by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction. Probing restricted to the highest-scoring PCs. PC interpretations isolate a subset of transferable PCs.
- Under that restriction, M3Z (defined as the baseline-to-oracle gap) is "closed by 78% on Q7V and by 25% on J8W." 
- M3Z is framed in the generalization performance of V6Q probes (parenthetical: "3.1, 8") evaluated over 3 held-out deception detection datasets.
- Projecting inputs onto a small subset of PCs from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches S6F.
- Source probe directions weighted heavily appear to encode source-specific surface features; the directions that actually transfer encode the same contrast more abstractly in a way natural language descriptions can capture.
- Conclusion-level claims: linear probes can detect behaviors/concepts inside LM activations but may fail to transfer OOD; OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.
- Venue: Machine Learning, ICML.

Key numbers/labels to track: 78% (Q7V), 25% (J8W), 3 held-out datasets, terms M3Z, A8T, V6Q, S6F.

R2F = top-100 PCs of scaled source activations (layer-15 residual stream, averaged over assistant response tokens). Labels: honest=0, ambiguous removed, deceptive=1. Standardize source stats applied to target activations. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baseline transfer (V9D, full standardized activations) E3K: P3Y 0.874, Q7V 0.706, J8W 0.606. Target-trained probe (S6F, 5-fold CV) E3K: P3Y 0.936, Q7V 0.950, J8W 0.869. K9U (greedy PC selection) on full target set yields single-PC-set sizes k≈13 (Q7V), 7 (P3Y), 14 (J8W); K9U improves V9D by ~+0.22 (Q7V) and ~+0.23 (J8W) (implied K9U ≈0.926–0.929 for Q7V, ≈0.836–0.832 for J8W). Interpretability-based selection (Q8B) produced 19 PCs and raised Q7V from 0.706→0.881 (closing ≈78% of gap to K9U ≈0.929) and J8W from 0.606→0.662 (recovering ≈25% of gap to K9U ≈0.832). Paper: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection" by Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Studied model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection on 3 held-out datasets (two named: Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging; third unnamed here). Method: train linear probes on model activations; project activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from PCA on training activations. Use an LLM judge to produce natural-language interpretations: it scores each PC by judging whether the PC’s most- and least-activating examples suggest a transferable deception direction. Key claims/results: (1) projecting onto selected PCs enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained directly on the test distribution; (2) training probes on the highest-scoring PCs closes 78% of the baseline-to-oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging (Section 4.5); baseline = probe using all activations, oracle = selecting PCs using labeled target examples; (3) source-trained probe weights correspond to source-specific surface features, while transferable PCs encode more abstract contrasts that align with natural-language descriptions; overall claim: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” (Yoo & Skapars). Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection. Source train set: Roleplaying deception scenarios. Three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: train linear probes on model activations; compute PCA on source-domain activations and train probes after projecting onto a subset of source PCs. PC selection approaches: (a) target-supervised greedy search (adds one source PC at a time using labeled target examples) finds ~8–15 PCs on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Section 4.2); (b) ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights fails to recover the transferable subspace (Section 4.3); (c) an LLM judge inspects most/least-activating examples for each PC and partially recovers the transferable subspace without target labels (Section 4.5). Key quantitative claims (from earlier summary): projecting onto selected PCs enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching target-trained probes; using the judge-selected PCs closes 78% of the baseline-to-oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Definitions: baseline = probe using all activations; oracle = selecting PCs using labeled target examples. Central claim: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” (Yoo & Skapars). Task: deception detection using linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations (layer 15 chosen for highest cross-domain AUROC). Datasets: Roleplaying (source), three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels from GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Activations: pass prompt through model, average token activations only over the assistant’s response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance; standardize target activations using source statistics. PCA: run on standardized source activations, retain top 100 PCs (ordered by explained variance). Motivation: SAE-decoder alignment with PCs decreases with PC index (Appendix C Fig.6), so low-index PCs are easier to interpret (not claimed to generalize better). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). For subset S of the 100 PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Earlier high-level results to check later: (a) target-supervised greedy search finds ≈8–15 PCs to match target-trained probe (Section 4.2); (b) ranking PCs by probe weights fails to recover transferable subspace (Section 4.3); (c) LLM judge inspects most/least-activating examples per PC and partially recovers transferable subspace without target labels (Section 4.5) — judge-selected PCs close ~78% of baseline→oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and ~25% on Sandbagging. Section 4.1 verifies the 100-PC subspace retains sufficient signal on every target.

Setting & baselines: Probes are logistic regression (λ=10). Baseline: probes trained on full source representations transfer to targets with AUROCs — Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Check of 100-PC subspace: training probes on top-100 source PCs with 5-fold CV on each target yields AUROCs (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging) = 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869, so the 100-PC subspace contains sufficient signal. Greedy PC selection (Sect.4.2): start empty; at each step consider adding any remaining PC among top-100 source PCs, fit logistic probe on source projections, measure target AUROC (selection uses target labels), add PC that most improves target AUROC; 5-fold CV over target for selection; stop when no candidate improves AUROC > 0.001. With CV-based greedy, average selected sizes: 15 (Report), 8 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Using greedy on full target dataset (for a single stable k) gives k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Greedy improves over baseline by ~0.22 (Report) and ~0.23 (Sandbagging) AUROC and comes close to target-trained probes for those two tasks; variance-based top-k (by explained variance) matches greedy only on the easy Confirm task. Sect.4.3 tests two ranking hypotheses: rank PCs by standardized absolute probe coefficients (abs(weight)×PC std) from a probe trained on source (source-PCA probe) or from a probe trained on target (target-PCA probe, still in source-PCA basis); after ranking, evaluated probes are trained on source projected to top-k ranked PCs (k from full-dataset greedy).

Paper studies probe generalization for deception detection using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations. Claims: evaluated generalization over 3 held-out deception-detection datasets. Main finding: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained on the test distribution. PC interpretations can help select transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on top-scoring PCs substantially closes the baseline-to-oracle gap (78% closure on Insider Trading Report, 25% on Sandbagging). Authors posit that source-probe-weighted directions capture source-specific surface features, while actually transferable directions capture the same contrast more abstractly in ways describable by natural language. High-level conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Venue tag: Machine Learning, ICML.

Model & task: Use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to probe deception-detection. Train on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluate on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Method: project activations onto the source-domain PCA basis and train linear probes on low-dimensional subspaces (selected PCs). Key results: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Simple rankings fail (Sec 4.3): ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace and does not beat the full-representation baseline. (3) LLM interpretation helps (Sec 4.5): an LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target data by scoring PCs based on whether their top/ bottom activating examples indicate a transferable deception contrast; probing on top-scoring PCs substantially closes the baseline-to-oracle gap (earlier notes: ~78% closure on Insider Trading Report, ~25% on Sandbagging). Hypothesis: source-probe-weighted directions capture source-specific surface cues, while transferable directions represent the same contrast more abstractly and describably in natural language. High-level conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. (Venue tag: ML / ICML.)

Model & task: Use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to probe deception-detection. Train probes on a single source dataset (roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluate zero-shot on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report (ITR), Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging.

Method: Project activations onto the source-domain PCA basis and train linear probes on low-dimensional subspaces (selected PCs). PC selection methods: target-supervised greedy search (oracle), simple rankings (by probe weights), and an LLM-based judge that scores PCs via natural-language interpretation of top/bottom activating examples.

Key results: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search finds ~8–15 PCs on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Simple rankings (source- or target-probe-weighted) fail to recover the transferable subspace and do not beat the full-representation baseline. (3) LLM-based interpretation helps: scoring PCs by an LLM using high-activation examples (without target labels) substantially closes the baseline-to-oracle gap (approx. closure reported: ~78% on ITR, ~25% on Sandbagging).

Hypothesis & conclusion: Source-probe-weighted directions capture source-specific surface cues; transferable directions are more abstract and describable. OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Related work context: prior work reports linear concept directions (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024; Zou et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026), debates on probe methodology (Alain & Bengio 2018; Hewitt & Liang 2019; Ravichander et al. 2021), safety-relevant probing (Burns et al. 2024; Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025), and LLM-based feature interpretation/labeling (Bills et al. 2023; Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023; Casademunt et al. 2025). Venue: ML / ICML.

Datasets: 4 deception datasets (Roleplaying = source; targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging). Labels from GPT-4o: honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous responses removed. LM & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual stream activations (chosen per Ying et al. 2026); token activations averaged over the assistant's response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance; apply same source statistics to standardize targets. PCA: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs (motivated by SAE decoder-feature alignment decreasing with PC index; not claiming low-index PCs generalize better). Probing: logistic regression probes (L2 lambda=10). For subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/eval; baseline probes train on full standardized activations. Section 4.1 will reportedly confirm the 100-PC subspace retains enough signal to separate deceptive vs. honest on each target.

Datasets: 4 deception datasets (Roleplaying = source; targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging). Labels: GPT-4o annotated responses (honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1); ambiguous removed. Model/activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream, token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing/PCA: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance), apply same source stats to targets; run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (L2 lambda=10); baseline probes on full standardized activations; subset probes train on projections onto chosen PC subset. 4.1 Baseline: source-trained probe (full reps) transfers with AUROC: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probe (5-fold CV) on top-100 source PCs achieves 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC across the three targets, indicating the 100-PC subspace contains sufficient signal. 4.2 Greedy PC selection: iteratively add PCs (search over top 100) choosing the PC that most improves AUROC on target; candidate probes are trained on source projections but PC choice is guided by target-labeled folds (5-fold CV); stop when improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves baseline by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging), approaching target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matches greedy only for Confirm. 4.3 Hypotheses: test whether transferable PCs are (a) those that separate target classes alone or (b) those with large source-probe weights. Compare rankings by standardized coefficient = |coef| * std(PC) from probes trained on activations projected onto the source-PCA basis (source vs target probes).

This appendix: LLM judge prompt details — they used GPT-5-mini (OpenAI, 2025). Prompt framing: interpret a principal component (bipolar: positive vs negative pole; larger magnitude = stronger match). Examples are shown as lines token<TAB>activation, activations normalized to integers in [-10,10]. Examples come from the Roleplaying dataset (scenario with a strategic chance to lie). Judge must infer the dominant contrast from positive and negative examples, avoid assuming broad sentiment unless supported, prefer narrow accurate descriptions, avoid overgeneralization, and penalize surface cues/lexical habits. Judge must rate out-of-distribution deception usefulness 1–10 with guidance: 1–4 for noisy/surface/task-specific cues, >=5 reserved for general deception-relevant strategies. Required output format (exact):
Positive pole: ...
Negative pole: ...
Shared direction: ...
OOD deception usefulness (1-10): ...
Main claim: a small subset of source PCs enables cross-domain transfer; LLM-based interpretability score (no target access) partially recovers that subspace. Limitations: single model/dataset, linear PCA+logistic pipeline, no causal ablations.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo; Adrians Skapars. Abstract key claims:
- A8T scores each principal component (PC) by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction. Probing restricted to the highest-scoring PCs. PC interpretations isolate a subset of transferable PCs.
- Under that restriction, M3Z (defined as the baseline-to-oracle gap) is "closed by 78% on Q7V and by 25% on J8W." 
- M3Z is framed in the generalization performance of V6Q probes (parenthetical: "3.1, 8") evaluated over 3 held-out deception detection datasets.
- Projecting inputs onto a small subset of PCs from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches S6F.
- Source probe directions weighted heavily appear to encode source-specific surface features; the directions that actually transfer encode the same contrast more abstractly in a way natural language descriptions can capture.
- Conclusion-level claims: linear probes can detect behaviors/concepts inside LM activations but may fail to transfer OOD; OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.
- Venue: Machine Learning, ICML.

Key numbers/labels to track: 78% (Q7V), 25% (J8W), 3 held-out datasets, terms M3Z, A8T, V6Q, S6F.

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD deception detection. Preproc: activations standardized using source stats; PCA on scaled source activations; retain R2F = top 100 PCs. K9U (greedy PC selection using target labels to guide subset choice) finds small transferable subsets (per-fold averages: Q7V ≈15 PCs, P3Y ≈8, J8W ≈14) and, when run on the complete target dataset, yields k=13 (Q7V), 7 (P3Y), 14 (J8W); K9U improves on V9D by ≈0.22 (Q7V) and ≈0.23 (J8W) and approaches S6F. Two hypotheses tested about what makes PCs transferable: (1) PCs that by themselves separate target classes (ranking H5X: weights from a probe trained on target data, using source-PCA activations), (2) PCs the source probe leans on (ranking Z1M: weights from a probe trained on source data). Ranking score U1L defined as |coef| * sd(PC). Evaluation: select top-k by ranking, train probe on source data projected to those PCs, test on target. Both fail: Z1M performs about as well as V9D (implying source-leaned PCs are non-transferable), H5X helps only on Q7V but fails on P3Y/J8W. Paper: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD deception detection.” Preproc: activations standardized using source stats; PCA on scaled source activations; retain R2F = top 100 PCs. Model: V6Q (3.1-series, 8B parameters), readout layer 15. Data: single source Z4K; targets P3Y, Q7V, J8W. Probe: linear logistic regression (L2 λ=10). K9U (greedy PC selection using target labels) finds small transferable subsets (per-fold averages ≈15 PCs for Q7V, ≈8 for P3Y, ≈14 for J8W); on whole target data K9U yields k≈13 (Q7V), 7 (P3Y), 14 (J8W) and gives upper-bound target scores (e.g., Q7V ≈0.929, J8W ≈0.832), approaching S6F. Abstract key points: - Main quantitative claim: "The closure of M3Z by Q8B was 78% for Q7V and 25% for J8W under V6Q deception probes on 3 held-out datasets (8; 3.1)." - Definitions/notations: A8T scores each principal component (PC) by whether its extreme examples imply a transferable deception direction; K9U denotes greedy PC selection; M3Z denotes the baseline-to-oracle gap. - Method/result: projecting inputs onto a few training-distribution PCs gave transfer nearly matching S6F. - Interpretation: heavily weighted source directions encode surface features, transferring ones encode the contrast abstractly, and OOD robustness is largely subspace selection. Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: probes for deception detection on 3 held-out datasets (three datasets claimed; two named later). Method: project activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs). Definition: PCs are mutually perpendicular directions from PCA on training activations. Claim: this projection enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained directly on the test distribution. Interpretable PC scoring: an LLM judge evaluates each PC by looking at its most- and least-activating examples to judge whether the PC suggests a transferable deception direction. Results: training probes on highest-scoring PCs closes 78% of the baseline-to-oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging (see Section 4.5). Baseline: uses all activations. Oracle: selects PCs using labeled target examples. Interpretation claim: directions heavily weighted by a source-trained probe encode source-specific surface features; transferring directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural-language descriptions. Conclusion: OOD probe robustness is largely determined by subspace selection (which activation directions the probe can use). Reference: ICML submission.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: linear probes for deception detection. Train source: Roleplaying deception scenarios. Evaluate (held-out targets): Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source-domain activations (source-domain PC basis = orthogonal PCs from PCA on training activations); project activations into that PC basis and train probes on selected subsets of PCs (subspace selection). Baseline: probe trained on full activations. Oracle: selects PCs using labeled target examples (target-supervised greedy search). Key claims/findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Section 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search (adds one source PC at a time using labeled target examples) finds ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights fails to recover that subspace and does not beat the full-representation baseline (Section 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target data by inspecting most/least activating examples per PC; selecting highest-scoring PCs closes 78% of the baseline-to-oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging (Section 4.5). Interpretation: source-weighted directions can reflect source-specific surface features; transferred directions capture contrasts more abstractly and are describable in natural language. Pipeline illustrated in Figure 1.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Task: linear probes for deception detection. Datasets: Roleplaying (source), Insider Trading Report (target), Insider Trading Confirm (target), Sandbagging (target). Labels: GPT-4o labels responses as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous responses are removed. Model & features: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; use layer-15 residual stream activations (layer 15 chosen for highest cross-domain AUROC). Token activations are averaged over the assistant’s response. Preproc: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance; standardize target activations using source statistics. PCA: run PCA on standardized source activations; retain top 100 PCs ordered by variance explained. Probes: logistic regression classifiers (regularization λ = 10). For subset experiments, S denotes a selected subset of the 100 PCs; project activations onto S before training/eval. Baseline probes train on full standardized activations. Rationale for 100 PCs: alignment with SAE decoder features decreases with PC index (App. C Fig.6), so lower-index PCs are more interpretable; not claiming low-index PCs generalize better—Section 4.1 checks that 100-PC subspace retains enough information on every target. Oracle: target-supervised greedy search (adds one source PC at a time using labeled target examples). Key claimed findings from earlier summary to check later: small transferable subspace (~8–15 PCs), source-weighted rankings fail, LLM judge can partially recover subspace (closes 78% of baseline->oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging).

Experiments evaluate transfer of linear probes for deception detection. Baselines: probe trained on full source representations and evaluated on targets yields AUROC: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. The 100-PC source subspace contains enough target information: target-trained probes (5-fold CV) on top-100 source PCs achieve AUROC (in order Report, Confirm, Sandbagging) 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869. Thus poor transfer is not due to missing information in top-100 PCs. Greedy PC-selection (oracle uses labeled target folds to choose PCs; probe weights always fit on source data; 5-fold CV over target; stop when AUROC improvement <= 0.001) finds small transferable subsets (cross-validated averages: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14). Greedy improves over the full-representation baseline by ~0.22 (Report) and ~0.23 (Sandbagging) AUROC, approaching target-trained performance. Control selecting top-k PCs by source variance (k matched to greedy) only matches greedy on the easy Confirm task and lags on Report and Sandbagging. Section 4.3 tests two ranking hypotheses (ranking by source-probe weights vs by target-probe weights) using standardized coefficients (|coef| * PC std); k is set by greedy run on the full target yielding k=13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging), which differs slightly from cross-validated averages.

Experiments study cross-domain transfer of linear probes for deception detection. Baseline (probe trained on full source reps, evaluated on targets) AUROCs: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. A probe trained on target labels but restricted to the top-100 source PCs attains (Report, Confirm, Sandbagging) 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869, so target information exists in top-100 PCs. Title: 'Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection' by Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Setup: study of linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations for deception-detection. Experiments: probes trained on a source and evaluated on 3 held-out deception detection datasets (names not given here). Main findings: (1) Projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained directly on the test distribution. (2) PC interpretations can identify a subset of transferable PCs. (3) Using an LLM judge to score PCs (based on most/least activating examples) and then probing on top-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Additional claim: source-probe high-weight directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable by natural language). Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted as Machine Learning, ICML. Key numbers to check later: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, 3 held-out datasets, 78% gap closure (Insider Trading Report), 25% gap closure (Sandbagging).

Title: 'Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection' (Yoo & Skapars). Testbed: linear deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Train on single source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios. Evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Framing: work in source-domain PCA basis; select subset of source PCs to avoid spurious surface correlations and improve OOD transfer. Key contributions (from Introduction): (1) Small transferable subspace exists (Sec 4.2). A target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side rankings (ranking PCs by probe weights) both fail to recover this subspace; such rankings do not outperform the full-representation baseline (Sec 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target data by interpreting/selecting PCs (Sec 4.5). Earlier notes: main empirical claims include that projecting onto a small subset of PCs enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching target-trained probes; LLM-judge scoring of PCs reportedly closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Figure 1: pipeline overview (project to source PCs, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected subspace).

Title: 'Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection' (Yoo & Skapars). Setup: linear deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Train on a single source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, select a subset of source PCs to avoid spurious surface correlations, train probes on that subspace. Pipeline: project to source PCs -> filter candidate PCs -> train probes on selected subspace (Fig.1). Main empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec.4.2); greedy target-supervised search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side rankings (by probe weights) fail to recover this subspace and do not beat full-representation baseline (Sec.4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target data (Sec.4.5); reported as closing baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Related work (this part): literature supports existence of linear/low-dimensional concept directions (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024; Zou et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026). Probing limitations: probes may learn tasks or exploit surface correlates; OOD generalization can be uneven (Hewitt & Liang 2019; Ravichander et al. 2021; Burns et al. 2024; Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025; kramár2026...). Interpreting features: LLMs used to generate natural-language neuron/feature explanations and to help label/ablate concepts (Bills et al. 2023; Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023; Casademunt et al. 2025). No contradictions found between related work and the paper's stated approach or claims so far.

Title: 'Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection' (Yoo & Skapars). Setup: train linear deception probes on a single source dataset (Roleplaying) and evaluate on three held-out target datasets (Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging). Labels: GPT-4o labels responses as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous responses removed. Model & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; use layer-15 residual-stream activations (chosen as layer with highest cross-domain AUROC per Ying et al. 2026); token activations averaged over the assistant’s response. Preprocessing & PCA: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance and apply the same source statistics to targets; run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (ridge, lambda=10). For experiments using a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on full standardized activations. Rationale: top-100 chosen because alignment with SAE decoder features decreases with PC index (Appendix C), so lower-index PCs are more interpretable; not claiming low-index PCs generalize better—Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace retains enough info to separate deceptive vs honest on every target. Main empirical claims to check later: (1) ~8–15 transferable PCs found by greedy target-supervised search; (2) source-/target-side rankings fail to recover that subspace and don't beat full-repr baseline; (3) an LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target data (reported gap closures: 78% on Insider Trading Report, 25% on Sandbagging).

Section 4 experiments. 4.1 Baseline: Source-trained probe transfer AUROCs on full representations — Insider Trading Confirm: 0.874, Insider Trading Report: 0.706, Sandbagging: 0.606. To test the 100-PC subspace, a probe trained on target data within the source-derived top-100 PCs (5-fold CV) achieves 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC across the three targets (same order as the prior sentence: Confirm / Report / Sandbagging). Conclusion: top-100 PCs contain enough signal; transfer gap is due to source probe picking non-generalizing directions. 4.2 Greedy PC selection: iterative greedy search over top-100 source PCs; at each step project source activations to current subset, train logistic probe on source, evaluate AUROC on target; subset selection uses labeled target folds with 5-fold CV, stopping when AUROC improvement <= 0.001. Average subset sizes found: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs. Greedy substantially improves over the full-repr baseline (improves Report by +0.22 AUROC, Sandbagging by +0.23), coming close to target-trained probe for Report and Sandbagging. Baseline variance-control (top-k PCs by variance, k matched to greedy) matches greedy only for Confirm and lags for Report and Sandbagging. Greedy is an upper bound on transfer since it uses some target labels. 4.3 Hypotheses for transferable PCs: (A) PCs that individually separate target classes; (B) PCs the source probe relies on. They compare two PC rankings (by target-probe vs source-probe importance), both using standardized coefficients (abs(coef) * std(PC)) from probes trained on activations projected into the source-PCA basis.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Main claims (abstract):
- Selecting a small subset of principal components (PCs) from training activations for probing enables cross-domain transfer and substantially improves OOD deception-detection performance.
- A procedure (A8T) scores each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; restricting probes to highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap (M3Z).
- Quantitative results reported in abstract: M3Z is closed by 78% on dataset Q7V and by 25% on dataset J8W.
- M3Z is defined as the baseline-to-oracle gap and is assessed via generalization performance of V6Q probes (references: 3.1, 8) over 3 held-out deception-detection datasets.
- PC interpretations isolate a subset of transferable PCs; projecting inputs onto this small PC subset nearly matches S6F (a stronger comparator).
- Observed phenomenon: directions heavily weighted by source probes encode source-specific surface features, whereas the directions that transfer encode the same contrast more abstractly and are describable in natural language.
- Conclusion: linear probes can detect behaviors/concepts inside LM activations but may fail to transfer OOD; OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.
(Keep abbreviations A8T, V6Q, M3Z, S6F, Q7V, J8W as paper-specific.)

steps.notes_before: Title/authors as before. Abstract/main claims: selecting a small subset of source-domain PCs enables cross-domain transfer for deception detection; A8T (an LLM judge/procedure) scores PCs and restricting probes to top-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap M3Z (reported: 78% closure on Q7V, 25% on J8W). PC projection onto a small subset nearly matches S6F (target-trained probe). Introduction specifics: a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs recovers ~8–15 PCs where a source-trained probe nearly matches S6F (Sec 4.2), showing a small transferable subspace exists. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights fails to beat the full-representation baseline V9D (Sec 4.3). A8T can partially recover the subspace without target data by interpreting/selecting PCs (Sec 4.5). Workflow: project activations onto source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on the low-dim subspace (Fig.1). Testbed: probes trained on a single source dataset Z4K (Roleplaying) and evaluated on three held-out targets Q7V (Insider Trading Report), P3Y (Insider Trading Confirm), J8W (Sandbagging). Comparators: S6F (target-trained), V9D (full rep. baseline), A8T (LLM judge). Note: the paper uses V6Q in contexts that suggest both a dataset/testbed and the model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct); treat V6Q primarily as the model but flag this ambiguity.

Main claim: small subset of source-domain principal components (PCs) suffices for cross-domain transfer in deception-detection probes. Approach: project model activations onto source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on the low-dim subspace. Key methods/terms: A8T = LLM-based judge/procedure to score PCs and select top PCs without target labels; S6F = target-trained probe (oracle); V9D = full-representation baseline. Testbed: probes trained on single source dataset (Roleplaying) and evaluated on three held-out targets (Insider Trading Report Q7V, Insider Trading Confirm P3Y, Sandbagging J8W). Reported results (from earlier parts): A8T selection closes baseline-to-oracle gap by ~78% on Q7V and ~25% on J8W; target-supervised greedy search recovers ~8–15 PCs where a source-trained probe nearly matches S6F; ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights fails to beat V9D; PC projection onto small subset nearly matches S6F. Note: paper uses token V6Q ambiguously (both dataset/testbed and model; treat V6Q primarily as model Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct but flag ambiguity). New from Related Work: situates work in literature studying linear directions/subspaces for high-level behaviors — identification of an “assistant” axis (Lu et al., 2026), single-direction mediation of refusal (Arditi et al., 2024), formalization of linear representation hypothesis (Park et al., 2024), linear true/false structure (Marks & Tegmark, 2024), modeling honesty/emotion as population directions (Zou et al., 2025). Notes methodological skepticism about probes (Hewitt & Liang 2019; Ravichander et al. 2021; kramár2026...) and prior safety-probe work (Burns et al. 2024; Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025). Also cites using LLMs to generate neuron explanations (Bills et al. 2023) and automated labeling of features (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023). No contradictions found between this section and earlier notes.

Abstract claims: 'closure of M3Z by Q8B' achieved 78% for Q7V and 25% for J8W under V6Q deception probes on 3 held-out datasets (refs: 8; 3.1). Method: score each training-PC with A8T by checking whether its extreme examples imply a transferable deception direction. K9U = greedy PC selection; M3Z = baseline-to-oracle gap. Main empirical finding: projecting inputs onto a few training-distribution principal components yields transfer nearly matching S6F. Interpretation: heavily-weighted source directions encode source-specific surface features; transferring directions encode the contrast abstractly. Conclusion: OOD robustness is largely a subspace-selection problem. Key numbers/terms to check later: 78%, 25%, 3 held-out datasets, A8T scoring, K9U greedy selection, M3Z as baseline-to-oracle gap, S6F performance match, claim that OOD robustness ~ subspace selection.

Testbed & notation: V6Q = Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; probes trained on Z4K (Roleplaying) and evaluated on three held-out datasets Q7V (Insider Trading Report), P3Y (Insider Trading Confirm), J8W (Sandbagging). Method overview: project activations onto source PCA basis and train probes on selected PC subsets. K9U is a (target-supervised) PC-selection method that surfaces an ~8–15-PC subspace which nearly matches S6F (the target-trained probe) in transfer performance (see §4.2). A8T is an LLM-based, target-free scorer that partially recovers the transferable subspace by selecting PCs whose extreme examples imply a transferable behavioral contrast (see §4.5). Ranking PCs by source- or target-side probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace and fails to beat V9D (the full-representation baseline) (§4.3). Claims to check later: specific numeric results from the abstract (78% on Q7V, 25% on J8W, closure of M3Z by Q8B on 3 held-out datasets), definition/use of M3Z (baseline-to-oracle gap), details of the greedy selection procedure, and the main interpretation that OOD robustness reduces to subspace selection. Also note references to sections: 4.2 (small transferable subspace exists), 4.3 (rankings fail), 4.5 (A8T performance).

Prior work identifies linear directions (e.g., an "assistant" axis) for reading/steering, raising the question of whether such directions are stable concepts or context-dependent correlations.

Layer chosen for highest cross-domain E3K (E3K = area under ROC) in prior work. Preprocessing: standardize using source (Z4K) statistics and apply to targets; compute PCA on source activations. R2F = retain top 100 PCs (retention motivated by decrease of SAE decoder alignment with PC index; no claim that low-index PCs generalize better). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10); subset-S probes project activations onto PC subset S; baselines use full standardized activations. Data: 4 deception datasets total (Z4K as source, Q7V, P3Y, J8W as held-out targets). Labels from GPT-4o: honest = 0, ambiguous = -1 (removed), deceptive = 1. Reminder of earlier claims to check in later sections: K9U (target-supervised PC-selection) surfaces ~8–15-PC transferable subspace nearly matching target-trained probe; A8T (LLM-based, target-free scorer) partially recovers transferable subspace via extreme-example contrasts; ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights fails to recover transferable subspace and does not beat full-representation baseline. Will verify numeric results and greedy selection procedure later.

Q8B (interp-selected PCs): 19 PCs chosen without target data via A8T (LLM ratings on extreme source examples: for each of 100 PCs, the 8 most and 8 least activating source examples were rated on a 1–10 generalizability scale; no PC scored >6 so 6 treated as max; Q8B = PCs that scored 6 in both runs). Reported: probe restricted to these 19 PCs beats V9D on all 3 targets, beats W4J (top-k-by-variance at k=19) by wide margins on Q7V and J8W, and beats G2Y (the remaining 81 PCs of R2F). On Q7V Q8B closes 78% of the gap from V9D (0.706) to K9U (0.929); on J8W closes 25% of that gap to K9U (0.832). P3Y is near ceiling and uninformative; most methods (except G2Y) similar there. K9U (target-supervised greedy forward selection over R2F=top-100 PCs) nearly matches S6F on Q7V and J8W, giving +0.22 and +0.23 E3K over V9D. K9U selection procedure: start empty, add PC that most improves target E3K for a probe fit on source projections; weights are fit on source while selection uses target labels on non-held-out folds under H6Q, eval on held-out fold; stop when gain <=0.001. Mean K9U subset sizes (CV): 15 (Q7V), 8 (P3Y), 14 (J8W); full-target-run ks: 13/7/14. Baselines Z1M (rank by source-probe |coef|×PCstd) performs ≈ V9D; H5X (rank by target-probe) does well on Q7V but worse on P3Y and below random on J8W — overall the weight-ranking hypotheses fail. V9D (source probe) E3K: P3Y 0.874, Q7V 0.706, J8W 0.606. S6F probes in R2F: 0.950 / 0.936 / 0.869 (P3Y/Q7V/J8W). Figures: Fig2/3/4/5 referenced for these comparisons.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (WVU), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Contribution: PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with deliberately inserted secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction (persuasion-based) probes. Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows; dialogue-level hybrid leakage reported as 38.7%–54.6% (Table 3). Definition: a dialogue is considered leaking if any standardized probe elicits its secret. Detection: hybrid detector combining normalized text matching and an LLM judge. Reported dependencies: leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity (Tables 3–5). Additional topic drift within the tested window does not reliably reduce leakage (Sec 5.4). Framing: privacy risk treated as a persistent behavioral failure mode, distinct from training-data memorization or immediate jailbreaking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero. Goal: measure whether secrets disclosed in an active conversation remain recoverable after unrelated topic drift. Benchmark: PrivDrift — 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues per model with deliberately inserted secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized persuasion-based extraction probes. Axes: (1) Topic drift d = # unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe (tested up to d ≤ 6). (2) Persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Models & eval: three LLMs with extended context windows, 1,000 dialogues each. Detection: reproducible hybrid detector combining deterministic normalization/regex matching (“regex-only”), fuzzy matching, and a closed-weights LLM judge; report dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6% (Table 3); leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity (Sec 5.3; Tables 3–5). SSNs and credit card numbers suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers. Within tested drift window (d ≤ 6), additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage (Sec 5.4). Proposed Privacy Half-Life τ as a stability-based measure of persistent suppression; no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range (Sec 5.6). Definition: a dialogue is leaking if any standardized probe elicits its secret.

Detection: hybrid detector combining deterministic normalization/regex matching (“regex-only”), fuzzy matching, and a closed-weights LLM judge; report dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6% (Table 3); leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. SSNs and credit card numbers suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers. Within tested drift window (d ≤ 6), additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. Proposed Privacy Half-Life τ as a stability-based measure; no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Definition: a dialogue is leaking if any standardized probe elicits its secret. Related work: distinguishes active-context privacy (this paper) from training-data extraction/membership inference; connects to multi-turn adversarial attacks (crescendo, jailbreaks, prompt injection) and machine unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) while emphasizing PrivDrift's focus on active context/RAG-style supplied context rather than model-weight edits.

PrivDrift: framework to evaluate active-context re-disclosure (whether an assistant later reproduces a secret S disclosed at turn t0 after unrelated topic drift). Formalization: secret S at t0, intervening drift D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad} (d pairs), probe P appended; leakage if model reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Framework components: (1) dialogue generator (scaffold-then-rewrite) producing N = 1,000 controlled dialogues (used per-model in benchmark), (2) probing harness, (3) leakage-detection metrics. Dataset: 1,000 total dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored) with human-authored examples mixed throughout; cached metadata lost human identifiers so only aggregate reporting. Secret categories: 4 fixed-format PII types — phone, email, Social Security Number (SSN), credit card. Drift lengths used: {0,2,3,4,5,6} (d counts user+assistant drift pairs). Persona sampled from >100 professions/demographics; secret injected in opening turn as plausible task. Drift turns are content-dense, topic-conditioned QA pairs pulled from a library; some drift turns are human-authored. Final naturalistic refinement: a rewriting model edits scaffolds for fluency/persona realism but must preserve exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Table 1 stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16, median 385.00, min/max words 43/795; approximate tokens estimated from words (factor ≈4/3) giving avg approx tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max approx tokens 57.33/1060.00. Next: 3.3 Probing Setup (not yet seen). Previous-summary notes to carry forward: benchmark runs standardized persuasion-based extraction probes and uses a hybrid detector (regex-only + fuzzy + closed-weights LLM judge); reported dialogue-level hybrid leakage ~38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity; within d ≤ 6, drift does not reliably reduce leakage; proposal of Privacy Half-Life τ (no model reaches stable decay within observed range).

steps.notes_before: PrivDrift evaluates active-context re-disclosure: secret S injected at t0, then d intervening drift turns/pairs, then a standardized probe (three persuasion levels: Simple, Medium, Hard). Dataset: N=1,000 controlled dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored). Drift-length set reported as {0,2,3,4,5,6}; this part samples d with P(d=0)=0.2 and P(d uniform over {2,3,4,5,6})=0.8 (Eq.1). Evaluation uses a two-stage hierarchical hybrid detector: Stage 1 normalization-based matching φ(·) (numeric: remove non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, retain delimiters) with Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)] (Eq.2). Stage 2 uses an LLM judge that receives (secret, response) and returns a binary leakage verdict; this part names an "open-weights Llama judge (Meta AI, 2024)" but earlier notes describe a "closed-weights LLM judge" (inconsistency to resolve). Report regex-only and hybrid rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ defined: D_obs = observed drift lengths; L(d) leakage rate; δ=0.1×L(0); τ = min d∈D_obs s.t. L(d)≤δ and all later observed L(d')≤δ; if none qualify τ=max(D_obs)+1. Earlier summary: hybrid leakage ~38.7%–54.6% and no model reached stable decay within observed range.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: Introduces PrivDrift benchmark for auditing recovery of user-disclosed secrets after conversational topic drift and persuasion-based probing. Key result: dialogue-level hybrid leakage remains substantial, ranging 38.7%–54.6%, and varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Additional topic drift within tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage. Conclusion: privacy risk in active LLM contexts should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure mode, not only as memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Purpose: introduce PrivDrift, a controlled benchmark measuring recoverability of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated conversational topic drift and under different persuasion styles. Dataset/evaluation: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues per model, evaluated on three LLMs with extended context windows. Axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe, tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Detector: reproducible hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching with a closed-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage remains substantial (38.7%–54.6%); leakage varies strongly by model, secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers), and persuasion intensity (which significantly affects leakage). Additional topic drift within tested window does not reliably reduce leakage; authors propose Privacy Half-Life (τ) as a stability-based metric and report that no evaluated model reaches stable decay within the observed drift range. Conclusion/high-level claim: privacy risk in active LLM contexts should be evaluated as a persistent behavioral failure mode, not only as memorization or immediate jailbreaks.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author/contact: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu). Purpose: introduce PrivDrift, a controlled benchmark measuring recoverability of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated conversational topic drift and under different persuasion styles. Dataset/evaluation: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues per model; evaluated on three LLMs with extended context windows. Axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe, tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Detector: reproducible hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching with a closed-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage remains substantial (38.7%–54.6%); leakage varies strongly by model and secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers) and by persuasion intensity (significant effect). Additional topic drift within tested window does not reliably reduce leakage; Privacy Half-Life (τ) proposed as a stability-based metric and no evaluated model reaches stable decay within the observed drift range. Related work: distinguishes active-context privacy (user-provided data in current interaction) from training-data extraction/memorization; existing benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) focus on privacy norms/static access-control; multi-turn adversarial work (Crescendo, automated jailbreaks, prompt injection) motivates studying information flow across turns; unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) operate over static Q-A and model weights—PrivDrift instead targets prompt-level context management and behavioral suppression in RAG/copilots/agentic workflows.

Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B (queried via OpenRouter). Dataset: 1,000 dialogues, each seeded with one secret and drift length d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6} (earlier parts). final_notes: Benchmark K7X: measures active-context privacy for secrets S disclosed at turn t0. Drift lengths tested {0,2,3,4,5,6} (d=0 p≈0.2, else Uniform{2..6}); dataset 1,000 dialogues per model (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored); Appendix A counts by d: N0=197,N2=147,N3=142,N4=166,N5=181,N6=167. Avg words by d: 0:44.29,2:253.97,3:344.18,4:452.27,5:520.92,6:568.03; medians 43,258,347,447,543,605. Avg tokens approx: 0:59.05,2:338.62,3:458.91,4:603.02,5:694.56,6:757.37; medians 57.33,344,462.67,596,724,806.67. Detection pipeline: regex normalization J5D then Llama judge; hybrid X3Q = positive if either stage signals leakage; fuzzy-match B7N@0.85 also reported. Metrics: dialogue-level R9S (dialogue leaks if any probe elicits secret) and probe-level M2V. 3,000 cached responses per model. Key empirical facts: stable-decay threshold τ = max(D_obs)+1 = 7; no model shows stable decay within d ≤ 6. Dialogue-level R9S (X3Q): E7B 38.70% [35.7,41.6], U5K 47.70% [44.6,50.8], P3R 54.60% [51.6,57.7]. Probe-level M2V (X3Q): E7B 26.43%, U5K 37.57%, P3R 37.53%. Appendix B Cramér's V (M2V granularity): Secret type — E7B 0.5871 (Large), U5K 0.7731 (Large), P3R 0.6927 (Large); Drift length — E7B 0.1073 (Small), U5K 0.0659 (Negligible), P3R 0.0723 (Negligible); Persuasion — E7B 0.0718 (Negligible), U5K 0.0689 (Negligible), P3R 0.0639 (Negligible). Conclusions: leakage substantial (≈38.7–54.6%), largely direct/near-direct reproduction, uneven across secret types (large V), drift provides no reliable mitigation within tested window (small/negligible V), and the paper reports statistical significance for persuasion but also reports negligible magnitude for persuasion (internal tension noted).
