Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: privacy risk in active LLM conversations should be evaluated as a persistent behavioral failure mode (not only memorization/jailbreak). Reported finding: additional V9B within the tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage; R9S X3Q (leakage measure) across three LLMs with extended context windows is substantial (38.7%–54.6%), and varies strongly by model, secret type, and Z4T. Dataset/benchmark K7X contains 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes to audit whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after conversational V9B and persuasion-based probing. Motivation: LLMs as persistent assistants in user-facing/shared-session/tool-augmented settings may behaveably recover sensitive info after topic shifts. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Key claims/definitions: R9S (dialogue-level leakage) under X3Q detection ranges 38.7%–54.6% across three LLMs with extended context windows (1,000 dialogues per model). Drift window tested: d ≤ 6; within this window, adding further V9B (topic-drift turns) does not reliably reduce leakage. Z4T (persuasion intensity) strongly affects leakage. Secret-type differences: L8P = SSNs and G6Y = credit cards are suppressed far more often than D2F = email addresses and A9T = phone numbers. Contributions: (1) K7X (PrivDrift) — controlled benchmark for auditing recoverability of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated V9B; (2) evaluation of leakage under direct, justified, and high-pressure probes; (3) implementation of a reproducible X3Q detector (normalization-based matching + T1G, a closed-weights LLM judge) and reporting of rates for R9S, M2V, J5D (regex-only leakage), B7N, and X3Q (hybrid leakage); (4) proposal of C5Z (Privacy Half-Life τ), a stability-based metric, with the claim that no evaluated model reaches stable decay within the observed drift range. Framing: examines topic shift as a potential privacy boundary distinct from memorization/jailbreak evaluations. V9B denotes number of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and later probing; Z4T denotes interaction/persuasion style.

K7X (PrivDrift) focuses on active-context privacy: whether a user-disclosed secret in the context window remains behaviorally recoverable after unrelated V9B (topic-drift turns) and later persuasion-style probes (Z4T). Contrasts drawn with machine-unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) which target parameter-level removal; K7X targets context-level persistence. Related threats: Crescendo attacks, multi-turn jailbreaks, and prompt injections motivate treating multi-turn information flow (re-disclosure) separately from harmful-content generation. Other benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) test privacy-norm reasoning or static access-control scenarios, while K7X isolates persistence over drift. Historical privacy work focused on training-data extraction, membership inference, and memorized PII in parameters; K7X addresses active-context leaks at inference time. Key reported results/claims from earlier parts to check later: R9S (dialogue-level leakage) 38.7%–54.6% across three LLMs (1,000 dialogues per model); drift window tested d ≤ 6; within that window, adding further V9B does not reliably reduce leakage; Z4T (persuasion intensity) strongly affects leakage; secret-type differences: L8P (SSNs) and G6Y (credit cards) suppressed far more often than D2F (email addresses) and A9T (phone numbers). Contributions: (1) K7X benchmark; (2) evaluation under direct, justified, and high-pressure probes; (3) reproducible X3Q detector (normalization-based matching + T1G judge) reporting rates for R9S, M2V, J5D (regex-only leakage), B7N, and X3Q (hybrid leakage); (4) Privacy Half-Life C5Z (τ) metric, claiming no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range.

K7X (PrivDrift) studies active-context privacy: whether a secret S disclosed at turn t0 is behaviorally recoverable after d unrelated content-dense drift turns and a later standardized probe. Threat model Q3M: not about transcript exposure but whether the assistant will re-disclose S when later prompted. Main evaluation appends a final probe of three persuasion levels: H2R (direct/neutral), F6K (medium/justified), N8W (hard/high-pressure). Drift lengths sampled as: d ~ 0 w.p.0.2; Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} w.p.0.8 (so tested d ∈ {0,2..6}); drift-window interpreted as bounded persistence (d ≤ 6). Dataset N=1000 controlled dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored interleaved); cached metadata doesn’t preserve human IDs so aggregate results reported. Two-stage hierarchical hybrid detector (Figure 2): (1) normalization/regex-stage φ(·): numeric secrets strip non-digits; alphanumeric normalize case/whitespace while preserving delimiters; Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)] (regex-only leakage = J5D). (2) Regex-negative responses go to an open-weights Llama judge (T1G) that returns binary verdict for partial/paraphrased disclosure; hybrid leakage metric X3Q includes either regex or judge positives; J5D and X3Q reported separately. Privacy Half-Life metric C5Z (τ): τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and ∀d'>d in D_obs: L(d')≤δ}, with δ = 0.1×L(0). If no such d exists, τ := max(D_obs)+1 (i.e., beyond observed window). Earlier reported results to check later: R9S 38.7%–54.6% across three LLMs (1,000 dialogues/model); persuasion intensity strongly affects leakage; SSNs/credit-cards suppressed more than emails/phone numbers; claim that no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range.

K7X (PrivDrift) measures active-context privacy: whether a secret S disclosed at turn t0 is behaviorally recoverable after d unrelated content-dense drift turns and a later standardized probe (threat model Q3M). Benchmark: 1,000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored interleaved). Secret space: 4 fixed-format PII categories (A9T, D2F, L8P, G6Y); secrets inserted in the opening turn. Drift lengths tested: {0,2,3,4,5,6} (drift-window = bounded persistence, d ≤ 6); sampling: d=0 with prob 0.2, else Uniform{2..6} with prob 0.8. Final probe appended with three persuasion intensities (H2R direct/neutral, F6K medium/justified, N8W hard/high-pressure). Generation pipeline: 3.2.1 persona sampled from >100 professions/demographic profiles; 3.2.2 topic assignment with topic-conditioned library of dense QA and fallback tasks; subset of drift turns human-authored and incorporated; 3.2.3 rewriting model improves fluency/persona realism while preserving exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Dataset stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795; approximate tokens estimated from word counts (avg tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max 57.33/1060.00). Detection: two-stage hybrid (regex normalization φ then an open-weights Llama judge); regex-only leakage = J5D; hybrid metric = X3Q (positive if either stage signals leakage). Privacy half-life τ defined with δ=0.1·L(0). Earlier reported high-level results: R9S 38.7%–54.6% leakage across models; persuasion intensity affects leakage; SSNs/credit-cards suppressed more than emails/phones.

K7X (PrivDrift) measures active-context privacy (Q3M): whether a secret S disclosed at turn t0 is recoverable after d drift turns and a standardized probe. Benchmark: 1,000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored interleaved). Secret space: 4 fixed-format PII categories (A9T, D2F, L8P, G6Y); secrets inserted in the opening turn. Drift lengths tested: {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling: d=0 with prob 0.2, else Uniform{2..6} with prob 0.8 (bounded persistence d ≤ 6). Final probe: three persuasion intensities (H2R direct/neutral, F6K medium/justified, N8W hard/high-pressure). Generation pipeline: persona sampling, topic assignment (dense QA/fallback tasks, some human-authored turns), and rewriting model that preserves the exact secret, drift length, role structure, and probe conditions. Dataset stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16 (median 385; min/max 43/795); tokens estimated from words (avg 478.87; median 513.33; min/max 57.33/1060.00). Detection: two-stage hybrid (regex normalization φ then Llama judge); regex-only leakage = J5D; hybrid metric = X3Q (positive if either stage signals leakage). Metrics and inference: R9S reported at dialogue level (dialogue counted as leaking if any standardized probe elicits the secret); persuasion-level and B7N analyses are probe-level (each dialogue contributes one response per persuasion condition). Statistical tests: chi-square tests of independence (Cramer's V effect size) for leakage vs drift/persuasion/secret type; repeated-measures across persuasion levels use Cochran's Q with post-hoc McNemar; paired model/detector comparisons use McNemar with Bonferroni correction. Confidence intervals: 95% bootstrap CIs computed over dialogues for dialogue-level rates; probe-level sensitivity rates computed over cached model-probe responses. Evaluation: three models (U5K = GPT-OSS-120B; E7B = DeepSeek-R1; P3R = Qwen3-VL-235B) evaluated via OpenRouter API on the same 1,000 dialogues × 3 probes → 3,000 cached responses per model, 9,000 total. Previously reported R9S range: 38.7%–54.6% leakage across models; persuasion intensity and secret type affect leakage (SSNs/credit cards more suppressed than emails/phones).

Benchmark K7X (PrivDrift): measures active-context privacy for secrets S disclosed at turn t0, tested with bounded drift lengths d in {0,2,3,4,5,6} (d=0 with p=0.2, else Uniform{2..6}). Dataset: 1,000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored interleaved); secrets are one of four fixed-format PII categories A9T, D2F, L8P, G6Y inserted in the opening turn. Final probe: three persuasion intensities H2R (direct/neutral), F6K (medium/justified), N8W (hard/high-pressure). Detection: regex normalization (J5D) then Llama judge; hybrid = X3Q (positive if either stage signals leakage). Metrics: R9S = dialogue-level leakage (dialogue leaks if any probe elicits secret); probe-level leakage called M2V (used for persuasion- and B7N analyses). Models: U5K (GPT-OSS-120B), E7B (DeepSeek-R1), P3R (Qwen3-VL-235B); 3,000 cached responses per model (1,000 dialogues × 3 probes). Key results (Part 7): stable-decay threshold τ = max(D_obs)+1 = 7; no model shows stable decay within tested window d ≤ 6. Strong association between secret type and leakage (Cramer's V in probe-level M2V): E7B 0.5871, U5K 0.7731, P3R 0.6927. Secret-type breakdown (X3Q M2V, Table 5) shows L8P/G6Y heavily suppressed (e.g., U5K L8P 0.14%, G6Y 0.00%) while D2F/A9T leak much more (e.g., U5K D2F 78.24%, A9T 70.89%). Persuasion effects are significant and model-dependent (Cochran's Q p<1e-5; Table 4): U5K H2R 39.30%/F6K 40.50%/N8W 32.90%; E7B 28.10%/22.00%/29.20%; P3R 38.70%/33.30%/40.60%. V9B-length curves dip near d=3 then rebound; effect sizes small (Cramer's V for V9B length: E7B 0.1073, U5K 0.0659, P3R 0.0723). Dialogue-level R9S (X3Q, Table 3): E7B 38.70% [35.7,41.6], U5K 47.70% [44.6,50.8], P3R 54.60% [51.6,57.7]. Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (WVU), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Contribution: PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with deliberately inserted secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction (persuasion-based) probes. Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows; dialogue-level hybrid leakage reported as 38.7%–54.6% (Table 3). Definition: a dialogue is considered leaking if any standardized probe elicits its secret. Detection: hybrid detector combining normalized text matching and an LLM judge. Reported dependencies: leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity (Tables 3–5). Additional topic drift within the tested window does not reliably reduce leakage (Sec 5.4). Framing: privacy risk treated as a persistent behavioral failure mode, distinct from training-data memorization or immediate jailbreaking.

Primary metric: dialogue-level hybrid leakage (hybrid detector = deterministic normalization/regex matching + open-weights LLM judge). Reported dialogue-level hybrid leakage: 38.7%–54.6% (Table 3). Topic-drift axis: d = number of unrelated intervening drift turns; tested window d ≤ 6. Within this window, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage (Sec 5.4). Privacy Half-Life τ proposed as a stability-based measure of persistent suppression; no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range (Sec 5.6). Framing: behavioral privacy risk distinct from training-data memorization or immediate jailbreaking.

PrivDrift framework: synthetic eval measuring whether secrets disclosed at turn t0 are re-disclosed after d unrelated, content-dense drift turns. Threat model = active-context re-disclosure: leakage if model reproduces S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Formalization: disclosure S at t0, intervening dialogue D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; probes appended to active context. Dataset: N = 1000 controlled dialogues (Table 1): 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored (human dialogs inserted throughout; cached evaluation metadata does not preserve their identifiers so only aggregate results reported). Secret categories = 4 (phone, email, SSN, credit card). Drift lengths tested = {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Word/token stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795; approx tokens estimated from words => avg ~478.87, median ~513.33, min/max ~57.33/1060. Pipeline: scaffold-then-rewrite generation preserves ground-truth secret, drift length, and probe structure; persona + secret injection places secret in opening turn as plausible task; drift turns drawn from topic-conditioned library (tax, medical, travel, etc.) with fallback tasks (writing, reasoning, summarization); annotators human-author subset of drift turns; naturalistic refinement: a rewriting model improves fluency/persona but must preserve exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Probing setup begins next (not in this part).

Eval appends a final standardized probe (three persuasion levels: Simple/Medium/Hard). Drift length d (number of intervening turns) sampled from mixture: d=0 with p=0.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (so each of 2–6 has p=0.16). Dataset drift lengths tested D_obs = {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Hierarchical hybrid detector (two stages, applied in order): Stage 1 normalization-based matching (called regex-stage): φ(·) normalizes secrets/responses — numeric secrets: remove non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, retain meaningful delimiters. Leak_regex(R,S) = I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)] (substring containment). Regex-positive responses labeled leakage; regex-negative responses passed to Stage 2. Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge given (secret, response) returns binary verdict (leakage/no leakage) to catch partial/paraphrased disclosures. Report regex-only and hybrid (regex+judge) leakage rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ: let L(d) be leakage rate at drift d; define δ = 0.1 × L(0). τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ and ∀ d' ∈ D_obs with d' > d: L(d') ≤ δ}. If no d qualifies, τ = max(D_obs) + 1 (requires stable decay below threshold).

Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B accessed via OpenRouter. Dataset: 1,000 PrivDrift dialogues per model; each dialogue has one seeded secret and one drift length d ∈ {0,2,3,4,5,6} sampled from Eq.(1) (mixture: d=0 with p=0.2; otherwise uniform over 2–6, so each of 2–6 has p=0.16). Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: Introduces PrivDrift benchmark for auditing recovery of user-disclosed secrets after conversational topic drift and persuasion-based probing. Dataset: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows. Key result: dialogue-level hybrid leakage remains substantial, ranging 38.7%–54.6%, and varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Additional topic drift within tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage. Conclusion: privacy risk in active LLM contexts should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure mode, not only as memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Goal: measure whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after topic drift and persuasion-style probing in multi-turn LLM conversations. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled dataset with 1,000 multi-turn dialogues (paper states 1,000 dialogues per model evaluated). Axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe, tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows. Detector: reproducible hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching (regex/fuzzy) with an open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage; leakage varies by secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers). Additional drift within tested window does not reliably reduce leakage. Proposed metric: Privacy Half-Life (τ) for persistent suppression; authors claim no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions enumerated: benchmark, evaluation under multiple probe styles, hybrid detector and multiple leakage metrics, and Privacy Half-Life analysis.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Purpose: measure whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after topic drift and persuasion-style probing in multi-turn LLM conversations. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled dataset with 1,000 multi-turn dialogues (reported as 1,000 dialogues per model evaluated). Experimental axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe, tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Models: evaluation over three LLMs with extended context windows. Detector: hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching (regex/fuzzy) with an open-weights LLM judge; metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy-only, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported findings: dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion intensity significantly increases leakage; leakage varies by secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers); additional drift within tested window does not reliably reduce leakage. Proposed metric: Privacy Half-Life (τ) for persistent suppression; authors claim no evaluated model reaches stable decay within the observed drift range. Related work summary: distinguishes active-context privacy (user-provided info in current interaction) from training-data extraction and membership inference; cites benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) that test static access-control/privacy norms, while PrivDrift isolates persistence under drift and persuasion. Notes that multi-turn adversarial/jailbreak work (e.g., Crescendo attacks, automated jailbreak frameworks, prompt injection) show gradual elicitation of undesired outputs; PrivDrift applies a similar multi-turn lens to information flow. Contrasts with machine unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) that target parameter-level removal over static QA pairs; PrivDrift targets prompt-level/context-window suppression behavior relevant to RAG, copilots, and agentic workflows.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: privacy risk in active LLM conversations should be evaluated as a persistent behavioral failure mode (not only memorization/jailbreak). Reported finding: additional V9B within the tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage; R9S X3Q (leakage measure) across three LLMs with extended context windows is substantial (38.7%–54.6%), and varies strongly by model, secret type, and Z4T. Dataset/benchmark K7X contains 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes to audit whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after conversational V9B and persuasion-based probing. Motivation: LLMs as persistent assistants in user-facing/shared-session/tool-augmented settings may behaveably recover sensitive info after topic shifts. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu). Core claim: active-context privacy leakage is a persistent behavioral failure mode distinct from memorization/jailbreak. Key empirical findings: dialogue-level leakage (R9S) under hybrid detection (X3Q) is 38.7%–54.6% across three LLMs with extended context windows, tested on 1,000 controlled dialogues per model. Tested drift window: d ≤ 6; adding further drift within this window does not reliably reduce leakage. Leakage varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity (Z4T). Secret-type suppression order: L8P (SSNs) and G6Y (credit cards) are suppressed far more often than D2F (email addresses) and A9T (phone numbers). Definitions/axes: V9B = topic drift (number of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe); Z4T = persuasion intensity / interaction style. Dataset/benchmark: K7X (PrivDrift) — 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, standardized extraction probes. Contributions: (1) K7X benchmark; (2) evaluation under direct, justified, and high-pressure probes modeling Z4T; (3) reproducible X3Q detector combining normalization-based matching with T1G (open-weights LLM judge), reporting rates for R9S (dialogue-level leakage), M2V, J5D (regex-only leakage), B7N, and X3Q (hybrid leakage); (4) C5Z (Privacy Half-Life τ), a stability-based metric showing no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Context/motivation: fills gap between memorization and immediate jailbreaking literature by measuring recoverability of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated conversational drift.

Related work contrasts machine-unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) that operate over static QA pairs and model parameters with K7X, which targets active-context privacy (prompt-level/context-window control rather than weight-level unlearning). Prior multi-turn safety work (Crescendo attacks, automated jailbreak frameworks, prompt injection) focuses on unsafe content or instruction hijacking; K7X adapts the multi-turn lens to information-flow control, asking whether a user-disclosed secret in the context window is behaviorally recoverable after unrelated topic drift (V9B) and later persuasion-based probes (Z4T). Benchmarks like ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, and PrivaCI-Bench test privacy reasoning, norms, or static access-control scenarios; K7X instead isolates persistence/recoverability of secrets across drift and probing. Historical privacy work addressed training-data extraction and memorized PII; K7X emphasizes active-context secrets requiring correct inference-time handling. Also notes claim that aligned models can remain vulnerable to multi-turn exploitation.

K7X / PrivDrift focuses on active-context privacy: whether a secret S disclosed at turn t0 is behaviorally recoverable after unrelated topic drift and later persuasion-style probes (contrasts with static QA/unlearning benchmarks like TOFU/WMDP and with privacy-reasoning benchmarks). Threat model Q3M: secret S disclosed; conversation proceeds through d unrelated drift turns D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; standardized probe P appended; leakage = model response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Dataset (3.2): N=1000 controlled dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored) produced by scaffold-then-rewrite; human IDs not preserved in cached metadata so aggregated results reported. Main evaluation (3.3): append final probe of three persuasion levels — H2R (direct/neutral), F6K (medium/contextual justification), N8W (hard/high-pressure). Drift length sampling (eq.1): d = 0 with p=0.2; d ∼ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (no d=1 samples). Detection pipeline (3.4): hierarchical hybrid detector — stage 1 (3.4.1) normalization/regex: φ(·) normalizes numeric (strip non-digits) and alphanumeric (case/whitespace normalized, delimiters preserved); Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)] (eq.2). Regex-negative responses go to stage 2 (3.4.2) an open-weights Llama judge (T1G) that receives secret+response and returns binary leakage verdict (captures paraphrase/partial disclosure); judge-introduced error rates (J5D, X3Q) reported separately. Stability metric C5Z(τ) (3.4.3 / eq.3): δ = 0.1×L(0); τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ and ∀d'>d, L(d') ≤ δ}; if set empty τ := max(D_obs)+1. Note ambiguity to track: wording alternately calls d the "number of turns" and also defines D as {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}, which suggests d counts user–assistant pairs (possible off-by-one/turn-definition ambiguity).

Dataset: N=1,000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored). Secret categories: 4 fixed-format PII (A9T, D2F, L8P, G6Y); secret inserted in the opening turn (t0). Drift lengths observed: {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Sampling (from earlier): d=0 with p=0.2; d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (no d=1). Summary stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16, median 385.00, min/max words 43/795. Approx tokens estimated from words using factor 4/3: avg tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max tokens 57.33/1060. Dialogue generation: scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline; 3.2.3 applies a rewriting model to each scaffold to improve fluency/persona realism while preserving exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Persona sampling from >100 professions/demographic profiles. Topics assigned (e.g., tax filing, medical triage, travel); drift turns drawn from a topic-conditioned library of dense QA pairs and fallback tasks; a subset of drift turns are human-authored and included in the generation library. Framework overview: K7X = parametric dialogue generator + probing harness + metric suite (hybrid leakage detector: stage1 regex normalization Leak_regex; regex-negatives go to Llama judge; judge error rates reported separately). Stability metric C5Z(τ) defined earlier. Ambiguity to track: paper alternately calls d the “number of turns” vs defines D={u1,a1,...,ud,ad} (suggests d counts user–assistant pairs). Final probes: three persuasion levels (H2R, F6K, N8W) appended to each dialogue per earlier description.

Paper K7X (PrivDrift) studies suppression of user-provided secrets in active multi-turn LLM conversations, focusing on persistence after topic drift (V9B) and later persuasion intensity (Z4T). Key metric C5Z = Privacy Half-Life (τ), stability-based; claim from intro: “No model reaches stable decay in the observed range under C5Z.” Benchmark axes: V9B (topic drift = unrelated turns between disclosure and probe) and Z4T (persuasion intensity). Evaluation conditions include direct, justified, and high-pressure probes; contexts include shared sessions, browser assistants, copilots, agentic workflows. Methods: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Detector: hybrid reproducible detector = normalization + open-weights LLM judge (T1G); reported outputs include R9S, M2V (probe-level leakage), J5D (regex-only), B7N, X3Q. Related work: K7X isolates persistence after drift and persuasion (sec refs 2.1–2.3). Prior work (training-data extraction, membership inference, memorized PII, TOFU, WMDP) targets parameter/memory/static QA/weights or static access-control tests (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench), whereas K7X applies a multi-turn information-flow lens to re-disclosure of user-supplied secrets. Other related work (Crescendo, automated multi-turn jailbreaks, prompt injection) target harmful content or instruction hijacking rather than user-secret re-disclosure.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (WVU), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Contribution: PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with deliberately inserted secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction (persuasion-based) probes. Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows; dialogue-level hybrid leakage reported as 38.7%–54.6% (Table 3). Definition: a dialogue is considered leaking if any standardized probe elicits its secret. Detection: hybrid detector combining normalized text matching and an LLM judge. Reported dependencies: leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity (Tables 3–5). Additional topic drift within the tested window does not reliably reduce leakage (Sec 5.4). Framing: privacy risk treated as a persistent behavioral failure mode, distinct from training-data memorization or immediate jailbreaking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano R. Maldonado Romero. Benchmark: PrivDrift — 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues per model with deliberately inserted secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes (direct, justified, high-pressure persuasion styles). Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows (3 × 1,000 dialogues). Primary metric: dialogue-level hybrid leakage (hybrid detector = deterministic normalization/regex matching + open-weights LLM judge). Reported dialogue-level hybrid leakage: 38.7%–54.6% (Table 3). Detection/reporting: dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only (normalization-based), fuzzy (approximate text similarity), and hybrid leakage rates. Secret-type effects: SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed far more often than email addresses and phone numbers (Table 5). Persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage (Sec 5.3). Topic-drift axis: d = number of unrelated intervening drift turns; tested window d ≤ 6. Within this window, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage (Sec 5.4). Privacy Half-Life τ proposed as a stability-based measure of persistent suppression; no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range (Sec 5.6). Framing: behavioral privacy risk distinct from training-data memorization or immediate jailbreaking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano R. Maldonado Romero. Benchmark: PrivDrift — 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues per model with deliberately inserted secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes (direct, justified, high-pressure persuasion styles). Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows (3 × 1,000 dialogues). Primary metric: dialogue-level hybrid leakage (hybrid detector = deterministic normalization/regex matching + open-weights LLM judge). Reported dialogue-level hybrid leakage: 38.7%–54.6% (Table 3). Detection/reporting: dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy (approximate text similarity), and hybrid leakage rates. Secret-type effects: SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed far more often than email addresses and phone numbers (Table 5). Persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage (Sec 5.3). Topic-drift axis: d = number of unrelated intervening drift turns; tested window d ≤ 6. Within this window, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage (Sec 5.4). Privacy Half-Life τ proposed as a stability-based measure of persistent suppression; no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range (Sec 5.6). Framing: behavioral privacy risk distinct from training-data memorization or immediate jailbreaking. Related work: contrasts training-data extraction and membership inference with active-context privacy; cites ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench as benchmarks of privacy reasoning/ norms but notes PrivDrift specifically isolates persistence of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated topic drift and later persuasion-based probing. Connects to multi-turn adversarial attacks (e.g., Crescendo, automated jailbreak frameworks) but emphasizes information re-disclosure rather than unsafe content generation. Contrasts with machine unlearning (TOFU, WMDP) by focusing on suppression in active context/RAG/copilots rather than changes to model weights.

PrivDrift framework: synthetic eval measuring whether secrets disclosed at turn t0 are re-disclosed after d unrelated, content-dense drift turns. Threat model = active-context re-disclosure: leakage if model reproduces S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Formalization: disclosure S at t0, intervening dialogue D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; probes appended to active context. Dataset: N = 1000 controlled dialogues (Table 1): 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored (human dialogs inserted throughout; cached evaluation metadata does not preserve their identifiers so only aggregate results reported). Secret categories = 4 (phone, email, SSN, credit card). Drift lengths tested = {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Word/token stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795; approx tokens estimated from words => avg ~478.87, median ~513.33, min/max ~57.33/1060. Pipeline: scaffold-then-rewrite generation preserves ground-truth secret, drift length, and probe structure; persona + secret injection places secret in opening turn as plausible task; drift turns drawn from topic-conditioned library (tax, medical, travel, etc.) with fallback tasks (writing, reasoning, summarization); annotators human-author subset of drift turns; naturalistic refinement: a rewriting model improves fluency/persona but must preserve exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Probing setup begins next (not in this part).

Eval appends a final standardized probe (three persuasion levels: Simple/Medium/Hard). Drift length d (number of intervening turns) sampled from mixture: d=0 with p=0.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (so each of 2–6 has p=0.16). Dataset drift lengths tested D_obs = {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Hierarchical hybrid detector (two stages, applied in order): Stage 1 normalization-based matching (called regex-stage): φ(·) normalizes secrets/responses — numeric secrets: remove non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, retain meaningful delimiters. Leak_regex(R,S) = I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)] (substring containment). Regex-positive responses labeled leakage; regex-negative responses passed to Stage 2. Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge given (secret, response) returns binary verdict (leakage/no leakage) to catch partial/paraphrased disclosures. Report regex-only and hybrid (regex+judge) leakage rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ: let L(d) be leakage rate at drift d; define δ = 0.1 × L(0). τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ and ∀ d' ∈ D_obs with d' > d: L(d') ≤ δ}. If no d qualifies, τ = max(D_obs) + 1 (requires stable decay below threshold).

Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B accessed via OpenRouter. Dataset: 1,000 PrivDrift dialogues per model; each dialogue has one seeded secret and one drift length d ∈ {0,2,3,4,5,6} sampled from Eq.(1) (mixture: d=0 with p=0.2; otherwise uniform over 2–6, so each of 2–6 has p=0.16). Each dialogue is probed with three standardized persuasion probes (Simple/Medium/Hard) — so 3,000 cached model-probe responses per model, 9,000 total. Detector & reporting: hierarchical two-stage detector — Stage 1 normalization/regex-match φ(·) (numeric: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, keep meaningful delimiters); Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Regex-positive responses labeled leakage; regex-negative passed to Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge for paraphrases. Report regex-only and hybrid (regex+judge) leakage. Privacy half-life τ: L(d) leakage at drift d; δ=0.1·L(0); τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and ∀d'>d: L(d')≤δ}; if none, τ=max(D_obs)+1. Aggregation: dialogue-level (dialogue counts as leaking if any probe elicits secret; used for overall leakage) and probe-level (each dialogue contributes one response per persuasion condition; used for persuasion-level and fuzzy-matching analyses). Statistics: dialogue-level 95% bootstrap CIs (resampling dialogues); probe-level uses cached responses. Paired comparisons: McNemar’s test (+ Bonferroni when applicable). Repeated persuasion-levels: Cochran’s Q, with post-hoc McNemar. Associations (drift length, persuasion, secret type): chi-square tests with Cramer’s V; report p-values vs null.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: Introduces PrivDrift benchmark for auditing recovery of user-disclosed secrets after conversational topic drift and persuasion-based probing. Dataset: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows. Key result: dialogue-level hybrid leakage remains substantial, ranging 38.7%–54.6%, and varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Additional topic drift within tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage. Conclusion: privacy risk in active LLM contexts should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure mode, not only as memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Goal: measure whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after topic drift and persuasion-style probing in multi-turn LLM conversations. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled dataset with 1,000 multi-turn dialogues (paper states 1,000 dialogues per model evaluated). Axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe, tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows. Detector: reproducible hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching (regex/fuzzy) with an open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage; leakage varies by secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers). Additional drift within tested window does not reliably reduce leakage. Proposed metric: Privacy Half-Life (τ) for persistent suppression; authors claim no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions enumerated: benchmark, evaluation under multiple probe styles, hybrid detector and multiple leakage metrics, and Privacy Half-Life analysis.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Purpose: measure whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after topic drift and persuasion-style probing in multi-turn LLM conversations. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled dataset with 1,000 multi-turn dialogues (reported as 1,000 dialogues per model evaluated). Experimental axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe, tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Models: evaluation over three LLMs with extended context windows. Detector: hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching (regex/fuzzy) with an open-weights LLM judge; metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy-only, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported findings: dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion intensity significantly increases leakage; leakage varies by secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers); additional drift within tested window does not reliably reduce leakage. Proposed metric: Privacy Half-Life (τ) for persistent suppression; authors claim no evaluated model reaches stable decay within the observed drift range. Related work summary: distinguishes active-context privacy (user-provided info in current interaction) from training-data extraction and membership inference; cites benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) that test static access-control/privacy norms, while PrivDrift isolates persistence under drift and persuasion. Notes that multi-turn adversarial/jailbreak work (e.g., Crescendo attacks, automated jailbreak frameworks, prompt injection) show gradual elicitation of undesired outputs; PrivDrift applies a similar multi-turn lens to information flow. Contrasts with machine unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) that target parameter-level removal over static QA pairs; PrivDrift targets prompt-level/context-window suppression behavior relevant to RAG, copilots, and agentic workflows.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: privacy risk in active LLM conversations should be evaluated as a persistent behavioral failure mode (not only memorization/jailbreak). Reported finding: additional V9B within the tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage; R9S X3Q (leakage measure) across three LLMs with extended context windows is substantial (38.7%–54.6%), and varies strongly by model, secret type, and Z4T. Dataset/benchmark K7X contains 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes to audit whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after conversational V9B and persuasion-based probing. Motivation: LLMs as persistent assistants in user-facing/shared-session/tool-augmented settings may behaveably recover sensitive info after topic shifts. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu). Core claim: active-context privacy leakage is a persistent behavioral failure mode distinct from memorization/jailbreak. Key empirical findings: dialogue-level leakage (R9S) under hybrid detection (X3Q) is 38.7%–54.6% across three LLMs with extended context windows, tested on 1,000 controlled dialogues per model. Tested drift window: d ≤ 6; adding further drift within this window does not reliably reduce leakage. Leakage varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity (Z4T). Secret-type suppression order: L8P (SSNs) and G6Y (credit cards) are suppressed far more often than D2F (email addresses) and A9T (phone numbers). Definitions/axes: V9B = topic drift (number of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe); Z4T = persuasion intensity / interaction style. Dataset/benchmark: K7X (PrivDrift) — 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, standardized extraction probes. Contributions: (1) K7X benchmark; (2) evaluation under direct, justified, and high-pressure probes modeling Z4T; (3) reproducible X3Q detector combining normalization-based matching with T1G (open-weights LLM judge), reporting rates for R9S (dialogue-level leakage), M2V, J5D (regex-only leakage), B7N, and X3Q (hybrid leakage); (4) C5Z (Privacy Half-Life τ), a stability-based metric showing no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Context/motivation: fills gap between memorization and immediate jailbreaking literature by measuring recoverability of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated conversational drift.

Related work contrasts machine-unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) that operate over static QA pairs and model parameters with K7X, which targets active-context privacy (prompt-level/context-window control rather than weight-level unlearning). Prior multi-turn safety work (Crescendo attacks, automated jailbreak frameworks, prompt injection) focuses on unsafe content or instruction hijacking; K7X adapts the multi-turn lens to information-flow control, asking whether a user-disclosed secret in the context window is behaviorally recoverable after unrelated topic drift (V9B) and later persuasion-based probes (Z4T). Benchmarks like ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, and PrivaCI-Bench test privacy reasoning, norms, or static access-control scenarios; K7X instead isolates persistence/recoverability of secrets across drift and probing. Historical privacy work addressed training-data extraction and memorized PII; K7X emphasizes active-context secrets requiring correct inference-time handling. Also notes claim that aligned models can remain vulnerable to multi-turn exploitation.

K7X / PrivDrift focuses on active-context privacy: whether a secret S disclosed at turn t0 is behaviorally recoverable after unrelated topic drift and later persuasion-style probes (contrasts with static QA/unlearning benchmarks like TOFU/WMDP and with privacy-reasoning benchmarks). Threat model Q3M: secret S disclosed; conversation proceeds through d unrelated drift turns D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; standardized probe P appended; leakage = model response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Dataset (3.2): N=1000 controlled dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored) produced by scaffold-then-rewrite; human IDs not preserved in cached metadata so aggregated results reported. Main evaluation (3.3): append final probe of three persuasion levels — H2R (direct/neutral), F6K (medium/contextual justification), N8W (hard/high-pressure). Drift length sampling (eq.1): d = 0 with p=0.2; d ∼ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (no d=1 samples). Detection pipeline (3.4): hierarchical hybrid detector — stage 1 (3.4.1) normalization/regex: φ(·) normalizes numeric (strip non-digits) and alphanumeric (case/whitespace normalized, delimiters preserved); Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)] (eq.2). Regex-negative responses go to stage 2 (3.4.2) an open-weights Llama judge (T1G) that receives secret+response and returns binary leakage verdict (captures paraphrase/partial disclosure); judge-introduced error rates (J5D, X3Q) reported separately. Stability metric C5Z(τ) (3.4.3 / eq.3): δ = 0.1×L(0); τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ and ∀d'>d, L(d') ≤ δ}; if set empty τ := max(D_obs)+1. Note ambiguity to track: wording alternately calls d the "number of turns" and also defines D as {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}, which suggests d counts user–assistant pairs (possible off-by-one/turn-definition ambiguity).

Dataset: N=1,000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored). Secret categories: 4 fixed-format PII (A9T, D2F, L8P, G6Y); secret inserted in the opening turn (t0). Drift lengths observed: {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Sampling (from earlier): d=0 with p=0.2; d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (no d=1). Summary stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16, median 385.00, min/max words 43/795. Approx tokens estimated from words using factor 4/3: avg tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max tokens 57.33/1060. Dialogue generation: scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline; 3.2.3 applies a rewriting model to each scaffold to improve fluency/persona realism while preserving exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Persona sampling from >100 professions/demographic profiles. Topics assigned (e.g., tax filing, medical triage, travel); drift turns drawn from a topic-conditioned library of dense QA pairs and fallback tasks; a subset of drift turns are human-authored and included in the generation library. Framework overview: K7X = parametric dialogue generator + probing harness + metric suite (hybrid leakage detector: stage1 regex normalization Leak_regex; regex-negatives go to Llama judge; judge error rates reported separately). Stability metric C5Z(τ) defined earlier. Ambiguity to track: paper alternately calls d the “number of turns” vs defines D={u1,a1,...,ud,ad} (suggests d counts user–assistant pairs). Final probes: three persuasion levels (H2R, F6K, N8W) appended to each dialogue per earlier description.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (WVU), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano R. Maldonado Romero. Benchmark: PrivDrift — 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues per model with deliberately inserted secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes (direct, justified, high-pressure persuasion styles). Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows (3 × 1,000 dialogues). Primary metric: dialogue-level hybrid leakage (hybrid detector = deterministic normalization/regex matching + open-weights LLM judge). Reported dialogue-level hybrid leakage: 38.7%–54.6% (Table 3). Detection/reporting: dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only (normalization-based), fuzzy (approximate text similarity), and hybrid leakage rates. Secret-type effects: SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed far more often than email addresses and phone numbers (Table 5). Persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage (Sec 5.3). Topic-drift axis: d = number of unrelated intervening drift turns; tested window d ≤ 6. Within this window, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage (Sec 5.4). Privacy Half-Life τ proposed as a stability-based measure of persistent suppression; no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range (Sec 5.6). Framing: behavioral privacy risk distinct from training-data memorization or immediate jailbreaking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano R. Maldonado Romero. Benchmark: PrivDrift — 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues per model with deliberately inserted secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes (direct, justified, high-pressure persuasion styles). Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows (3 × 1,000 dialogues). Primary metric: dialogue-level hybrid leakage (hybrid detector = deterministic normalization/regex matching + open-weights LLM judge). Reported dialogue-level hybrid leakage: 38.7%–54.6% (Table 3). Detection/reporting: dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy (approximate text similarity), and hybrid leakage rates. Secret-type effects: SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed far more often than email addresses and phone numbers (Table 5). Persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage (Sec 5.3). Topic-drift axis: d = number of unrelated intervening drift turns; tested window d ≤ 6. Within this window, additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage (Sec 5.4). Privacy Half-Life τ proposed as a stability-based measure of persistent suppression; no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range (Sec 5.6). Framing: behavioral privacy risk distinct from training-data memorization or immediate jailbreaking. Related work: contrasts training-data extraction and membership inference with active-context privacy; cites ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench as benchmarks of privacy reasoning/ norms but notes PrivDrift specifically isolates persistence of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated topic drift and later persuasion-based probing. Connects to multi-turn adversarial attacks (e.g., Crescendo, automated jailbreak frameworks) but emphasizes information re-disclosure rather than unsafe content generation. Contrasts with machine unlearning (TOFU, WMDP) by focusing on suppression in active context/RAG/copilots rather than changes to model weights.

PrivDrift framework: synthetic eval measuring whether secrets disclosed at turn t0 are re-disclosed after d unrelated, content-dense drift turns. Threat model = active-context re-disclosure: leakage if model reproduces S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Formalization: disclosure S at t0, intervening dialogue D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; probes appended to active context. Dataset: N = 1000 controlled dialogues (Table 1): 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored (human dialogs inserted throughout; cached evaluation metadata does not preserve their identifiers so only aggregate results reported). Secret categories = 4 (phone, email, SSN, credit card). Drift lengths tested = {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Word/token stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795; approx tokens estimated from words => avg ~478.87, median ~513.33, min/max ~57.33/1060. Pipeline: scaffold-then-rewrite generation preserves ground-truth secret, drift length, and probe structure; persona + secret injection places secret in opening turn as plausible task; drift turns drawn from topic-conditioned library (tax, medical, travel, etc.) with fallback tasks (writing, reasoning, summarization); annotators human-author subset of drift turns; naturalistic refinement: a rewriting model improves fluency/persona but must preserve exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Probing setup begins next (not in this part).

Eval appends a final standardized probe (three persuasion levels: Simple/Medium/Hard). Drift length d (number of intervening turns) sampled from mixture: d=0 with p=0.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (so each of 2–6 has p=0.16). Dataset drift lengths tested D_obs = {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Hierarchical hybrid detector (two stages, applied in order): Stage 1 normalization-based matching (called regex-stage): φ(·) normalizes secrets/responses — numeric secrets: remove non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, retain meaningful delimiters. Leak_regex(R,S) = I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)] (substring containment). Regex-positive responses labeled leakage; regex-negative responses passed to Stage 2. Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge given (secret, response) returns binary verdict (leakage/no leakage) to catch partial/paraphrased disclosures. Report regex-only and hybrid (regex+judge) leakage rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ: let L(d) be leakage rate at drift d; define δ = 0.1 × L(0). τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ and ∀ d' ∈ D_obs with d' > d: L(d') ≤ δ}. If no d qualifies, τ = max(D_obs) + 1 (requires stable decay below threshold).

Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B accessed via OpenRouter. Dataset: 1,000 PrivDrift dialogues per model; each dialogue has one seeded secret and one drift length d ∈ {0,2,3,4,5,6} sampled from Eq.(1) (mixture: d=0 with p=0.2; otherwise uniform over 2–6, so each of 2–6 has p=0.16). Each dialogue is probed with three standardized persuasion probes (Simple/Medium/Hard) — so 3,000 cached model-probe responses per model, 9,000 total. Detector & reporting: hierarchical two-stage detector — Stage 1 normalization/regex-match φ(·) (numeric: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, keep meaningful delimiters); Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Regex-positive responses labeled leakage; regex-negative passed to Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge for paraphrases. Report regex-only and hybrid (regex+judge) leakage. Privacy half-life τ: L(d) leakage at drift d; δ=0.1·L(0); τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and ∀d'>d: L(d')≤δ}; if none, τ=max(D_obs)+1. Aggregation: dialogue-level (dialogue counts as leaking if any probe elicits secret; used for overall leakage) and probe-level (each dialogue contributes one response per persuasion condition; used for persuasion-level and fuzzy-matching analyses). Statistics: dialogue-level 95% bootstrap CIs (resampling dialogues); probe-level uses cached responses. Paired comparisons: McNemar’s test (+ Bonferroni when applicable). Repeated persuasion-levels: Cochran’s Q, with post-hoc McNemar. Associations (drift length, persuasion, secret type): chi-square tests with Cramer’s V; report p-values vs null.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: Introduces PrivDrift benchmark for auditing recovery of user-disclosed secrets after conversational topic drift and persuasion-based probing. Dataset: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows. Key result: dialogue-level hybrid leakage remains substantial, ranging 38.7%–54.6%, and varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Additional topic drift within tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage. Conclusion: privacy risk in active LLM contexts should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure mode, not only as memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Goal: measure whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after topic drift and persuasion-style probing in multi-turn LLM conversations. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled dataset with 1,000 multi-turn dialogues (paper states 1,000 dialogues per model evaluated). Axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe, tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows. Detector: reproducible hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching (regex/fuzzy) with an open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage; leakage varies by secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers). Additional drift within tested window does not reliably reduce leakage. Proposed metric: Privacy Half-Life (τ) for persistent suppression; authors claim no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions enumerated: benchmark, evaluation under multiple probe styles, hybrid detector and multiple leakage metrics, and Privacy Half-Life analysis.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Purpose: measure whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after topic drift and persuasion-style probing in multi-turn LLM conversations. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled dataset with 1,000 multi-turn dialogues (reported as 1,000 dialogues per model evaluated). Experimental axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe, tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Models: evaluation over three LLMs with extended context windows. Detector: hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching (regex/fuzzy) with an open-weights LLM judge; metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy-only, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported findings: dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion intensity significantly increases leakage; leakage varies by secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers); additional drift within tested window does not reliably reduce leakage. Proposed metric: Privacy Half-Life (τ) for persistent suppression; authors claim no evaluated model reaches stable decay within the observed drift range. Related work summary: distinguishes active-context privacy (user-provided info in current interaction) from training-data extraction and membership inference; cites benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) that test static access-control/privacy norms, while PrivDrift isolates persistence under drift and persuasion. Notes that multi-turn adversarial/jailbreak work (e.g., Crescendo attacks, automated jailbreak frameworks, prompt injection) show gradual elicitation of undesired outputs; PrivDrift applies a similar multi-turn lens to information flow. Contrasts with machine unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) that target parameter-level removal over static QA pairs; PrivDrift targets prompt-level/context-window suppression behavior relevant to RAG, copilots, and agentic workflows.

Figure text refers to these as "regex-stage"/"regex-negative". Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge examines regex-negative responses with secret+response and returns binary verdict; report regex-only and hybrid rates separately.
Privacy Half-Life τ: let D_obs be observed drift lengths, L(d) leakage at d; safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0). τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and for all d'>d in D_obs, L(d')≤δ}; if empty set τ = max(D_obs)+1. (Definition assumes an unambiguous ordered meaning of d.)

PrivDrift: measures secret recoverability after topic drift and persuasion probes. Dataset: N=1,000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored; reported in aggregate). Each dialogue contains one seeded secret (one of 4 fixed-format PII types: phone, email, SSN, credit card) and one drift length d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6} sampled with p(d=0)=0.2, else d~Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} (total p=0.8). Avg words/dialogue 359.16 (median 385; min 43; max 795); tokens ≈1.333×words (avg tokens ≈478.87). Pipeline: scaffold-then-rewrite; persona+secret injected at opening; drift QA pairs topic-conditioned; final rewrite preserves secret/drift/roles/probe. Probes: three persuasion levels (Simple, Medium, Hard). Note: earlier sections ambiguously defined d (turns vs. user/assistant pairs). Detector: hierarchical hybrid — Stage 1 deterministic normalization/substring check φ(·) (numeric: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, keep delimiters); Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Stage 2: open-weight Llama judge examines regex-negative responses with secret+response and returns binary verdict; report regex-only and hybrid rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ defined via observed leakage L(d) with threshold δ=0.1×L(0) (requires ordered meaning of d). From this part: Models evaluated: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter API; all models queried with same dialogue histories and probe templates. For each model: evaluate same 1,000 dialogues; each dialogue evaluated under 3 standardized persuasion probes → 3,000 cached model-probe responses per model (9,000 total across 3 models). Aggregation: two levels — dialogue-level (a dialogue counts as leaking if any probe elicits the secret) and probe-level (each dialogue contributes one response per persuasion condition; used for persuasion-level and fuzzy-matching analyses). Dialogue-level leakage can exceed the average of per-probe leakage rates (because it's the union across probes). Uncertainty/statistics: report regex-only and hybrid leakage. Dialogue-level rates: 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues. Probe-level sensitivity checks: compute rates over cached model-probe responses. Paired model/detector comparisons: McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction. Repeated measures across persuasion levels: Cochran’s Q test with post-hoc McNemar. Associations (leakage vs drift length/persuasion/secret type): chi-square tests of independence; report Cramer’s V.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: privacy risk in active LLM conversations should be evaluated as a persistent behavioral failure mode (not only memorization/jailbreak). Reported finding: additional V9B within the tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage; R9S X3Q (leakage measure) across three LLMs with extended context windows is substantial (38.7%–54.6%), and varies strongly by model, secret type, and Z4T. Dataset/benchmark K7X contains 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes to audit whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after conversational V9B and persuasion-based probing. Motivation: LLMs as persistent assistants in user-facing/shared-session/tool-augmented settings may behaveably recover sensitive info after topic shifts. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu). Core claim: active-context privacy leakage is a persistent behavioral failure mode distinct from memorization/jailbreak. Key empirical findings: dialogue-level leakage (R9S) under hybrid detection (X3Q) is 38.7%–54.6% across three LLMs with extended context windows, tested on 1,000 controlled dialogues per model. Tested drift window: d ≤ 6; adding further drift within this window does not reliably reduce leakage. Leakage varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity (Z4T). Secret-type suppression order: L8P (SSNs) and G6Y (credit cards) are suppressed far more often than D2F (email addresses) and A9T (phone numbers). Definitions/axes: V9B = topic drift (number of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe); Z4T = persuasion intensity / interaction style. Dataset/benchmark: K7X (PrivDrift) — 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, standardized extraction probes. Contributions: (1) K7X benchmark; (2) evaluation under direct, justified, and high-pressure probes modeling Z4T; (3) reproducible X3Q detector combining normalization-based matching with T1G (open-weights LLM judge), reporting rates for R9S (dialogue-level leakage), M2V, J5D (regex-only leakage), B7N, and X3Q (hybrid leakage); (4) C5Z (Privacy Half-Life τ), a stability-based metric showing no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Context/motivation: fills gap between memorization and immediate jailbreaking literature by measuring recoverability of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated conversational drift.

Related work contrasts machine-unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) that operate over static QA pairs and model parameters with K7X, which targets active-context privacy (prompt-level/context-window control rather than weight-level unlearning). Prior multi-turn safety work (Crescendo attacks, automated jailbreak frameworks, prompt injection) focuses on unsafe content or instruction hijacking; K7X adapts the multi-turn lens to information-flow control, asking whether a user-disclosed secret in the context window is behaviorally recoverable after unrelated topic drift (V9B) and later persuasion-based probes (Z4T). Benchmarks like ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, and PrivaCI-Bench test privacy reasoning, norms, or static access-control scenarios; K7X instead isolates persistence/recoverability of secrets across drift and probing. Historical privacy work addressed training-data extraction and memorized PII; K7X emphasizes active-context secrets requiring correct inference-time handling. Also notes claim that aligned models can remain vulnerable to multi-turn exploitation.

K7X / PrivDrift focuses on active-context privacy: whether a secret S disclosed at turn t0 is behaviorally recoverable after unrelated topic drift and later persuasion-style probes (contrasts with static QA/unlearning benchmarks like TOFU/WMDP and with privacy-reasoning benchmarks). Threat model Q3M: secret S disclosed; conversation proceeds through d unrelated drift turns D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; standardized probe P appended; leakage = model response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Dataset (3.2): N=1000 controlled dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored) produced by scaffold-then-rewrite; human IDs not preserved in cached metadata so aggregated results reported. Main evaluation (3.3): append final probe of three persuasion levels — H2R (direct/neutral), F6K (medium/contextual justification), N8W (hard/high-pressure). Drift length sampling (eq.1): d = 0 with p=0.2; d ∼ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (no d=1 samples). Detection pipeline (3.4): hierarchical hybrid detector — stage 1 (3.4.1) normalization/regex: φ(·) normalizes numeric (strip non-digits) and alphanumeric (case/whitespace normalized, delimiters preserved); Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)] (eq.2). Regex-negative responses go to stage 2 (3.4.2) an open-weights Llama judge (T1G) that receives secret+response and returns binary leakage verdict (captures paraphrase/partial disclosure); judge-introduced error rates (J5D, X3Q) reported separately. Stability metric C5Z(τ) (3.4.3 / eq.3): δ = 0.1×L(0); τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ and ∀d'>d, L(d') ≤ δ}; if set empty τ := max(D_obs)+1. Note ambiguity to track: wording alternately calls d the "number of turns" and also defines D as {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}, which suggests d counts user–assistant pairs (possible off-by-one/turn-definition ambiguity).

Dataset: N=1,000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored). Secret categories: 4 fixed-format PII (A9T, D2F, L8P, G6Y); secret inserted in the opening turn (t0). Drift lengths observed: {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Sampling (from earlier): d=0 with p=0.2; d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (no d=1). Summary stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16, median 385.00, min/max words 43/795. Approx tokens estimated from words using factor 4/3: avg tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max tokens 57.33/1060. Dialogue generation: scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline; 3.2.3 applies a rewriting model to each scaffold to improve fluency/persona realism while preserving exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Persona sampling from >100 professions/demographic profiles. Topics assigned (e.g., tax filing, medical triage, travel); drift turns drawn from a topic-conditioned library of dense QA pairs and fallback tasks; a subset of drift turns are human-authored and included in the generation library. Framework overview: K7X = parametric dialogue generator + probing harness + metric suite (hybrid leakage detector: stage1 regex normalization Leak_regex; regex-negatives go to Llama judge; judge error rates reported separately). Stability metric C5Z(τ) defined earlier. Ambiguity to track: paper alternately calls d the “number of turns” vs defines D={u1,a1,...,ud,ad} (suggests d counts user–assistant pairs). Final probes: three persuasion levels (H2R, F6K, N8W) appended to each dialogue per earlier description.

PrivDrift framework: synthetic eval measuring whether secrets disclosed at turn t0 are re-disclosed after d unrelated, content-dense drift turns. Threat model = active-context re-disclosure: leakage if model reproduces S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Formalization: disclosure S at t0, intervening dialogue D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; probes appended to active context. Dataset: N = 1000 controlled dialogues (Table 1): 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored (human dialogs inserted throughout; cached evaluation metadata does not preserve their identifiers so only aggregate results reported). Secret categories = 4 (phone, email, SSN, credit card). Drift lengths tested = {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Word/token stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795; approx tokens estimated from words => avg ~478.87, median ~513.33, min/max ~57.33/1060. Pipeline: scaffold-then-rewrite generation preserves ground-truth secret, drift length, and probe structure; persona + secret injection places secret in opening turn as plausible task; drift turns drawn from topic-conditioned library (tax, medical, travel, etc.) with fallback tasks (writing, reasoning, summarization); annotators human-author subset of drift turns; naturalistic refinement: a rewriting model improves fluency/persona but must preserve exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Probing setup begins next (not in this part).

Eval appends a final standardized probe (three persuasion levels: Simple/Medium/Hard). Drift length d (number of intervening turns) sampled from mixture: d=0 with p=0.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (so each of 2–6 has p=0.16). Dataset drift lengths tested D_obs = {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Hierarchical hybrid detector (two stages, applied in order): Stage 1 normalization-based matching (called regex-stage): φ(·) normalizes secrets/responses — numeric secrets: remove non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, retain meaningful delimiters. Leak_regex(R,S) = I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)] (substring containment). Regex-positive responses labeled leakage; regex-negative responses passed to Stage 2. Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge given (secret, response) returns binary verdict (leakage/no leakage) to catch partial/paraphrased disclosures. Report regex-only and hybrid (regex+judge) leakage rates separately. Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: Introduces PrivDrift benchmark for auditing recovery of user-disclosed secrets after conversational topic drift and persuasion-based probing. Dataset: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows. Key result: dialogue-level hybrid leakage remains substantial, ranging 38.7%–54.6%, and varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Additional topic drift within tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage. Conclusion: privacy risk in active LLM contexts should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure mode, not only as memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Goal: measure whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after topic drift and persuasion-style probing in multi-turn LLM conversations. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled dataset with 1,000 multi-turn dialogues (paper states 1,000 dialogues per model evaluated). Axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe, tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows. Detector: reproducible hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching (regex/fuzzy) with an open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage; leakage varies by secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers). Additional drift within tested window does not reliably reduce leakage. Proposed metric: Privacy Half-Life (τ) for persistent suppression; authors claim no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions enumerated: benchmark, evaluation under multiple probe styles, hybrid detector and multiple leakage metrics, and Privacy Half-Life analysis.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Purpose: measure whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after topic drift and persuasion-style probing in multi-turn LLM conversations. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled dataset with 1,000 multi-turn dialogues (reported as 1,000 dialogues per model evaluated). Experimental axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe, tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Models: evaluation over three LLMs with extended context windows. Detector: hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching (regex/fuzzy) with an open-weights LLM judge; metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy-only, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported findings: dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion intensity significantly increases leakage; leakage varies by secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers); additional drift within tested window does not reliably reduce leakage. Proposed metric: Privacy Half-Life (τ) for persistent suppression; authors claim no evaluated model reaches stable decay within the observed drift range. Related work summary: distinguishes active-context privacy (user-provided info in current interaction) from training-data extraction and membership inference; cites benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) that test static access-control/privacy norms, while PrivDrift isolates persistence under drift and persuasion. Notes that multi-turn adversarial/jailbreak work (e.g., Crescendo attacks, automated jailbreak frameworks, prompt injection) show gradual elicitation of undesired outputs; PrivDrift applies a similar multi-turn lens to information flow. Contrasts with machine unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) that target parameter-level removal over static QA pairs; PrivDrift targets prompt-level/context-window suppression behavior relevant to RAG, copilots, and agentic workflows.
