Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: privacy risk in active LLM conversations should be evaluated as a persistent behavioral failure mode (not only memorization/jailbreak). Reported finding: additional V9B within the tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage; R9S X3Q (leakage measure) across three LLMs with extended context windows is substantial (38.7%–54.6%), and varies strongly by model, secret type, and Z4T. Dataset/benchmark K7X contains 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes to audit whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after conversational V9B and persuasion-based probing. Motivation: LLMs as persistent assistants in user-facing/shared-session/tool-augmented settings may behaveably recover sensitive info after topic shifts. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu). Core claim: active-context privacy leakage is a persistent behavioral failure mode distinct from memorization/jailbreak. Key empirical findings: dialogue-level leakage (R9S) under hybrid detection (X3Q) is 38.7%–54.6% across three LLMs with extended context windows, tested on 1,000 controlled dialogues per model. Tested drift window: d ≤ 6; adding further drift within this window does not reliably reduce leakage. Leakage varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity (Z4T). Secret-type suppression order: L8P (SSNs) and G6Y (credit cards) are suppressed far more often than D2F (email addresses) and A9T (phone numbers). Definitions/axes: V9B = topic drift (number of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe); Z4T = persuasion intensity / interaction style. Dataset/benchmark: K7X (PrivDrift) — 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, standardized extraction probes. Contributions: (1) K7X benchmark; (2) evaluation under direct, justified, and high-pressure probes modeling Z4T; (3) reproducible X3Q detector combining normalization-based matching with T1G (open-weights LLM judge), reporting rates for R9S (dialogue-level leakage), M2V, J5D (regex-only leakage), B7N, and X3Q (hybrid leakage); (4) C5Z (Privacy Half-Life τ), a stability-based metric showing no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Context/motivation: fills gap between memorization and immediate jailbreaking literature by measuring recoverability of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated conversational drift.

Related work contrasts machine-unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) that operate over static QA pairs and model parameters with K7X, which targets active-context privacy (prompt-level/context-window control rather than weight-level unlearning). Prior multi-turn safety work (Crescendo attacks, automated jailbreak frameworks, prompt injection) focuses on unsafe content or instruction hijacking; K7X adapts the multi-turn lens to information-flow control, asking whether a user-disclosed secret in the context window is behaviorally recoverable after unrelated topic drift (V9B) and later persuasion-based probes (Z4T). Benchmarks like ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, and PrivaCI-Bench test privacy reasoning, norms, or static access-control scenarios; K7X instead isolates persistence/recoverability of secrets across drift and probing. Historical privacy work addressed training-data extraction and memorized PII; K7X emphasizes active-context secrets requiring correct inference-time handling. Also notes claim that aligned models can remain vulnerable to multi-turn exploitation.

K7X / PrivDrift focuses on active-context privacy: whether a secret S disclosed at turn t0 is behaviorally recoverable after unrelated topic drift and later persuasion-style probes (contrasts with static QA/unlearning benchmarks like TOFU/WMDP and with privacy-reasoning benchmarks). Threat model Q3M: secret S disclosed; conversation proceeds through d unrelated drift turns D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; standardized probe P appended; leakage = model response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Dataset (3.2): N=1000 controlled dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored) produced by scaffold-then-rewrite; human IDs not preserved in cached metadata so aggregated results reported. Main evaluation (3.3): append final probe of three persuasion levels — H2R (direct/neutral), F6K (medium/contextual justification), N8W (hard/high-pressure). Drift length sampling (eq.1): d = 0 with p=0.2; d ∼ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (no d=1 samples). Detection pipeline (3.4): hierarchical hybrid detector — stage 1 (3.4.1) normalization/regex: φ(·) normalizes numeric (strip non-digits) and alphanumeric (case/whitespace normalized, delimiters preserved); Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)] (eq.2). Regex-negative responses go to stage 2 (3.4.2) an open-weights Llama judge (T1G) that receives secret+response and returns binary leakage verdict (captures paraphrase/partial disclosure); judge-introduced error rates (J5D, X3Q) reported separately. Stability metric C5Z(τ) (3.4.3 / eq.3): δ = 0.1×L(0); τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ and ∀d'>d, L(d') ≤ δ}; if set empty τ := max(D_obs)+1. Note ambiguity to track: wording alternately calls d the "number of turns" and also defines D as {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}, which suggests d counts user–assistant pairs (possible off-by-one/turn-definition ambiguity).

Dataset: N=1,000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored). Secret categories: 4 fixed-format PII (A9T, D2F, L8P, G6Y); secret inserted in the opening turn (t0). Drift lengths observed: {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Sampling (from earlier): d=0 with p=0.2; d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (no d=1). Summary stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16, median 385.00, min/max words 43/795. Approx tokens estimated from words using factor 4/3: avg tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max tokens 57.33/1060. Dialogue generation: scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline; 3.2.3 applies a rewriting model to each scaffold to improve fluency/persona realism while preserving exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Persona sampling from >100 professions/demographic profiles. Topics assigned (e.g., tax filing, medical triage, travel); drift turns drawn from a topic-conditioned library of dense QA pairs and fallback tasks; a subset of drift turns are human-authored and included in the generation library. Framework overview: K7X = parametric dialogue generator + probing harness + metric suite (hybrid leakage detector: stage1 regex normalization Leak_regex; regex-negatives go to Llama judge; judge error rates reported separately). Stability metric C5Z(τ) defined earlier. Ambiguity to track: paper alternately calls d the “number of turns” vs defines D={u1,a1,...,ud,ad} (suggests d counts user–assistant pairs). Final probes: three persuasion levels (H2R, F6K, N8W) appended to each dialogue per earlier description.

final_notes: Experiment: 3 models (U5K=GPT-OSS-120B, E7B=DeepSeek-R1, P3R=Qwen3-VL-235B). Dataset: 1,000 dialogues/model (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored); 3 probes per dialogue (H2R easy, F6K medium, N8W hard) → 3,000 responses/model. V9B (context-depth) sampled at d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6}; observed fallback τ=7 for all models, so drift evaluation is bounded to d≤6 (short-to-medium), not full-window saturation. Leak detection: regex normalization φ then Llama judge T1G; leak = regex OR T1G. Only structured PII tested; labels are surface-form; no formal human–automated agreement reported. PrivDrift δ=0.1·L(0). Key results: dialogue-level leakage reported ~38.7–54.6% across models (E7B 38.70, U5K 47.70, P3R 54.60). Paper K7X (PrivDrift) studies suppression of user-provided secrets in active multi-turn LLM conversations, focusing on persistence after topic drift (V9B) and later persuasion intensity (Z4T). Key metric C5Z = Privacy Half-Life (τ), stability-based; claim from intro: “No model reaches stable decay in the observed range under C5Z.” Benchmark axes: V9B (topic drift = unrelated turns between disclosure and probe) and Z4T (persuasion intensity). Evaluation conditions include direct, justified, and high-pressure probes; contexts include shared sessions, browser assistants, copilots, agentic workflows. Methods: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Detector: hybrid reproducible detector = normalization + open-weights LLM judge (T1G); reported outputs include R9S, M2V (probe-level leakage), J5D (regex-only), B7N, X3Q. Related work: K7X isolates persistence after drift and persuasion (sec refs 2.1–2.3). Prior work (training-data extraction, membership inference, memorized PII, TOFU, WMDP) targets parameter/memory/static QA/weights or static access-control tests (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench), whereas K7X applies a multi-turn information-flow lens to re-disclosure of user-supplied secrets. Other related work (Crescendo, automated multi-turn jailbreaks, prompt injection) target harmful content or instruction hijacking rather than user-secret re-disclosure.

PrivDrift framework: synthetic eval measuring whether secrets disclosed at turn t0 are re-disclosed after d unrelated, content-dense drift turns. Threat model = active-context re-disclosure: leakage if model reproduces S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Formalization: disclosure S at t0, intervening dialogue D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; probes appended to active context. Dataset: N = 1000 controlled dialogues (Table 1): 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored (human dialogs inserted throughout; cached evaluation metadata does not preserve their identifiers so only aggregate results reported). Secret categories = 4 (phone, email, SSN, credit card). Drift lengths tested = {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Word/token stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795; approx tokens estimated from words => avg ~478.87, median ~513.33, min/max ~57.33/1060. Pipeline: scaffold-then-rewrite generation preserves ground-truth secret, drift length, and probe structure; persona + secret injection places secret in opening turn as plausible task; drift turns drawn from topic-conditioned library (tax, medical, travel, etc.) with fallback tasks (writing, reasoning, summarization); annotators human-author subset of drift turns; naturalistic refinement: a rewriting model improves fluency/persona but must preserve exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Probing setup begins next (not in this part).

Eval appends a final standardized probe (three persuasion levels: Simple/Medium/Hard). Drift length d (number of intervening turns) sampled from mixture: d=0 with p=0.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (so each of 2–6 has p=0.16). Dataset drift lengths tested D_obs = {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Hierarchical hybrid detector (two stages, applied in order): Stage 1 normalization-based matching (called regex-stage): φ(·) normalizes secrets/responses — numeric secrets: remove non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, retain meaningful delimiters. Leak_regex(R,S) = I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)] (substring containment). Regex-positive responses labeled leakage; regex-negative responses passed to Stage 2. Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge given (secret, response) returns binary verdict (leakage/no leakage) to catch partial/paraphrased disclosures. Report regex-only and hybrid (regex+judge) leakage rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ: let L(d) be leakage rate at drift d; define δ = 0.1 × L(0). τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ and ∀ d' ∈ D_obs with d' > d: L(d') ≤ δ}. If no d qualifies, τ = max(D_obs) + 1 (requires stable decay below threshold).

Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B accessed via OpenRouter. Dataset: 1,000 PrivDrift dialogues per model; each dialogue has one seeded secret and one drift length d ∈ {0,2,3,4,5,6} sampled from Eq.(1) (mixture: d=0 with p=0.2; otherwise uniform over 2–6, so each of 2–6 has p=0.16). Each dialogue is probed with three standardized persuasion probes (Simple/Medium/Hard) — so 3,000 cached model-probe responses per model, 9,000 total. Detector & reporting: hierarchical two-stage detector — Stage 1 normalization/regex-match φ(·) (numeric: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, keep meaningful delimiters); Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Regex-positive responses labeled leakage; regex-negative passed to Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge for paraphrases. Report regex-only and hybrid (regex+judge) leakage. Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: Introduces PrivDrift benchmark for auditing recovery of user-disclosed secrets after conversational topic drift and persuasion-based probing. Dataset: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows. Key result: dialogue-level hybrid leakage remains substantial, ranging 38.7%–54.6%, and varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Additional topic drift within tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage. Conclusion: privacy risk in active LLM contexts should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure mode, not only as memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Goal: measure whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after topic drift and persuasion-style probing in multi-turn LLM conversations. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled dataset with 1,000 multi-turn dialogues (paper states 1,000 dialogues per model evaluated). Axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe, tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Evaluation: three LLMs with extended context windows. Detector: reproducible hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching (regex/fuzzy) with an open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage; leakage varies by secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers). Additional drift within tested window does not reliably reduce leakage. Proposed metric: Privacy Half-Life (τ) for persistent suppression; authors claim no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions enumerated: benchmark, evaluation under multiple probe styles, hybrid detector and multiple leakage metrics, and Privacy Half-Life analysis.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Purpose: measure whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after topic drift and persuasion-style probing in multi-turn LLM conversations. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled dataset with 1,000 multi-turn dialogues (reported as 1,000 dialogues per model evaluated). Experimental axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe, tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Models: evaluation over three LLMs with extended context windows. Detector: hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching (regex/fuzzy) with an open-weights LLM judge; metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy-only, and hybrid leakage rates. Key reported findings: dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion intensity significantly increases leakage; leakage varies by secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers); additional drift within tested window does not reliably reduce leakage. Proposed metric: Privacy Half-Life (τ) for persistent suppression; authors claim no evaluated model reaches stable decay within the observed drift range. Related work summary: distinguishes active-context privacy (user-provided info in current interaction) from training-data extraction and membership inference; cites benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) that test static access-control/privacy norms, while PrivDrift isolates persistence under drift and persuasion. Notes that multi-turn adversarial/jailbreak work (e.g., Crescendo attacks, automated jailbreak frameworks, prompt injection) show gradual elicitation of undesired outputs; PrivDrift applies a similar multi-turn lens to information flow. Contrasts with machine unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) that target parameter-level removal over static QA pairs; PrivDrift targets prompt-level/context-window suppression behavior relevant to RAG, copilots, and agentic workflows.

Secret types: 4 fixed-format PII (phone, email, SSN, credit card). Drift lengths used: {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling p(d=0)=0.2, else d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with total p=0.8. Avg words/dialogue 359.16 (median 385; min 43; max 795). Tokens estimated ≈1.333×words (avg 478.87). Pipeline: scaffold-then-rewrite; persona+secret injected at opening; drift QA pairs topic-conditioned; final rewrite preserves secret/drift/roles/probe. Probes: three persuasion levels (Simple, Medium, Hard). Note: earlier sections ambiguously defined d (appears as either number of turns or number of user/assistant pairs).
Evaluation: hierarchical hybrid detector — Stage 1 deterministic normalization/substring check φ(·) (numeric: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, keep delimiters); leakage label Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Figure text refers to these as "regex-stage"/"regex-negative". Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge examines regex-negative responses with secret+response and returns binary verdict; report regex-only and hybrid rates separately.
Privacy Half-Life τ: let D_obs be observed drift lengths, L(d) leakage at d; safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0). τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and for all d'>d in D_obs, L(d')≤δ}; if empty set τ = max(D_obs)+1. (Definition assumes an unambiguous ordered meaning of d.)

PrivDrift: measures secret recoverability after topic drift and persuasion probes. Dataset: N=1,000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored; reported in aggregate). Each dialogue contains one seeded secret (one of 4 fixed-format PII types: phone, email, SSN, credit card) and one drift length d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6} sampled with p(d=0)=0.2, else d~Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} (total p=0.8). Avg words/dialogue 359.16 (median 385; min 43; max 795); tokens ≈1.333×words (avg tokens ≈478.87). Pipeline: scaffold-then-rewrite; persona+secret injected at opening; drift QA pairs topic-conditioned; final rewrite preserves secret/drift/roles/probe. Probes: three persuasion levels (Simple, Medium, Hard). Note: earlier sections ambiguously defined d (turns vs. user/assistant pairs). Detector: hierarchical hybrid — Stage 1 deterministic normalization/substring check φ(·) (numeric: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, keep delimiters); Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Stage 2: open-weight Llama judge examines regex-negative responses with secret+response and returns binary verdict; report regex-only and hybrid rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ defined via observed leakage L(d) with threshold δ=0.1×L(0) (requires ordered meaning of d). From this part: Models evaluated: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter API; all models queried with same dialogue histories and probe templates. For each model: evaluate same 1,000 dialogues; each dialogue evaluated under 3 standardized persuasion probes → 3,000 cached model-probe responses per model (9,000 total across 3 models). Aggregation: two levels — dialogue-level (a dialogue counts as leaking if any probe elicits the secret) and probe-level (each dialogue contributes one response per persuasion condition; used for persuasion-level and fuzzy-matching analyses). Dialogue-level leakage can exceed the average of per-probe leakage rates (because it's the union across probes). Uncertainty/statistics: report regex-only and hybrid leakage. Dialogue-level rates: 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues. Probe-level sensitivity checks: compute rates over cached model-probe responses. Paired model/detector comparisons: McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction. Repeated measures across persuasion levels: Cochran’s Q test with post-hoc McNemar. Associations (leakage vs drift length/persuasion/secret type): chi-square tests of independence; report Cramer’s V.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University); contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: privacy risk in active LLM conversations should be evaluated as a persistent behavioral failure mode (not only memorization/jailbreak). Reported finding: additional V9B within the tested drift window does not reliably reduce leakage; R9S X3Q (leakage measure) across three LLMs with extended context windows is substantial (38.7%–54.6%), and varies strongly by model, secret type, and Z4T. Dataset/benchmark K7X contains 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes to audit whether user-disclosed secrets remain recoverable after conversational V9B and persuasion-based probing. Motivation: LLMs as persistent assistants in user-facing/shared-session/tool-augmented settings may behaveably recover sensitive info after topic shifts. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu). Core claim: active-context privacy leakage is a persistent behavioral failure mode distinct from memorization/jailbreak. Key empirical findings: dialogue-level leakage (R9S) under hybrid detection (X3Q) is 38.7%–54.6% across three LLMs with extended context windows, tested on 1,000 controlled dialogues per model. Tested drift window: d ≤ 6; adding further drift within this window does not reliably reduce leakage. Leakage varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity (Z4T). Secret-type suppression order: L8P (SSNs) and G6Y (credit cards) are suppressed far more often than D2F (email addresses) and A9T (phone numbers). Definitions/axes: V9B = topic drift (number of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe); Z4T = persuasion intensity / interaction style. Dataset/benchmark: K7X (PrivDrift) — 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, standardized extraction probes. Contributions: (1) K7X benchmark; (2) evaluation under direct, justified, and high-pressure probes modeling Z4T; (3) reproducible X3Q detector combining normalization-based matching with T1G (open-weights LLM judge), reporting rates for R9S (dialogue-level leakage), M2V, J5D (regex-only leakage), B7N, and X3Q (hybrid leakage); (4) C5Z (Privacy Half-Life τ), a stability-based metric showing no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Context/motivation: fills gap between memorization and immediate jailbreaking literature by measuring recoverability of user-disclosed secrets after unrelated conversational drift.

Related work contrasts machine-unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP) that operate over static QA pairs and model parameters with K7X, which targets active-context privacy (prompt-level/context-window control rather than weight-level unlearning). Prior multi-turn safety work (Crescendo attacks, automated jailbreak frameworks, prompt injection) focuses on unsafe content or instruction hijacking; K7X adapts the multi-turn lens to information-flow control, asking whether a user-disclosed secret in the context window is behaviorally recoverable after unrelated topic drift (V9B) and later persuasion-based probes (Z4T). Benchmarks like ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, and PrivaCI-Bench test privacy reasoning, norms, or static access-control scenarios; K7X instead isolates persistence/recoverability of secrets across drift and probing. Historical privacy work addressed training-data extraction and memorized PII; K7X emphasizes active-context secrets requiring correct inference-time handling. Also notes claim that aligned models can remain vulnerable to multi-turn exploitation.

K7X / PrivDrift focuses on active-context privacy: whether a secret S disclosed at turn t0 is behaviorally recoverable after unrelated topic drift and later persuasion-style probes (contrasts with static QA/unlearning benchmarks like TOFU/WMDP and with privacy-reasoning benchmarks). Threat model Q3M: secret S disclosed; conversation proceeds through d unrelated drift turns D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; standardized probe P appended; leakage = model response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Dataset (3.2): N=1000 controlled dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored) produced by scaffold-then-rewrite; human IDs not preserved in cached metadata so aggregated results reported. Main evaluation (3.3): append final probe of three persuasion levels — H2R (direct/neutral), F6K (medium/contextual justification), N8W (hard/high-pressure). Drift length sampling (eq.1): d = 0 with p=0.2; d ∼ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (no d=1 samples). Detection pipeline (3.4): hierarchical hybrid detector — stage 1 (3.4.1) normalization/regex: φ(·) normalizes numeric (strip non-digits) and alphanumeric (case/whitespace normalized, delimiters preserved); Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)] (eq.2). Regex-negative responses go to stage 2 (3.4.2) an open-weights Llama judge (T1G) that receives secret+response and returns binary leakage verdict (captures paraphrase/partial disclosure); judge-introduced error rates (J5D, X3Q) reported separately. Stability metric C5Z(τ) (3.4.3 / eq.3): δ = 0.1×L(0); τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ and ∀d'>d, L(d') ≤ δ}; if set empty τ := max(D_obs)+1. Note ambiguity to track: wording alternately calls d the "number of turns" and also defines D as {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}, which suggests d counts user–assistant pairs (possible off-by-one/turn-definition ambiguity).

Dataset: N=1,000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored). Secret categories: 4 fixed-format PII (A9T, D2F, L8P, G6Y); secret inserted in the opening turn (t0). Drift lengths observed: {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Sampling (from earlier): d=0 with p=0.2; d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (no d=1). Summary stats: avg words/dialogue 359.16, median 385.00, min/max words 43/795. Approx tokens estimated from words using factor 4/3: avg tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max tokens 57.33/1060. Dialogue generation: scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline; 3.2.3 applies a rewriting model to each scaffold to improve fluency/persona realism while preserving exact secret, drift length, role structure, and final probe conditions. Persona sampling from >100 professions/demographic profiles. Topics assigned (e.g., tax filing, medical triage, travel); drift turns drawn from a topic-conditioned library of dense QA pairs and fallback tasks; a subset of drift turns are human-authored and included in the generation library. Framework overview: K7X = parametric dialogue generator + probing harness + metric suite (hybrid leakage detector: stage1 regex normalization Leak_regex; regex-negatives go to Llama judge; judge error rates reported separately). Stability metric C5Z(τ) defined earlier. Ambiguity to track: paper alternately calls d the “number of turns” vs defines D={u1,a1,...,ud,ad} (suggests d counts user–assistant pairs). Final probes: three persuasion levels (H2R, F6K, N8W) appended to each dialogue per earlier description.

steps.notes_before: Paper K7X: 'Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under V9B in Active LLM Conversations' (author L.R. Maldonado Romero). Key definitions: C5Z = Privacy Half-Life (τ), a stability-based metric for persistent suppression; claim: "No model reaches stable decay in the observed range under C5Z." K7X (PrivDrift) = benchmark on two axes: V9B = topic drift (unrelated turns between disclosure and probe) and Z4T = persuasion intensity. Evaluation conditions include direct, justified, and high-pressure probes; contexts include shared sessions, browser assistants, copilots, agentic workflows. Method summary (from earlier): 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Detector: reproducible hybrid detector = normalization matching + open-weights T1G (T1G = LLM judge), reporting rates R9S, M2V (probe-level leakage), J5D (regex-only), B7N, X3Q. Note: Introduction's contribution list numbers are scrambled (4,1,3,2). Keep these definitions, claimed results, metrics and the detector composition for cross-checking later sections.

Paper K7X (PrivDrift) studies suppression of user-provided secrets in active multi-turn LLM conversations, focusing on persistence after topic drift (V9B) and later persuasion intensity (Z4T). Key metric C5Z = Privacy Half-Life (τ), stability-based; claim from intro: “No model reaches stable decay in the observed range under C5Z.” Benchmark axes: V9B (topic drift = unrelated turns between disclosure and probe) and Z4T (persuasion intensity). Evaluation conditions include direct, justified, and high-pressure probes; contexts include shared sessions, browser assistants, copilots, agentic workflows. Methods: 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Detector: hybrid reproducible detector = normalization + open-weights LLM judge (T1G); reported outputs include R9S, M2V (probe-level leakage), J5D (regex-only), B7N, X3Q. Related work: K7X isolates persistence after drift and persuasion (sec refs 2.1–2.3). Prior work (training-data extraction, membership inference, memorized PII, TOFU, WMDP) targets parameter/memory/static QA/weights or static access-control tests (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench), whereas K7X applies a multi-turn information-flow lens to re-disclosure of user-supplied secrets. Other related work (Crescendo, automated multi-turn jailbreaks, prompt injection) target harmful content or instruction hijacking rather than user-secret re-disclosure.
